Sure, below is a refined email draft:

:::writing{variant="email" id="48291" subject="Pending Applications, Withholding Details and Input Tax Ageing"}
Dear [Name],

We refer to your recent email wherein you communicated your understanding that the earlier application was filed due to a system glitch, as a result of which the status was inadvertently changed, and that a subsequent application was filed for restoration of the correct status.

However, upon perusal of the application shared with us, the relevant background and context do not appear to be clearly reflected therein. The application primarily seems to relate to the updation of addresses in SGL’s profile, and it does not clearly establish any linkage with the matter of restoration of status as communicated by you. If the same application was intended to cover both matters, then, on a plain reading, the status restoration issue is not clearly coming out from the contents of the application.

Having said that, if this is indeed the relevant pending application, we can place the same before the Commissioner in order to provide background and context. However, we would request you to kindly recheck the matter at your end, as the application presently pending in the profile does not appear to support or establish the position communicated in your email.

Furthermore, you had informed us that the withholding tax details would be shared by Monday. However, the same have not yet been received. You are requested to kindly share the said details at the earliest so that we may appropriately review and respond to the matter.

In addition, we had already shared the draft intimation letter with you for review and comments. However, we have not yet received any response from your side. The said draft intimation letter is being attached again with this email for your review. You are requested to kindly examine the same and share your feedback so that the matter may be finalized accordingly.

With respect to the input tax position, as already discussed and also requested through our earlier emails, we would require invoice-wise ageing of the unclaimed input tax appearing in the name of ICL. The purpose of obtaining this ageing is to identify the amount of input tax which falls within the six-month period and the amount which pertains to periods older than six months. This distinction is important, as input tax older than six months may create additional complications if the same is not transferred or otherwise adjusted in time.

Accordingly, you are requested to kindly provide invoice-wise ageing of the unclaimed input tax balance at the earliest, so that we may evaluate the position and, if required, prepare and submit an appropriate application before the Commissioner for transfer/adjustment of the input tax.

Regards,  
[Your Name]
:::

If you are asking about platforms similar to **Befiler** in Pakistan, then the closest category would be online tax filing and compliance service platforms. Some comparable options are:

1. **TaxApp / TaxApp.pk**  
   Provides online tax return filing, NTN registration, and related tax support.

2. **FBR IRIS Portal**  
   This is the official FBR system where income tax returns, statements, and registration matters are actually filed. Platforms like Befiler ultimately facilitate filing through IRIS.

3. **Online tax advisory portals**  
   Some tax firms and consultants provide online filing support through websites, forms, WhatsApp, or client portals, but many are not as app-based or automated as Befiler.

4. **Digital services by tax firms**  
   Several professional firms now provide digital onboarding for income tax return filing, NTN registration, sales tax registration, and business compliance.

In practical terms, **Befiler’s main competitors are not only apps**, but also tax consultants and firms offering remote filing services.

A stronger Befiler-style business model in Pakistan could include:

**Income tax return filing, NTN registration, business registration, sales tax registration, monthly sales tax returns, withholding tax compliance, bookkeeping, tax notices handling, and automated compliance reminders** — all under one dashboard.

That would make it more useful than a simple annual return filing app because Pakistani businesses usually need continuous compliance support, not just one-time return filing.
I’ll look at this as a market scan: who is offering app/portal-based tax return filing in Pakistan, what Befiler is known for, and why it has gained recall among taxpayers.

Based on a quick market scan, **Befiler is still one of the most visible private app/website-based tax filing platforms in Pakistan**. There are some alternatives, but many of them are either official FBR apps, basic tax calculators, web-view apps, or consultant-led portals rather than a fully developed Befiler-style platform.

## 1. Platforms/apps similar to Befiler

### 1. Befiler

Befiler offers tax filing, NTN registration, business NTN registration, sales tax registration, business tax filing, tax calculator, business registration, trademark/IP services, and even USA LLC/tax-related services. Its own website claims **1 million app downloads** and positions it as a leading tax filing and NTN registration portal for individuals and SMEs. citeturn154427search20

Befiler’s Google Play listing describes it as an app for individuals and businesses in Pakistan to manage **tax filing, NTN registration and related tasks**, with automated calculations, a digital process, and expert assistance through chat, phone and email. citeturn154427search5

### 2. FBR Tax Asaan App

This is the **official FBR-supported app**, not a private competitor. It offers easy wizard-based income tax return filing for salaried and normal returns, income tax registration, sales tax registration, online verification services, e-payment, withholding deduction data, and password recovery. citeturn154427search0

However, from a business-model perspective, Tax Asaan is not the same as Befiler because it is more of a government facilitation app. It does not appear to provide the same commercial service layer, expert review, customer support, or bundled business compliance services.

### 3. Scounts – Digital Tax Partner

Scounts appears to be a private tax consultancy app in Pakistan. Its Play Store listing says it provides income tax return filing, NTN registration assistance, and a step-by-step process for sharing tax return data with consultants. citeturn154427search17

This is closer to the Befiler model because it combines app-based onboarding with consultant support, but it does not appear to have the same brand recall or service breadth as Befiler.

### 4. TaxFiler App

There is also a “Tax Filer” app on Google Play that describes itself as a tax and business compliance solution, including NTN registration and related services. citeturn154427search25

This may be relevant as an emerging category player, but again, its market presence appears much smaller compared with Befiler.

### 5. TaxINN

TaxINN is another app that presents itself as a tax calculation, filing, and tax management app for individuals and businesses. Its listing highlights tax calculations, secure account management, and simplified tax management. citeturn154427search34

### 6. Pak Filer

Pak Filer is more of an online tax filing service/portal than clearly an app-first platform. It promotes FBR tax returns, NTN/GST registration, salary tax calculator, and CA-certified professionals. citeturn166863search9

## 2. Why Befiler is known in the market

Befiler is known mainly because it solved a very specific taxpayer pain point: **ordinary salaried individuals and small businesses do not want to deal directly with IRIS, tax forms, wealth statements, reconciliations, and FBR jargon**.

The official FBR position is that income tax returns are filed through **IRIS**, and first-time filers must complete registration/e-enrollment before filing. citeturn154427search4 Befiler built a business around simplifying that journey for the taxpayer.

Its recognition is mainly due to these reasons:

### 1. Strong positioning around “Become a filer”

In Pakistan, the word **“filer”** itself has strong commercial importance because non-filers face higher withholding taxes on banking transactions, property, vehicles, dividends, and other transactions. Befiler’s branding directly connects with that public pain point: become a filer, avoid unnecessary higher tax incidence, and stay compliant.

### 2. App + website convenience

Befiler is not only a tax advisory firm. It presents itself as a **digital app and website-based platform**. That makes it more scalable and accessible than traditional tax consultants who operate through office visits, email, or WhatsApp only. citeturn166863search17

### 3. Simple onboarding

Their own product positioning is built around easy steps like register, upload and pay for NTN registration, and “file taxes within minutes” without appointments or office visits. citeturn154427search20

From a user-behaviour angle, this is powerful because the average salaried person does not want a technical consultation; he wants a simple outcome: **return filed, ATL status updated, and documentation handled**.

### 4. Expert-assisted model

Befiler’s blog explains that after the user enters information, Befiler prepares the return, gets it reviewed by tax experts, and submits particulars in FBR’s IRIS system. citeturn166863search12

This is important. Pure DIY filing is difficult for many taxpayers, while pure consultant filing feels slow or old-fashioned. Befiler sits in the middle: **technology-driven process plus human tax review**.

### 5. Service bundling

Befiler has expanded beyond simple return filing into NTN registration, business registration, sales tax registration, business tax filing, trademark/IP services, and USA LLC-related services. citeturn154427search20

This creates a wider customer journey. A salaried person may start with annual return filing, then later need sole proprietor registration, sales tax registration, company incorporation, trademark registration, or business tax compliance.

### 6. Partnerships and brand visibility

Befiler displays partners/collaborators such as Engro, ICMAP, UBL, Allied Bank, KCCI, PSEB, Telenor, and JS on its website. citeturn154427search20 That improves trust, especially in a market where people are hesitant to share CNIC, IRIS credentials, salary certificates, bank data, and asset details with unknown service providers.

## 3. Main conclusion

At present, the closest Befiler-style options appear to be **Scounts, TaxFiler, TaxINN, Pak Filer, and some consultant-led online filing services**, while **Tax Asaan** remains the official FBR facilitation app. However, Befiler appears more established because it combines:

**mobile app + web portal + simple filing flow + expert review + NTN/business services + strong “become a filer” branding + visible partnerships + broader compliance services.**

For your own business idea, the opportunity is not merely to copy Befiler’s annual return filing model. The stronger gap is to build a platform around **continuous compliance**, such as monthly sales tax returns, withholding statements, bookkeeping, ATL tracking, notice management, CPR recordkeeping, wealth reconciliation, and client reminders. That is where Pakistani taxpayers and SMEs still face practical difficulty.

Below is a refined draft reply focusing mainly on lack of reasonable opportunity, FBR’s own 15-day instruction, and the point that the alleged decline is only around 2.6–3%, which cannot by itself be treated as a “material decline” or basis for drastic action like suspension of sales tax registration.

:::writing{variant="email" id="48291" subject="Reply to Show Cause Notice under Section 21(2) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990"}
To,  
The Commissioner Inland Revenue, Zone-VI,  
Large Taxpayers’ Office, Karachi.  

**Subject: Reply to Show Cause Notice under Section 21(2) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 read with Rule 12 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006 – Non-compliance with S.R.O. 376(I)/2023**

Dear Sir,

We refer to Show Cause Notice No. CIR/Zone-VI/LTO/Khi/2025-26/341 dated May 19, 2026, issued under section 21(2) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 read with Rule 12 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006, whereby the Company has been called upon to show cause as to why its sales tax registration should not be suspended on account of alleged non-compliance with S.R.O. 376(I)/2023.

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the impugned notice has fixed the hearing on May 20, 2026, i.e. on the very next day of issuance of the notice. The notice seeks reconciliation and explanation of data spanning multiple tax periods, including billing, recovery and sales tax figures for the periods June 2024 to February 2025 and June 2025 to February 2026. It is submitted that such voluminous and technical information cannot reasonably be compiled, reconciled, verified and responded to within one day. The opportunity provided is, therefore, neither meaningful nor reasonable and is contrary to the settled principles of natural justice.

In this regard, reference is invited to FBR’s own instructions issued vide C.No.6(4)Rev.Bud/2018 dated July 23, 2018, wherein the Board specifically directed that sufficient time of at least fifteen days / fair opportunity should be given to the taxpayer after receipt of notice to make necessary compliance. The said instructions were issued precisely to ensure taxpayer facilitation and to avoid adverse proceedings being initiated without proper opportunity of compliance. The present notice, by fixing the hearing on the very next day, is not in conformity with the aforesaid instructions. fileciteturn0file0

Without prejudice to the above, it is further submitted that the allegation of “material decline” in recovery ratio is also misconceived. As per the comparison reproduced in the notice itself, the recovery ratio has moved from 92.2% to 89.6%, reflecting a variation of approximately 2.6 percentage points only. Such variation, particularly in the electric power sector where recoveries are influenced by seasonal consumption patterns, consumer mix, billing cycles, delayed payments, government receivables, operational recoveries and other commercial factors, cannot be treated as an abnormal or material decline so as to presume suppression of output tax or reduction of sales tax liability.

It is also respectfully submitted that the Company is a regulated electric power utility and its billing and recovery mechanisms are subject to regulatory, commercial and operational controls. Normal fluctuations in recovery ratios may arise due to timing differences between billing and actual realization, delayed recoveries, consumer category-wise recovery patterns and other sector-specific factors. Therefore, a marginal movement in recovery ratio, without first examining the complete underlying reconciliation and supporting record, cannot constitute a valid basis for invoking the drastic provisions of section 21(2) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990.

The notice appears to proceed on the assumption that the declared recoveries are not verifiable. However, no proper opportunity has been allowed to the Company to furnish the requisite reconciliation, supporting data and explanations. The proposed action of suspension of sales tax registration is an extremely harsh and coercive measure and cannot be invoked mechanically, particularly where the matter essentially relates to reconciliation of billing, recovery and sales tax data under S.R.O. 376(I)/2023.

In view of the above, it is respectfully requested that the instant proceedings may kindly be withdrawn or, in the alternative, the Company may be granted reasonable time of at least fifteen days, in line with FBR’s own instructions, to compile and furnish the requisite reconciliation and supporting documents. The Company remains fully committed to providing all relevant data and explanations required for proper verification of its sales tax position.

This reply is submitted without prejudice to any other legal or factual submissions which may be furnished at the time of hearing or through subsequent correspondence.

Yours faithfully,  
For and on behalf of  
**M/s K-Electric Limited**  
:::

I would suggest attaching the FBR letter dated July 23, 2018 as **Annexure-A** and specifically referring to it in the covering submission.

Such variation, particularly in the electric power sector where recoveries are influenced by seasonal consumption patterns, consumer mix, billing cycles, delayed payments, government receivables, operational recoveries and other commercial factors, cannot be treated as an abnormal or material decline so as to presume suppression of output tax or reduction of sales tax liability.

It is also respectfully submitted that our client is a regulated electric power utility and its billing and recovery mechanisms are subject to regulatory, commercial and operational controls. Normal fluctuations in recovery ratios may arise due to timing differences between billing and actual realization, delayed recoveries, consumer category-wise recovery patterns and other sector-specific factors. Therefore, a marginal movement in recovery ratio, without first examining the complete underlying reconciliation and supporting record, cannot constitute a valid basis for invoking the drastic provisions of section 21(2) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990.

The notice appears to proceed on the assumption that the declared recoveries are not verifiable. However, no proper opportunity has been allowed to our client to furnish the requisite reconciliation, supporting data and explanations. The proposed action of suspension of sales tax registration is an extremely harsh and coercive measure and cannot be invoked mechanically, particularly where the matter essentially relates to reconciliation of billing, recovery and sales tax data under S.R.O. 376(I)/2023.

In view of the above, it is respectfully requested that the instant proceedings may kindly be withdrawn or, in the alternative, our client may be granted reasonable time of at least fifteen days, in line with FBR’s own instructions, to compile and furnish the requisite reconciliation and supporting documents. Our client remains fully committed to providing all relevant data and explanations required for proper verification of its sales tax position.

This reply is submitted without prejudice to any other legal or factual submissions which may be furnished at the time of hearing or through subsequent correspondence.

Yours faithfully,  
For and on behalf of  
**[Your Firm Name]**  

Authorized Tax Consultants  
M/s K-Electric Limited
:::

:::writing{variant="standard" id="73926"}
**Date:** [●]

**To**  
Mr. Ahsan [●]  
[Designation]  
[Department/Office]  
[Address]

**Subject: Request for Review of Case Record and Intimation of Further Documents, if Required — Appeal No. 660/2024 Pending before the Commissioner (Appeals)**

Dear Sir,

This is with reference to Appeal No. 660/2024 filed by K-Electric Limited, which is presently pending adjudication before the learned Commissioner (Appeals). The said appeal was earlier fixed for hearing on May 18, 2026, and has now been adjourned and fixed for hearing on June 3, 2026.

During our meeting/hearing on May 18, 2026, we had briefly explained the background and factual position of the matter for your review and assistance. In this regard, we also furnished copies of the initial notice issued by the department, our reply thereto, the subsequent notice, the reply filed in response thereto, and the impugned order passed in the matter.

It was also explained during the said meeting/hearing that the initial observation raised by the department was approximately Rs. 21 million. The Company submitted its detailed response against the said observation, along with relevant supporting documents and explanations. Thereafter, the matter was reconsidered by the department and the subsequent notice was issued on a reduced/refined amount of approximately Rs. 12 million, being the amount which, according to the department, remained unverified.

However, while finalizing the proceedings and passing the impugned order, the officer appears to have considered certain parties/transactions from the original show cause notice, as well as certain parties/transactions from the subsequent notice. This has created a serious factual and procedural inconsistency. Once the department itself had refined the original observation of Rs. 21 million to approximately Rs. 12 million in the subsequent notice, logically and legally the final order ought to have been confined only to the parties/transactions forming part of the subsequent notice, or such parties/transactions out of the refined amount which, according to the officer, remained unresolved. Instead, the impugned order appears to have carried forward certain defects from the original notice, despite the fact that the scope of the matter had already been narrowed through the subsequent notice.

It was further explained that a major portion of the adverse treatment in the impugned order appears to be based on the alleged inactive status of certain suppliers/parties. In this regard, it is respectfully submitted that the relevant inactive taxpayer rule/regime was introduced in the year 2023, whereas the payments/transactions under consideration pertain to periods prior to the introduction of the said regime. Therefore, the subsequent inactive status of any party cannot, by itself, be used as a basis to adversely treat or disallow transactions which had already taken place before the said rule came into field, particularly where the Company had made payments and maintained supporting documentation in the normal course of business.

Further, as advised by you, the complete set of the aforesaid documents was also subsequently shared again through email at the email address provided by you. Along with the above, we also furnished copies of the relevant invoices of the concerned parties involved in the matter, so that the facts and supporting record may be reviewed in proper perspective before the next date of hearing.

In view of the above, you are kindly requested to review the documents already provided and let us know whether any further information, clarification, or supporting documents are required from our side. If considered appropriate, you may also kindly call a brief hearing/meeting before the next date fixed before the Commissioner (Appeals), so that any factual or documentary requirement may be addressed in advance.

We would appreciate if any further requirement may kindly be communicated before June 3, 2026, enabling us to furnish the same timely and ensure that the matter may be properly explained and concluded on the next date of hearing before the learned Commissioner (Appeals).

We remain available to provide any further assistance or documentation that may be required in this regard.

Yours faithfully,  
For and on behalf of  
**K-Electric Limited**

__________________  
Authorized Signatory  
:::

آج ایک لیٹر ڈرافٹ کریں فار دی آفیسرز ٹھیک ہے ایس آر بی اس میں یہ بولیں کہ اینگرو ایل این سی ٹرمینل پرائیویٹ لمیٹڈ کی جو اپیل بیفور کمشنر اپیلز ہے جس میں اپیل نمبر ففٹی ٹو آف دو ہزار اٹھارہ اور ففٹی سکس آف دو ہزار انیس اور جو ٹیکس پیریڈ انوال ہے جنوری ٹو دسمبر دو ہزار چودہ اور جنوری ٹو دسمبر دو ہزار پندرہ اس میں جو ہے وہ اپیل ہماری فکس تھی بیفور کمشنر اپیلز فورٹین میں کو جس کے اندر کمشنر اپیلز نے جو ہے نا اس کو ایڈجورن کر کے اور فائنل اوپورچونٹی دی ہے اور ٹو سمٹ دا رپورٹ اور نائنز جو ڈیٹ آف ہیئرنگ ہے وہ جون چار کو فکس کی ہے اور اس کے سلسلے میں ہم نے فرائیڈے جو کہ تھرسڈے کو تھائی ہوئے آن فرائیڈے نیکسٹ ڈے جو تھا میے پندرہ کو ہم آپ کے پاس آئے تھے اس کے اندر آپ اوکوپائیڈ تھے اور ہم نے آپ کو جو ہے جو کنسٹرکشن کوسٹ ہے اس کا جو فورٹین اور ففٹین کا جو بریک اپ ہے وہ دیا تھا ہم نے آپ کو اکاؤنٹس کے زو دس سے لے کر پچس تک کے اکاؤنٹس کے موومنٹس دی تھیں اور ہم نے آپ کو ایس ایس ڈی سی کا ایموٹائزیشن شیڈول دیا تھا ٹھیک ہے اور ہم نے ایس ایس ڈی سی کا جو کنسٹرکشن کانٹریکٹ تھا وہ اس کی کاپی بھی دی تھی پلس ہم نے اس کی ایس آر پی کی رجسٹریشن کی پروفائل بھی آپ کو دی تھی اور ہم نے آپ کو کہا تھا کہ ہمیں کائنلی ایک ہیئرنگ ہماری آفٹر ڈاکومنٹس کو دیکھ کے ایک ہیئرنگ فکس کر دیں تاکہ ہم اس کو آپ کو فردر اور بھی ایکسپلین کر سکیں اور تھرو دیس لیٹر ہم نے ارلیئر بھی آپ سے ملٹیپل ٹائم ریکویسٹ کی ہے اور آپ سے ایک ہیئرنگ ہم نے اس میں کی بھی تھی جس کے اندر ہم نے جو آپ نے فردر ڈاکومنٹس ہم جمع کرائے تھے وہ بھی ہم نے آپ کو فنش کر دی ہے تو تھرو دیس لیٹر ہم یہ تمام چیزیں دوبارہ سے آپ کو فنش کر رہے ہیں اور ہم کہہ رہے ہیں آپ کو ڈاؤن کر دیں کہ یہ ڈاکومنٹس ہم دوبارہ دے دیں اور ہمیں کائنلی جو ہے نا آپ اس کو ڈاکومنٹس کو دیکھ لیں اور ہمیں بتائیں کہ اگر آپ کو کوئی فردر اور ڈاکومنٹس پرووائڈ ہیں اور اس میں اس سلسلے میں کوئی ہیئرنگ فکس کر دیں تاکہ جو نیکسٹ ڈیٹ آف ہیئرنگ ہے جو کہ چار سے پہلے کوئی ڈیٹ فکس کر دیں ہمیں کائنلی لیٹرس نو کر دیں تاکہ ہم اس میں کوئی آپ کو فردر ایکسپلینیشن کوئی اس چیزیں چاہیے تو ہم پھر وہ ٹائم آپ کو چیزیں پرووائڈ کر سکیں

I’ll extract the key news items from the uploaded PDF, shortlist the most public-facing points, and convert them into three polished social media posts with strong headings and explanatory paragraphs.

## 1. **Electric Vehicles May Get 1% GST — Not 18%: Pakistan Pushes for Affordable EV Adoption**

Pakistan’s Ministry of Industries has opposed the IMF’s proposal to impose **18% GST on electric vehicles** and has instead proposed a concessional **1% GST on New Energy Vehicles** under the upcoming auto policy framework. This proposal covers electric cars, buses, trucks, tractors, pickups, two-wheelers, three-wheelers and light commercial vehicles.

The key issue is that EV adoption in Pakistan is still at an early stage. If EVs are taxed at the standard 18% rate, the upfront cost may increase significantly, making electric mobility less attractive for consumers and businesses. The ministry has argued that since hybrid vehicles already enjoy a reduced GST rate of **8.5%**, electric vehicles should also receive concessional treatment to encourage local demand and investment.

Another important point is the imbalance in the EV supply chain. Imported EV parts are reportedly subject to **1% GST**, while locally manufactured parts face **18% GST**, creating refund accumulation and cashflow issues for local manufacturers. A uniform 1% GST across the EV supply chain could support local assembly, reduce pricing pressure and make Pakistan’s EV policy more practical.

---

## 2. **FBR’s “Digital Eye” Expands to Milk, Steel, Edible Oil & Ghee — Real-Time Production Monitoring Begins**

Through **SRO 880(I)/2026 dated May 20, 2026**, FBR has expanded its digital tax monitoring system to manufacturers of **packaged milk, iron and steel, edible oil and ghee**. These sectors will now be subject to real-time electronic monitoring of production lines through video surveillance, video analytics and digital monitoring technology.

This development is part of FBR’s broader shift from traditional post-facto audits to technology-based enforcement. Instead of relying only on sales tax returns and records submitted by taxpayers, the tax authority is now moving towards real-time monitoring of production activity. The objective is to reduce underreporting, improve transparency and strengthen tax collection from high-volume manufacturing sectors.

For affected businesses, this is not merely a tax update; it is an operational compliance matter. Manufacturers will need to review their production processes, system readiness, internal controls, data accuracy and coordination with tax teams. Where production, sales and stock records are not properly reconciled, digital monitoring may create immediate exposure during scrutiny or audit.

---

## 3. **INGOs Face Stricter FBR Registration Rules — More Documents, More Disclosure, More Compliance**

FBR has issued **SRO 879(I)/2026 dated May 20, 2026**, amending the Income Tax Rules, 2002 to make registration and documentation requirements more stringent for **International Non-Governmental Organizations operating in Pakistan**. The amendment follows draft **SRO 856(I)/2026 dated May 11, 2026** and introduces an expanded disclosure framework under Rule 80B.

Under the revised framework, INGOs will be required to provide detailed information including taxpayer name, business address, accounting period, principal activity, details of principal officer or authorized representative, authorization letter, contact details, foreign tax registration or incorporation documents, embassy verification, local residence proof, Ministry of Interior NOC, MoU with the Government of Pakistan, and details of directors, trustees or major shareholders holding 10% or more stake.

This amendment shows a clear regulatory direction: foreign-funded organizations will be expected to maintain stronger documentation and transparent operating records in Pakistan. INGOs should proactively review their registration status, authorization documents, local office documentation, government approvals and tax records to avoid delays, objections or compliance complications before FBR.

Yes, you are right. The email should not simply list implications in isolation. Each restriction should be supported with the relevant **section / rule reference**, otherwise the client may not be able to verify the position.

One important point after double-checking: **Rule 12 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006 still reflects the older procedural timelines of 7 days / 90 days in the FBR’s Rules updated up to January 1, 2025, whereas section 21(2A), inserted through Finance Act, 2025, now provides 10 days for issuance of show cause notice and 30 days from receipt of reply for passing an appealable speaking order for blacklisting.** Since the Act is the parent law and later amendment, the safer position is to quote **section 21(2A)** for timelines, while referring to **Rule 12** for procedural and operational consequences. citeturn751824view0turn385775view1

:::writing{variant="email" id="58429" subject="Implications of Suspension and Blacklisting of Sales Tax Registration under the Sales Tax Act, 1990"}
Dear [Name],

We have reviewed the legal and practical implications of suspension and blacklisting of sales tax registration under the Sales Tax Act, 1990 and the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

At the outset, it is important to note that suspension and blacklisting are two distinct legal stages. Suspension is generally an interim action pending further inquiry, whereas blacklisting is a more serious consequential action which may be taken after issuance of show cause notice, consideration of reply, opportunity of hearing and passing of an appealable speaking order.

Under section 21(2) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, where the Commissioner is satisfied that a registered person has issued fake invoices or has otherwise committed tax fraud, he may issue an order of suspension and blacklisting or suspend the registration in accordance with the prescribed procedure. Further, under section 21(2A), the Commissioner is required to issue a show cause notice within ten days of the order of suspension and, after receipt of reply and providing opportunity of hearing, may either revoke the suspension or issue an appealable speaking order for blacklisting within thirty days of receipt of reply.

Reference: Section 21(2) and section 21(2A) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990.

In addition, Rule 12 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006 provides the procedural framework for suspension and blacklisting. Under Rule 12(a), suspension may be initiated where the Commissioner has reason to believe that the registered person has issued fake invoices, evaded tax or committed tax fraud. The basis for such satisfaction may include, among others, non-availability at the registered address, refusal to allow access to business premises or records, abnormal tax profile such as excessive input tax adjustment or continuous carry-forward, substantial purchases from or supplies to blacklisted/suspended persons, non-filing of sales tax returns, recommendation of another Commissioner, or any other reason specified by the Commissioner.

Reference: Rule 12(a)(i)(A) to (G) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

The immediate implications of suspension are summarized below:

1. During the period of suspension, invoices issued by the suspended person are not to be entertained for purposes of sales tax refund or input tax credit.

Reference: Section 21(3) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990.

2. No input tax adjustment or refund is admissible to the suspended person during the currency of suspension.

Reference: Rule 12(a)(v) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

3. Other registered persons/customers are also exposed because no input tax adjustment or refund is allowed to them on the strength of invoices issued by such suspended person during the currency of suspension, whether such invoices were issued prior to or after suspension.

Reference: Rule 12(a)(v) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

4. Since a suspended person falls outside the definition of an “active taxpayer”, the person automatically becomes a non-active taxpayer and is removed from the Active Taxpayers List maintained by the Board.

Reference: Section 2(1A)(a) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 read with Rule 12A(1) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

5. A non-active taxpayer is not entitled to file Goods Declarations for import or export.

Reference: Rule 12A(2)(a) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

6. A non-active taxpayer is not entitled to issue sales tax invoices.

Reference: Rule 12A(2)(b) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

7. A non-active taxpayer is not entitled to claim input tax or refund.

Reference: Rule 12A(2)(c) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

8. A non-active taxpayer is not entitled to avail any concession under the Sales Tax Act, 1990 or the rules made thereunder.

Reference: Rule 12A(2)(d) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

9. No person, including government departments, autonomous bodies and public sector organizations, is allowed to make purchases from a non-active taxpayer.

Reference: Rule 12A(3) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

10. If a registered buyer enters an invoice issued by a non-active taxpayer in Annexure-A of its sales tax return, the system reflects that the supplier is a non-active taxpayer and no input tax credit is admissible against such invoice.

Reference: Rule 12A(4) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

The implications of blacklisting are more severe and may extend beyond the period of suspension. Once a person is blacklisted, refund or input tax credit claimed against invoices issued by such person, whether prior to or after blacklisting, may be rejected. However, such rejection is required to be made through a self-speaking appealable order after providing an opportunity of being heard.

Reference: Section 21(3) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990.

Further, Rule 12(b) provides that where, after opportunity of hearing, the alleged offence is confirmed, the Commissioner shall issue an appealable self-speaking order for blacklisting and proceed to take legal and penal action under the relevant provisions of the Sales Tax Act, 1990. The blacklisting order is required to contain reasons for blacklisting, the time period for which any refund or input tax claimed by the blacklisted person or any other registered person on the strength of invoices issued by him shall be inadmissible, any recovery payable and penalties to be imposed.

Reference: Rule 12(b)(i) and Rule 12(b)(ii) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

Rule 12 further provides that copies of the blacklisting order are to be endorsed to the concerned registered person, other LTUs/RTOs, FBR/PRAL system, STARR system and Customs Wing system, and the relevant lists are to be circulated to refund sections, audit sections and other concerned officers for implementation.

Reference: Rule 12(b)(iv) and Rule 12(b)(v) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

Where officers receive the list of invoices issued by a blacklisted person, they are required to issue show cause notice to the registered persons who claimed input tax/refund on the strength of such invoices and decide the matter through a self-speaking appealable order after providing reasonable opportunity of hearing.

Reference: Rule 12(b)(vi) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006 read with section 21(3) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990.

Separately, section 21(4) empowers the Board, Commissioner or authorized officer to block refunds or input tax adjustments where there are reasons to believe that a registered person is engaged in issuing fake or flying invoices, claiming fraudulent input tax or refunds, does not physically exist or conduct actual business, or is committing any other fraudulent activity. Such action requires reasons to be recorded in writing and may be followed by further investigation and appropriate legal action.

Reference: Section 21(4) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990.

From a commercial perspective, suspension or blacklisting can have serious business consequences. It may disrupt sales tax invoicing, input tax adjustment, refunds, import/export GD filing, customer/vendor confidence, procurement from government and public sector entities, and the taxpayer’s standing within the supply chain. In particular, customers may become reluctant to transact with the suspended/blacklisted person because their own input tax credit/refund may be challenged.

In view of the above, if a taxpayer’s registration is suspended, the matter should be handled urgently. The immediate response should include documentary evidence of physical existence, actual business activity, tax return filing, sales and purchase reconciliations, stock movement, bank payments, tax payments, customer/vendor details, and rebuttal of each allegation mentioned in the suspension/show cause notice. The objective should be to secure revocation of suspension before the matter proceeds to blacklisting.

Regards,

[Your Name]
:::

For internal checking, the most important references are:

**Suspension / blacklisting power:** section 21(2), Sales Tax Act, 1990.  
**Post-suspension procedure and timelines:** section 21(2A), Sales Tax Act, 1990.  
**Invoices not entertained during suspension / blacklisting effect:** section 21(3), Sales Tax Act, 1990.  
**Blocking of refund/input adjustment:** section 21(4), Sales Tax Act, 1990.  
**Grounds and procedure for suspension:** Rule 12(a), Sales Tax Rules, 2006.  
**Consequences during suspension:** Rule 12(a)(v), Sales Tax Rules, 2006.  
**Blacklisting order and its contents:** Rule 12(b)(i) and (ii), Sales Tax Rules, 2006.  
**Non-active taxpayer restrictions:** Rule 12A(1) to (4), Sales Tax Rules, 2006.  
**Definition of active taxpayer:** section 2(1A), Sales Tax Act, 1990.

Revised wording is below:

:::writing{variant="email" id="69284" subject="Further Implication of Suspension on Customers’ April Input Tax Claims"}
Dear [Name],

Further to our earlier email, one additional important practical implication also needs to be considered.

Sales tax returns are initially processed on the basis of declarations made by the respective registered persons. However, where the supplier’s sales tax registration is suspended / reflected as non-active in the FBR system, the corresponding input tax claimed by customers may be treated as inadmissible in their respective sales tax returns.

In the present case, since your sales tax return for the relevant tax period has not yet been submitted, the position may create an immediate impact for your customers. Practically, by the end of the month, i.e. around the 21st when the relevant return position/payment liability is finalized in the system, the input tax claimed by your customers for the month of April may appear as payable / inadmissible in their respective sales tax returns.

Therefore, even if any customer had claimed input tax against your invoices before the date of suspension, such input tax may still be reflected as payable once the return is processed in the system. This may result in a direct payable amount for the respective customers for the month of April, corresponding to the output tax charged by you on those invoices.

This is a significant commercial implication because the issue may not remain limited to your own sales tax profile. It may also affect customers’ input tax adjustments, payable position and return reconciliation, and may result in immediate queries from customers once the payable amount starts reflecting in their respective returns.

The above position is also supported by Rule 12(a)(v) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006, which provides that no input tax adjustment or refund shall be admissible to the suspended registered person or to any other registered person on the strength of invoices issued by such suspended person during the currency of suspension. Further, Rule 12A(2)(b) and Rule 12A(2)(c) restrict a non-active taxpayer from issuing sales tax invoices and claiming input tax / refund, while Rule 12A(4) provides that where an invoice of a non-active taxpayer is entered in Annexure-A of the buyer’s return, the system reflects the supplier as non-active and no input tax credit is admissible against such invoice.

Accordingly, apart from the legal consequences already highlighted in our earlier email, the immediate customer-side exposure for the April tax period should also be assessed carefully, as the disallowance / payable impact may arise in customers’ respective returns by the end of the month.

Regards,

[Your Name]
:::

Below is a continuation paragraph/email that can be sent in the same thread:

:::writing{variant="email" id="31742" subject="Further Implication of Suspension on Customers’ Input Tax Claims"}
Dear [Name],

Further to our earlier email, one additional important practical implication also needs to be considered.

Sales tax returns are initially processed on the basis of the declarations made by the respective registered persons. Therefore, even if any customer has already claimed input tax against invoices issued before the date of suspension, such input tax may still be impacted once the supplier’s status is reflected as suspended / non-active in the FBR system.

In the present case, since your sales tax return for the relevant period has not yet been submitted, there is a significant possibility that the corresponding input tax claimed by customers against your output tax invoices may be reflected as inadmissible / payable in their respective sales tax returns. Practically, this means that the output tax declared or chargeable by you may create a corresponding exposure for your customers, as the input tax claimed by them for the month of April may appear as payable / disallowed in their return position, particularly when the return is processed after the suspension status is reflected in the system.

This is a very significant commercial implication because the issue may not remain limited to your own sales tax profile only. It may also directly affect your customers’ return positions, input tax adjustments, payable amounts and reconciliations. As a result, customers may raise immediate concerns once their respective returns reflect such input tax as payable / inadmissible.

This position is also supported by Rule 12(a)(v) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006, which provides that no input tax adjustment or refund shall be admissible to the suspended registered person or to any other registered person on the strength of invoices issued by such suspended person during the currency of suspension. Further, Rule 12A(2)(b) and Rule 12A(2)(c) restrict a non-active taxpayer from issuing sales tax invoices and claiming input tax / refund, while Rule 12A(4) provides that where an invoice of a non-active taxpayer is entered in Annexure-A of the buyer’s return, the system reflects the supplier as non-active and no input tax credit is admissible against such invoice.

Accordingly, apart from the legal consequences already highlighted in our earlier email, the immediate customer-side exposure also needs to be assessed carefully, particularly for the April tax period, as the disallowance / payable impact may start appearing in customers’ respective returns.

Regards,

[Your Name]
:::

Below is a researched position and a client-ready email draft. I have kept the language practical, but legally anchored in **section 21 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990**, **Rule 12 and Rule 12A of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006**, and the Finance Act, 2025 update.

### Key legal position

Under the **Sales Tax Act, 1990**, the Commissioner may suspend or blacklist a registered person where he is satisfied that the person has issued fake invoices or otherwise committed tax fraud. After the Finance Act, 2025, section 21(2A) now requires the Commissioner to issue show cause notice within **ten days** of suspension and, after reply and hearing, either revoke the suspension or pass an appealable speaking order for blacklisting within **thirty days of receipt of reply**. citeturn550205view0turn989535view1

Under **Rule 12 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006**, the grounds for suspension may include non-availability at registered address, refusal to provide access to premises/records, abnormal tax profile, excessive input adjustment, continuous carry-forward, substantial transactions with suspended/blacklisted persons, non-filing of returns, or any other specified reason. citeturn745458view0

During suspension, the most serious legal consequence is that **no input tax adjustment/refund is admissible to the suspended person**, and other registered persons are also not allowed input/refund on the strength of invoices issued by the suspended person during the currency of suspension. citeturn745458view1 Further, because a suspended or blacklisted person ceases to qualify as an “active taxpayer”, Rule 12A consequences also apply: such person cannot file Goods Declarations for import/export, issue sales tax invoices, claim input tax/refund, or avail concessions under the Act/rules; purchasers, including government departments and public sector bodies, are also barred from purchasing from a non-active taxpayer. citeturn354848view0turn745458view3

Once blacklisted, the consequences become more severe and may operate against invoices issued **prior to or after blacklisting**, subject to a self-speaking appealable order and opportunity of hearing. The blacklisting order must state reasons, the period for which refund/input tax becomes inadmissible, any recovery payable, and penalties to be imposed. citeturn550205view0turn745458view2

:::writing{variant="email" id="72948" subject="Legal and Practical Implications of Suspension and Blacklisting of Sales Tax Registration"}
Dear [Name],

We have reviewed the implications of suspension and blacklisting of sales tax registration under the Sales Tax Act, 1990 and the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

At the outset, it is important to appreciate that suspension and blacklisting are not merely procedural statuses appearing on FBR’s system. Both carry serious legal and commercial consequences. Suspension is generally an interim action pending inquiry or further proceedings, whereas blacklisting is a more serious final action which may be taken after issuance of show cause notice, opportunity of hearing, and confirmation of the alleged offence.

Under section 21 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, the Commissioner may suspend registration or blacklist a registered person where he is satisfied that such person has issued fake invoices or has otherwise committed tax fraud. After the Finance Act, 2025, the law now specifically requires that, within ten days of the suspension order, a show cause notice should be issued to the registered person. After receipt of reply and after providing an opportunity of hearing, the Commissioner may either revoke the suspension or pass an appealable speaking order for blacklisting within thirty days of receipt of reply.

From a practical perspective, where a person’s sales tax registration is suspended, the following key restrictions and consequences may arise:

1. The suspended person cannot claim input tax adjustment or sales tax refund during the currency of suspension.

2. Invoices issued by the suspended person are not entertained for purposes of input tax credit or sales tax refund.

3. Buyers/customers dealing with the suspended person may also be denied input tax adjustment or refund on the strength of invoices issued by such suspended person.

4. Since a suspended person does not remain an active taxpayer for sales tax purposes, such person may not be able to file Goods Declarations for import or export, issue sales tax invoices, claim input tax/refund, or avail any concession available under the Act or the Rules.

5. Purchasers, including government departments, autonomous bodies and public sector organizations, are restricted from making purchases from a non-active taxpayer.

6. Commercially, suspension may result in customers withholding purchases, vendors placing the taxpayer on hold, disruption in imports/exports, blockage of refund/input adjustments, and reputational risk in the supply chain.

However, suspension should not be treated as equivalent to blacklisting. Suspension is generally an interim measure pending inquiry, and the taxpayer has the right to respond to the show cause notice, provide supporting documents, seek hearing, and request revocation of suspension where the allegations are factually or legally incorrect.

Blacklisting, on the other hand, has more severe implications. If, after hearing, the alleged offence is confirmed, the Commissioner may pass an appealable self-speaking order for blacklisting and may also initiate legal and penal action under the relevant provisions of the Sales Tax Act, 1990. The blacklisting order is required to specify the reasons for blacklisting, the period for which refund or input tax claimed by the taxpayer or by any other registered person on the strength of invoices issued by such taxpayer shall be inadmissible, and any recovery or penalty proposed to be imposed.

The most critical distinction is that, once blacklisting is ordered, the rejection of input tax credit/refund may extend to invoices issued prior to or after blacklisting, subject to the procedure prescribed under law, including issuance of a self-speaking appealable order and provision of opportunity of hearing. This can expose not only the blacklisted person but also its buyers/customers to adverse proceedings for rejection of input tax/refund claims.

Accordingly, in case of suspension, the immediate strategy should be to respond within the prescribed time, provide complete documentary evidence, establish physical existence and actual business activity, reconcile sales and purchases, demonstrate filing/payment compliance, and request revocation of suspension before the matter proceeds to blacklisting. Where any allegation relates to fake invoices, abnormal input adjustment, non-filing, non-availability at address, or transactions with suspended/blacklisted persons, each allegation should be separately rebutted with documentary support.

In our view, suspension should be handled on urgent basis because delay or incomplete compliance may expose the taxpayer to blacklisting, denial of input/refund claims, supply-chain disputes, and further legal/penal action.

Regards,

[Your Name]
:::

**Practical note:** I would avoid saying that a suspended person is “absolutely barred from carrying on business” unless a specific order seals premises or blocks operations. The safer legal wording is that the person cannot issue **effective/admissible sales tax invoices**, cannot claim input/refund, cannot file import/export GDs as non-active taxpayer, cannot avail concessions, and its customers’ input/refund claims become exposed.

We refer to Show Cause Notice C.No. CIR/Zone-VI/Suspension-ST/LTO/Khi/2025-26/348 dated May 21, 2026, issued under section 21(2A) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 read with Rule 12(a)(vi) of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006, whereby K-Electric Limited [the “Company”] has been called upon to show cause as to why it may not be blacklisted on account of alleged persistent violation of the provisions of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 read with S.R.O. 376(I)/2023 dated 21 March 2023.
At the outset, the Company respectfully denies the allegations contained in the impugned notice. The notice proceeds on an incorrect appreciation of facts, overlooks prior compliance already made by the Company, misconstrues the special recovery-based mechanism prescribed for DISCOs under S.R.O. 376(I)/2023, and seeks to invoke the extreme consequence of blacklisting without identifying any specific instance of deliberate suppression, false declaration, non-deposit of recovered tax, or tax fraud within the meaning of the Sales Tax Act, 1990.
It is respectfully submitted that the Company is a regulated electric power distribution company operating under a distinct commercial, regulatory and recovery framework. The difference between sales tax billed through electricity bills and sales tax actually recovered from consumers is an inherent feature of the DISCO recovery model and has specifically been recognized through S.R.O. 376(I)/2023. Such difference, by itself, cannot be equated with suppression of output tax or tax fraud.
IMPUGNED BLACKLISTING NOTICE MATERIALLY CHANGES THE BASIS OF THE EARLIER SUSPENSION PROCEEDINGS
The present notice appears to have been issued in continuation of earlier proceedings initiated through Show Cause Notice No. CIR/Zone-VI/LTO/Khi/2025-26/341 dated May 19, 2026, whereby the Company was called upon to explain why its sales tax registration should not be suspended under section 21(2) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 read with Rule 12 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.
It is important to highlight that the earlier notice dated May 19, 2026 was premised primarily on an alleged decline in recovery ratio from 92.2% for the period June 2024 to February 2025 to 89.6% for the period June 2025 to February 2026. The allegation in the earlier notice was, therefore, confined to a comparative recovery-ratio observation for two limited periods.
Nevertheless, the present blacklisting notice has substantially altered the nature, scope and basis of the allegation. Instead of remaining confined to the recovery-ratio comparison referred to in the earlier notice, the present notice extends tax periods to February 2023 to March 2026 and alleges that against total output sales tax billed of Rs 326,567,252,303, the Company declared collection of 
Rs 289,041,889,607.
This is not a mere continuation of the earlier proceedings. Rather, it constitutes a fresh and materially expanded allegation based on a different period, different computation and different factual premise. The Company respectfully submits that a drastic action such as blacklisting cannot be founded upon shifting and enlarged allegations unless the precise basis, working, period-wise detail and supporting material are first provided to the taxpayer and a meaningful opportunity is allowed to respond.
The proceedings are therefore vitiated on account of serious procedural unfairness, as the Company is being confronted with an enlarged allegation at the blacklisting stage without being provided the underlying computation and without being granted reasonable time to reconcile the same.
PRIOR COMPLIANCE ALREADY MADE BY THE COMPANY HAS BEEN COMPLETELY IGNORED
The allegation that the Company has failed to comply with S.R.O. 376(I)/2023 or failed to furnish the requisite information is factually incorrect and contrary to the record. 
In this regard, reference is invited to letter bearing reference DST-1806 dated 17 June 2025, submitted through the Company’s authorized representative in response to notice No. DCIR/U-4/Z-VI/LTO/S-147/2024-25/e-dox-11588 dated June 10, 2025. Through the said letter, the Company had already furnished complete information pertaining to overall movement, including recoveries and defaulting consumers, for the tax periods February 2023 to May 2025. A copy of letter DST-1806 dated 17 June 2025, along with acknowledgment, is enclosed herewith as Annexure ‘A’.
It is therefore evident that a substantial part of the very period now referred to in the impugned blacklisting notice had already been responded to by the Company. The relevant information had been furnished earlier and was available with the department. The impugned notice, however, proceeds on the assumption that no compliance was made, which is grossly incorrect.
The Company respectfully submits that once the relevant data had already been provided for February 2023 to May 2025, the same could not have been ignored while alleging persistent non-compliance. At the very least, the department was required to examine the information already submitted, identify any specific deficiency therein, and allow the Company an opportunity to explain or supplement the same. Instead, the impugned notice proceeds directly towards blacklisting, which is not justified.
It is further submitted that the Company has, from time to time and whenever required by the department, been furnishing detailed information relating to recovery of sales tax, including consumer-wise/record-wise details, in the manner requested by the concerned officers. Such information is not always capable of being reported through the standard fields available in the monthly sales tax return; however, as a responsible and compliant taxpayer, the Company has continued to provide the relevant data manually on an “as and when required” basis. Therefore, it is factually incorrect to allege that the Company has failed to furnish the requisite information or has not complied with the requirements of S.R.O. 376(I)/2023.
Without prejudice to the Company’s legal objections, including the defective assumption of tax fraud, the factual incorrectness of the impugned notice, the absence of any specific allegation of tax actually recovered but not deposited, and the prior compliance already made for the period February 2023 to May 2025, it is respectfully requested that the complete basis and working of the alleged differential amount of approximately Rs. 37.525 billion may kindly be provided. The impugned notice merely states aggregate figures of billed sales tax and recovered sales tax for the period February 2023 to March 2026, without providing tax-period-wise breakup, consumer/category-wise details, return-wise mapping, or identification of any amount allegedly recovered but not deposited. Since substantial details for February 2023 to May 2025 have already been furnished to the department, any remaining query, if at all, must be identified with precision so that the Company may reconcile and respond to the same in a meaningful manner.
THE COMPANY HAS BEEN REPORTING INFORMATION IN THE MONTHLY SALES TAX RETURNS TO THE EXTENT PERMITTED BY IRIS
The Company has been duly declaring relevant information in the monthly sales tax returns in the manner and to the extent permitted by the IRIS portal.
As already explained in the earlier correspondence, the relevant annexure/tab in the sales tax return contains pre-defined fields. The IRIS portal does not provide an unrestricted facility for uploading detailed consumer-wise, party-wise or customized defaulting-consumer data beyond the system fields made available by FBR. A taxpayer cannot be expected to upload information in a format or field which the system itself does not provide.
This limitation is not attributable to the Company. It arises from the design of the return and the system-based reporting mechanism. Therefore, the Company cannot be penalized or treated as non-compliant for not furnishing data in a manner which is not supported by the prescribed electronic return.
The Company respectfully reiterates that where the IRIS system does not provide a specific facility for uploading detailed party-wise or consumer-wise information in the monthly sales tax return, no adverse inference can be drawn against the taxpayer for not furnishing such data electronically.
The Company has no control over the structure of the return, the design of IRIS, or the fields enabled by FBR. If FBR requires any additional format, structured annexure or separate electronic filing facility for DISCOs under S.R.O. 376(I)/2023, the same may be prescribed and enabled formally. Until such mechanism is available, the taxpayer cannot be treated as non-compliant merely because the system does not allow the desired level of reporting.
This point was already explained in the earlier letter dated 17 June 2025. Despite this, the impugned notice shifts the entire burden of system limitation to the Company, which is neither fair nor sustainable.
THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN BILLED SALES TAX AND RECOVERED SALES TAX IS NOT TAX FRAUD
The principal assumption in the impugned notice appears to be that the difference between output sales tax billed and output sales tax recovered represents suppressed output tax. This assumption is legally and factually misconceived in the case of a DISCO operating under S.R.O. 376(I)/2023.
S.R.O. 376(I)/2023 was issued precisely to address the peculiar nature of the electric power distribution sector, where sales tax is billed to consumers through electricity bills, but actual realization depends upon subsequent recovery from consumers. The special procedure recognizes the distinction between billing and recovery and prescribes a mechanism for collection and payment accordingly.
In the electricity distribution sector, recoveries are affected by several factors, including delayed consumer payments, instalment arrangements, disputed bills, government receivables, category-wise consumer behavior, operational constraints, litigation, delayed realization and defaulting consumers. These factors are commercial and regulatory realities of the sector. They cannot be treated as evidence of suppression unless the department identifies a specific amount of tax that was actually recovered from consumers but not deposited by the Company.
The impugned notice does not identify any such amount. It does not point out any specific consumer, bill, receipt, tax period, return entry, bank recovery or collection record showing that sales tax was recovered by the Company but not deposited into the Government treasury. In the absence of such evidence, the difference between billed and recovered sales tax cannot be converted into an allegation of tax fraud.
In the absence of aforesaid details, the Company is unable to verify the figures stated in the notice or provide a meaningful reconciliation. The Company respectfully requests that if the department still maintains the above allegation, complete period-wise and annexure-wise working may first be provided so that the Company may examine and respond to the same in an appropriate manner.
Ingredients for blacklisting under section 21(2A) and Rule 12(a)(vi) are not established
Blacklisting is an extraordinary and highly prejudicial action. It has serious commercial, regulatory and reputational consequences. Such action cannot be invoked merely because a reconciliation is required or because there is a difference between billed and recovered amounts under a special procedure.
The impugned notice alleges persistent violation and tax fraud. However, the essential ingredients of such allegation have not been established. The notice does not demonstrate that the Company has:
a. issued fake or false invoices;
b. suppressed taxable supplies;
c. recovered sales tax from consumers and failed to deposit the same;
d. made false declarations in the sales tax returns;
e. concealed any material record;
f. failed to provide information despite reasonable and specific requisition; or
g. deliberately violated any mandatory requirement of S.R.O. 376(I)/2023.
On the contrary, the record shows that the Company has been filing sales tax returns, reporting available information in the prescribed system fields, depositing recovered sales tax, responding to departmental notices, and furnishing manual data when called upon.
Therefore, the case does not fall within the scope of blacklisting. At most, the matter requires reconciliation of billed, recovered and unpaid amounts under the special procedure. Such reconciliation issue cannot be converted into proceedings for blacklisting.
COMPLIANT TAXPAYER AND THE ALLEGATION OF TAX FRAUD IS WHOLLY UNWARRANTED
The Company is one of the largest regulated taxpayers and contributors to the national exchequer. It collects and deposits substantial amounts of sales tax and withholding taxes on a continuous monthly basis and remains subject to extensive regulatory and tax oversight.
In such circumstances, serious allegations such as tax fraud, suppression and persistent non-compliance should not be made casually or mechanically. These allegations carry significant legal and reputational consequences and must be supported by clear evidence. The impugned notice, however, does not identify any specific instance where tax was recovered by the Company and not deposited.
The Company respectfully submits that the impugned proceedings appear to have been initiated on a misunderstanding of the recovery-based mechanism applicable to DISCOs and without appreciating the prior compliance already made by the Company.
Without prejudice to the legal, factual and procedural objections raised hereinabove, and without admitting any default, the Company remains committed to full compliance with the Sales Tax Act, 1990, the Sales Tax Rules, 2006 and S.R.O. 376(I)/2023.
The Company is willing to re-submit the data already furnished earlier and to provide further reconciliation for the remaining period, if any, in a reasonable and mutually workable format. However, any such submission should not be treated as an admission of non-compliance, particularly where the Company has already complied to the extent permitted by IRIS and has already provided manual information when required.
The Company respectfully requests that the department may first share complete working of the figures mentioned in the impugned notice so that the same may be reconciled in a structured manner.
