**Subject: Review of Procurement Services Agreement and Invoicing Arrangement**

Dear Usman,

Thank you for your email and for sharing the draft agreement for 2023 along with the executed agreement for 2022.

We have reviewed the draft agreement from a tax perspective. Broadly, the arrangement appears to be in line with the earlier practice, whereby United Energy (Beijing) Limited provides international procurement support services to United Energy Pakistan Limited in relation to international procurement. The scope of services, as currently drafted, covers procurement management support, strategy and consultancy, sourcing and market intelligence, vendor pre-qualification, bid evaluation, negotiations, vendor management, expediting, logistics coordination and related procurement support services. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file1

With respect to the procurement service fee of **3.1% of international procurement**, we understand that this rate has been commercially agreed between the parties. However, we are not aware of the underlying basis, benchmarking, analogy or internal analysis on the basis of which this percentage has been determined. We assume that appropriate commercial and business consideration has been applied while agreeing the rate. Since this is an associated enterprise transaction, the arm’s length nature of the charge may separately be examined from a transfer pricing perspective. Accordingly, UEPL should maintain adequate supporting evidence, including the basis of rate determination, actual services rendered, benefit received by UEPL, year-wise procurement values, correspondence, service records and, where required, transfer pricing study / benchmarking support. Our comments are therefore limited to the tax and documentation aspects, and we are not commenting on the commercial reasonableness or arm’s length benchmarking of the 3.1% rate.

From an income tax withholding perspective, the tax implications will arise at the time of payment / remittance to United Energy (Beijing) Limited. The applicable withholding position should be evaluated and discharged based on the nature of payment, relevant provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, and any applicable treaty position, subject to availability of supporting documents such as tax residency certificate, beneficial ownership / no-PE declaration and other remittance documentation. Since the payment for 2023, 2024 and 2025 is proposed to be made during June 2026, the withholding would practically be made in the tax year in which payment is made. You may also check with the corresponding foreign entity whether claiming foreign tax credit in its jurisdiction for the entire withholding in one year would create any issue. If they require year-wise tax credit evidence, then separate payments and separate CPRs for each year may be more appropriate.

In addition to income tax withholding, Sindh Sales Tax on Services implications under the reverse charge mechanism should also be considered. Where taxable services are received by a resident person in Sindh from a non-resident / foreign service provider, the service recipient is generally required to discharge Sindh sales tax under the reverse charge mechanism, subject to the nature and classification of the service. This implication would therefore need to be evaluated for the proposed procurement support services. We also understand that the validity of the reverse charge mechanism has been supported in recent judicial proceedings; accordingly, the SRB exposure should not be ignored while processing the remittance. The agreement and invoices should therefore clearly describe the nature of services, relevant period, value of services and the party responsible for compliance, so that the income tax withholding and SRB reverse charge positions can both be properly documented.

As regards the agreement structure, in our view, it is acceptable to have one continuing / master agreement for recurring procurement support services, as this is commonly done for recurring intra-group service arrangements. However, the current draft appears to contain a sunset / expiry mechanism by linking the agreement to a specific year. If the intention is to continue the same arrangement for multiple years, then either the sunset clause may be removed and the agreement may be made more general in nature with an annual invoicing and computation mechanism, or alternatively, the existing structure may be retained and each year may be covered through a short supplementary agreement / addendum extending the duration while keeping the remaining commercial terms unchanged.

For invoicing, even where a single master agreement is executed, we would recommend that the invoices should clearly identify the relevant period and year-wise computation. This will help in maintaining a clean audit trail for expense booking, withholding tax compliance, transfer pricing documentation, SRB reverse charge compliance and foreign remittance support. Separate invoices for 2023, 2024 and 2025 would be preferable from a documentation standpoint, even if the payments are processed together in June 2026.

We would also suggest that the agreement should include a clear tax clause stating that all payments shall be subject to applicable withholding taxes and indirect taxes in Pakistan, including any applicable Sindh sales tax under the reverse charge mechanism. UEPL should also provide relevant tax deduction / payment evidence, including CPRs, to United Energy (Beijing) Limited. If the tax cost is not to be borne by UEPL, the agreement should avoid any gross-up obligation.

In view of the above, there is no fundamental tax objection to executing a single continuing agreement, provided the drafting is aligned accordingly and the annual invoicing / computation mechanism is clearly built into the agreement. Alternatively, the parties may execute short annual supplementary agreements for each year. In either case, please quantify and share the expected income tax withholding and SRB reverse charge impact so that the tax treatment, CPRs and related documentation can be properly aligned before remittance.

Kind regards,  
Zuhair

Draft reply:

**Subject: Review of Procurement Services Agreement and Proposed Invoicing Arrangement**

Dear Usman,

Thank you for your email and for sharing the draft agreement for 2023 along with the executed agreement for 2022.

We have reviewed the draft from a tax perspective. Broadly, the arrangement appears to be in line with the earlier executed agreement, whereby United Energy (Beijing) Limited is providing international procurement support services to United Energy Pakistan Limited, with the service fee computed at 3.1% of the actual international procurement for the relevant year. The scope includes procurement management support, contract strategy, sourcing, market intelligence, vendor pre-qualification, bid evaluation, negotiations, vendor management, expediting, logistics coordination and related support services. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file1

From a Pakistan tax perspective, the key issue is withholding tax at the time of payment/remittance to United Energy (Beijing) Limited, being a non-resident. Considering the nature of services, the payment may fall within the scope of fee for technical services / managerial or consultancy services. Under Pakistan domestic law, payments of Pakistan-source fee for technical services to a non-resident are chargeable under section 6, and withholding is required under section 152. citeturn728133view0 Further, under the Pakistan–China tax treaty, fees for technical services may be taxed in the source state, but where the recipient is the beneficial owner, the tax is capped at 12.5% of the gross amount. citeturn536291view0 Accordingly, before remittance, UEPL should ensure availability of the tax residency certificate of United Energy (Beijing) Limited, beneficial ownership / no-PE declaration, invoice, agreement, computation of procurement base, and proper withholding tax challan / treaty documentation, as applicable.

We would also recommend maintaining strong supporting documentation from a transfer pricing and deductibility perspective, since the transaction is between associated enterprises. The 3.1% charge should be supported through year-wise computation, details of international procurements, evidence of services actually rendered, benefit received by UEPL, correspondence, vendor support, bid evaluation / negotiation records, and any internal benchmarking or basis adopted for the fee. This will be important in case the department questions the commercial justification, arm’s length nature, or allowability of the expense.

On the agreement itself, a few drafting corrections are required. The 2023 draft still contains overlapping year references such as “2022 2023” in the effective date, contract price clause and invoice clause. These should be cleaned so that the agreement clearly states that it relates to the period January 1, 2023 to December 31, 2023. The agreement should also avoid backdating the signature date. It may be executed currently, but should clearly state that it covers procurement services rendered during the relevant historical period. We would also suggest adding a tax clause confirming that all payments shall be subject to applicable withholding taxes in Pakistan, and that UEPL shall provide tax deduction evidence / CPR to United Energy (Beijing) Limited. If the commercial understanding is that the tax is to be borne by United Energy (Beijing) Limited, the agreement should not contain any gross-up obligation on UEPL.

Regarding whether one consolidated agreement and invoice may be used for 2023, 2024 and 2025, our preference would be to execute separate year-wise agreements or, alternatively, a master agreement with separate annual schedules / addenda for each year. In either case, separate invoices should be raised for each year. This will provide a cleaner audit trail, allow proper matching of expense with the relevant tax year, support year-wise transfer pricing documentation, and avoid unnecessary questions on prior-period booking, withholding tax reporting and foreign remittance documentation. A single consolidated invoice for all three years may create avoidable complications, particularly if the department asks for year-wise basis, services performed and procurement value.

Separately, provincial sales tax / reverse charge implications on import of services should also be evaluated based on the nature of services and the place where the services are received / consumed. For this purpose, the invoices should clearly describe the nature of services and the relevant period to which the charges relate.

In view of the above, there is no fundamental tax objection to the arrangement, provided the agreement is cleaned up, year-wise documentation is maintained, applicable withholding tax / treaty documentation is completed before remittance, and separate invoices are raised for each year.

Kind regards,  
Zuhair

## Post 1: **Crypto Gains Under Tax Net — Budget 2026 May Change the Game**

Cryptocurrency transactions are likely to come under a formal tax framework through the Finance Bill 2026. One key proposal under consideration is to expand the scope of **section 37 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**, so that gains from crypto trading may be taxed as capital gains.

This means that where a person buys a digital asset and later sells it at a profit, the gain may become taxable. Reports suggest that the possible tax rate may fall between **20% and 30%**, although the final position will only become clear once the Finance Bill is officially presented.

The bigger challenge for FBR will not only be taxation, but documentation. Crypto transactions often take place through offshore exchanges, P2P transfers, stablecoins and private wallets. Unless the reporting mechanism is practical and clear, the law may become difficult to enforce. For crypto investors, the message is simple: the era of completely undocumented digital asset gains may be coming to an end. fileciteturn2file0

---

## Post 2: **Tax Refunds by June 15 — A Big Test for FBR’s Delivery**

In pre-budget consultations, the Prime Minister directed FBR to clear all pending tax refund cases by **June 15**. This is a major development for exporters and businesses whose working capital often remains stuck due to delayed refunds.

Refund delays are not just a compliance issue; they directly affect cash flows, production planning and export competitiveness. When businesses are forced to finance government-held refunds from their own pockets, the cost of doing business increases and expansion becomes difficult.

The government has also indicated that the export refinance scheme rate will remain capped at **4.5% until June 2027**, giving exporters some certainty in a tight monetary environment. However, the real impact will depend on execution. For businesses, the key question is not whether the announcement is good, but whether refunds are actually processed within the promised timeline. fileciteturn1file3

---

## Post 3: **FTO Draws the Line: Inquiry Powers Are Not Recovery Powers**

The Federal Tax Ombudsman has clarified an important taxpayer protection principle: investigative powers under **section 175C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** do not independently authorize coercive recovery or collection of tax without lawful determination of liability.

In the reported case, the taxpayer deposited **Rs. 1.5 million** during monitoring/inquiry proceedings, after which the department discontinued the proceedings without passing a proper speaking order or determining actual tax liability. The FTO treated such conduct as maladministration and recommended inquiry into the circumstances under which the amount was obtained.

This ruling is highly relevant for taxpayers facing field visits, monitoring proceedings or pressure for “voluntary” payments. Tax can only be recovered through due process, after proper determination under law. An inquiry notice cannot be converted into a shortcut recovery tool. fileciteturn1file1

With reference to the captioned appeal, it is respectfully submitted that the matter was fixed for hearing before the Hon’ble Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue, Division-II, Karachi, on May 18, 2026, wherein detailed arguments were advanced on behalf of the Appellant on the issues involved in the appeal.

During the course of hearing, while addressing the issue relating to Windfall Levy, it was specifically submitted that the same issue had already been considered and decided in favour of the Appellant in earlier proceedings. In this regard, reliance was placed on the submissions already filed through the earlier appeal note as well as the rejoinder, wherein it was brought on record that the Department itself, in the assessment order for tax year 2019, had taken a favourable view on the same issue, whereas for tax years 2020 and 2021, the learned Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals) had also decided the issue in favour of the Appellant.

It is further submitted that, during the hearing, the relevant extracts relating to tax year 2019 were placed before the Hon’ble Bench. However, with respect to the favourable orders passed by the learned Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals) for tax years 2020 and 2021, the Hon’ble Bench was pleased to direct that copies of the said appellate orders may also be furnished for proper appreciation of the Appellant’s contention.

In compliance with the aforesaid direction, the Appellant respectfully submits herewith copies of the relevant orders passed by the learned Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals) as **Annexure “A”**, whereby the issue relating to Windfall Levy was decided in favour of the Appellant for the aforesaid tax years.

It is also respectfully submitted that, based on the information presently available with the Appellant and upon review of the available record, it appears that the Department did not prefer any further appeal before this Hon’ble Tribunal against the favourable findings recorded by the learned Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals) on the issue of Windfall Levy. Accordingly, the said findings, to the best of the Appellant’s understanding and based on the record available, appear to have remained undisturbed.

In view of the above, it is respectfully prayed that the enclosed appellate orders, along with the earlier submissions already placed on record, may kindly be taken into consideration while adjudicating the captioned appeal.

Submitted for your honour’s kind perusal and record.

**Subject: Opinion on Classification of Vendor Contracts under Section 153**

Dear [Name],

We have reviewed the attached contracts executed with Rizwan Electric Works, particularly the scope appearing in Annexure-A, to evaluate whether withholding tax should continue to be applied under section 153(1)(b) as “services” or whether the contracts are more appropriately covered under section 153(1)(c) as “execution of contract”.

At the outset, the classification should not be determined merely on the basis of the title used in the contract, such as “service contract” or “procurement of services”. For withholding tax purposes, the more relevant test is the **dominant nature, commercial substance and actual obligation assumed by the vendor**. Where the vendor is mainly required to provide manpower, technical support, emergency response, supervision or routine operational assistance on an as-needed basis, without undertaking a defined independent deliverable, the arrangement generally leans towards **services**. However, where the vendor undertakes installation, rehabilitation, construction, dismantling, energization, replacement, cable laying, foundation work or completion of a defined scheme / feeder / project, the arrangement is more appropriately viewed as **execution of contract**, even if the contract document uses service-related terminology.

On this principle, **Contract No. 5210000258** appears to be more inclined towards **services under section 153(1)(b)**. The scope is for emergency support and primarily requires the vendor to provide SSM, UGM and OH maintenance gangs during rain / emergency situations, comprising supervisors, fitters, jointers, linemen and helpers. The contract also indicates that the vendor is required to arrange services on a necessary basis, respond within short notice, and submit daily cluster-wise gang deployment attendance for invoicing. These features show that the arrangement is largely manpower / emergency maintenance support driven, rather than an independent works contract with a defined project deliverable. fileciteturn5file0

In contrast, **Contract No. 5210000293** appears to be more appropriately classifiable as **execution of contract under section 153(1)(c)**. Although the document uses service-related wording, the subject itself is “Network Rehabilitation of Distribution Network Cluster – Baldia”. The scope includes PMT rehabilitation, conversion of OH bare spans, sub-station rehabilitation / maintenance, installation or replacement of HT poles, cable termination / jointing, LBS works and PMT shifting. The contract also contains strong execution indicators, including completion of each feeder, lump-sum / BOQ-based pricing, performance bond, defect liability period, work commencement, completion timeline, delay penalties, material reconciliation and restrictions on unauthorized execution. These are not merely support services; they reflect outcome-based electrical and network rehabilitation works. fileciteturn5file1

Similarly, **Contract No. 5210000407**, despite being titled “Distribution Electrical Services”, is substantially in the nature of **execution of contract under section 153(1)(c)**. The contract covers extensive distribution-related execution items, including installation of HT/LT poles, cable laying, excavation, foundation works, installation/removal of equipment, energization, dismantling, meter installation, PMT/RMU works and scheme-based distribution activities. The terms further refer to completed schemes, RO/CRO-based execution, risk-and-cost consequences, performance bond, material stock / reconciliation, project scope and performance obligations. These factors collectively indicate that the vendor is assuming responsibility for execution of physical / electrical works rather than merely rendering general services. fileciteturn5file2

Accordingly, our overall view is that **Contract No. 5210000258 may reasonably be retained under section 153(1)(b)**, being primarily an emergency manpower / maintenance support arrangement. However, **Contracts No. 5210000293 and 5210000407 are more defensibly classifiable under section 153(1)(c)** as execution of contracts, since the dominant scope involves network rehabilitation, installation, replacement, dismantling, cable laying, foundation and energization works.

From a rate perspective, once the classification is finalized, the applicable withholding rate should be applied as per the relevant entry of section 153 read with the First Schedule and the Tenth Schedule, after confirming the vendor’s legal status, ATL position and availability of any valid exemption or reduced-rate certificate. The rate should therefore follow the classification: **section 153(1)(b) for services** and **section 153(1)(c) for execution of contract**.

We would also suggest that, going forward, the contract title and description should be aligned with the actual nature of the arrangement. Where the arrangement is execution-based, the contract should preferably be titled and described as **“Works Contract”, “Execution of Electrical Works”, “Network Rehabilitation Works” or “Distribution Network Execution Works”**, instead of a generic “Service Contract”. Although the title is not conclusive, inconsistent terminology may unnecessarily create room for dispute during withholding tax review, vendor reconciliation or departmental audit. A clearer title, supported by consistent invoice descriptions and PO/RO tax coding, would make the withholding position more defensible.

As a further control point, invoices should also describe the actual work performed rather than using generic wording such as “services rendered”. For example, invoices under execution-based contracts should ideally refer to the relevant feeder / scheme / BOQ item / RO or CRO and state the nature of work completed, such as installation, rehabilitation, cable laying, dismantling or energization. Where any invoice contains a clearly separable manpower-only component, that component may be evaluated separately; however, where the invoice is raised for completion of scheme-based or BOQ-based works, the stronger position would remain classification under section 153(1)(c).

Regards,  
Zuhair Ahmed Minhas

**Proposed response:**

Dear [Name],

We have reviewed the attached contracts and the scope of work mentioned in Annexure-A. Under section 153, a distinction needs to be made between payments for rendering/providing of services under section 153(1)(b) and payments on execution of contracts under section 153(1)(c). As per FBR’s WHT Rate Card for Tax Year 2026, general services under section 153(1)(b) attract 15% for ATL persons and 30% for non-ATL persons, whereas execution of contracts under section 153(1)(c) attracts 7.5% for ATL companies and 8% in other ATL cases, with non-ATL rates of 15% and 16%, respectively. citeturn222915view0

Based on the scope, Contract No. **5210000258** appears to be more in the nature of emergency manpower/gang deployment services, i.e. provisioning of SSM/UGM/OH maintenance gangs with supervisors, fitters, jointers, linemen and helpers, along with MTL and related support. fileciteturn2file0 Accordingly, applying withholding under section **153(1)(b)** appears supportable. However, since the scope has characteristics of manpower outsourcing / emergency maintenance support, the possibility of applying the reduced rate for specified services may also be examined, provided the vendor’s profile, ATL status and other conditions are satisfied. In the absence of such comfort, deduction at **15% under section 153(1)(b)** remains a conservative position.

For Contract No. **5210000293**, the scope is not merely routine services; it includes network rehabilitation works such as installation/replacement of PMT leading, conversion of OH spans, sub-station rehabilitation/maintenance, installation/replacement of HT poles, LBS-related work, PMT shifting and related electrical/civil works. The contract also refers to lump-sum/BOQ-based work, completion of feeders, performance bond, defect liability period and execution obligations. fileciteturn2file1 On substance, this appears closer to an **execution of works contract** rather than ordinary services. Therefore, withholding under section **153(1)(c)** may be more appropriate for this contract.

Similarly, Contract No. **5210000407** covers extensive distribution electrical works, including installation of HT/LT poles, cable laying, excavation, foundation works, installation/removal of equipment, energization, dismantling and other execution-based activities, with performance bond, CRO/RO-based execution and scheme completion requirements. fileciteturn2file2 This also appears to fall more appropriately under **section 153(1)(c)** as execution of contract, rather than general services under section 153(1)(b).

Accordingly, for Contracts **5210000293** and **5210000407**, if the vendor is a company and appears on ATL, the applicable rate would be **7.5%**; if the vendor is other than a company and appears on ATL, the rate would be **8%**. If the vendor is not on ATL, the applicable rate would increase under the Tenth Schedule, i.e. **15% for company** and **16% for other than company**. For prior invoices where 15% has already been deducted under section 153(1)(b), there should not be any short-deduction exposure from KE’s perspective; however, it may represent excess withholding for the vendor if the correct classification is section 153(1)(c) and the vendor is on ATL.

We would therefore recommend confirming the vendor’s legal status and ATL position from IRIS/ATL before updating the withholding tax code. On the basis of the attached scope, our recommended treatment is: **Contract 5210000258 — section 153(1)(b), subject to review for specified services; Contracts 5210000293 and 5210000407 — section 153(1)(c), execution of contract.**

Please use the below refined email:

---

**Subject: Opinion on Classification of Vendor Contracts under Section 153**

Dear [Name],

We have reviewed the attached contracts executed with Rizwan Electric Works, particularly the scope of work appearing in Annexure-A, to evaluate whether withholding tax should continue to be applied under section 153(1)(b) as “services” or whether the contracts are more appropriately covered under section 153(1)(c) as “execution of contract”.

At the outset, the classification should not be determined merely on the basis of the title used in the contract, such as “service contract” or “procurement of services”. For purposes of section 153, the more relevant test is the **real nature and dominant substance of the arrangement**. Where the vendor is mainly required to provide manpower, technical assistance, operational support, supervision, maintenance support, or emergency response on an as-needed basis, without undertaking a defined project or deliverable, the arrangement generally leans towards **services**. Conversely, where the vendor assumes responsibility for completing an identifiable work, project, scheme, feeder, rehabilitation activity, installation, dismantling, construction, energization, or similar physical/electrical execution, particularly where the contract contains BOQ/lump-sum pricing, completion milestones, performance bond, defect liability, risk-and-cost consequences, material reconciliation and project-wise invoicing, the arrangement is more appropriately viewed as **execution of contract**.

In the present case, **Contract No. 5210000258** appears to be more inclined towards **services under section 153(1)(b)**. The contract is for emergency support and primarily requires the vendor to arrange and deploy SSM, UGM and OH maintenance gangs for rain/emergency situations, including supervisors, fitters, jointers, linemen and helpers. The terms also indicate that services are to be provided on a necessary basis, on short notice, with payment based on actual work done and supported by daily attendance / deployment records. The substance is therefore closer to provision of emergency manpower and maintenance support rather than execution of an independent project or defined deliverable. fileciteturn3file4 fileciteturn3file12

However, **Contract No. 5210000293** appears to be more appropriately classified as **execution of contract under section 153(1)(c)**. Although the document uses service-related terminology, the underlying scope is network rehabilitation of the distribution network, including PMT rehabilitation, conversion of OH bare spans, sub-station rehabilitation/maintenance, installation or replacement of HT poles, cable termination/jointing, LBS works and PMT shifting. The contractual terms also refer to completion of each feeder, lump-sum/BOQ-based pricing, performance bond, material reconciliation, completion timelines, delay penalties and defect liability period. These features indicate that the vendor is not merely providing services but is undertaking defined execution-based electrical works with an outcome-oriented obligation. fileciteturn3file8 fileciteturn3file5 fileciteturn3file1

Similarly, **Contract No. 5210000407**, despite being titled “Distribution Electrical Services”, is also substantially in the nature of **execution of contract under section 153(1)(c)**. The contract covers a large number of execution-based line items, including installation of HT/LT poles, cable laying, excavation, foundations, equipment installation/removal, energization, dismantling, meter installation, repair of foundations, PMT/RMU-related works, and other scheme-based distribution works. The terms further refer to CRO/RO-based execution, completed schemes, risk-and-cost consequences, performance bond, project scope, additional resources for completion of project scope and adjustment of balance material. These are strong indicators of a works/execution arrangement rather than ordinary rendering of services. fileciteturn3file6 fileciteturn3file9

Accordingly, our view is that only **Contract No. 5210000258** may reasonably continue to be treated under section **153(1)(b)**, as the dominant element is emergency manpower / maintenance support. On the other hand, **Contracts No. 5210000293 and 5210000407** are more appropriately classifiable under section **153(1)(c)**, being contracts for execution of electrical/network rehabilitation and distribution works.

For rate purposes, as per FBR’s Withholding Tax Rate Card for Tax Year 2026 updated up to June 30, 2025, services under section 153(1)(b), other than specified reduced-rate services, attract withholding at 15% for ATL and 30% for non-ATL persons, whereas execution of contracts under section 153(1)(c) attracts 7.5% for ATL companies, 8% for other ATL persons, and 15% / 16% for non-ATL cases, respectively. The applicable rate should therefore be applied after confirming the vendor’s legal status, ATL position and availability of any valid exemption/reduced-rate certificate. citeturn719150view0 citeturn850099view0

In case any invoice under the larger contracts contains a clearly separable and independently identifiable manpower-only component, the position may be reviewed separately on invoice-level facts. However, where the invoice is raised under a RO/CRO for completion of scheme-based, installation, rehabilitation, dismantling, cable laying, foundation, energization or similar execution work, the stronger and more defensible position would be to treat the payment as falling under section **153(1)(c)**.

Regards,  
Zuhair Ahmed Minhas

**Subject:** RE: New Supply Model – Dealers (Retailer) & Shell Card

Dear Hashim Sb,

Thank you for your confirmation and the additional clarifications.

Based on the facts now confirmed, our understanding is that the proposed arrangement should not disturb the existing primary supply model between WEPL and the dealer/retailer. WEPL will continue to make the normal sale of petroleum products to the dealer under the existing retail supply mechanism, and the dealer’s existing economics, including dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax on franchise fee and withholding tax treatment, will continue to apply in the ordinary course. The Shell Card arrangement appears to operate as a separate commercial mechanism whereby WEPL, at its own discretion, offers discount to Shell Card customers, while a portion of the discount cost is commercially recovered from the dealer through a per-litre debit note based on Shell Card volumes.

On this basis, the discount offered to Shell Card customers should remain a discount offered by WEPL and not by the dealer, particularly since you have confirmed that the dealer has no concern with the quantum or manner of discount offered by WEPL to the Shell Card customer. Since the customer-facing manual invoice will reflect the discount and the same will also be declared in the sales tax return, WEPL should ensure that the invoicing, sales tax reporting and accounting treatment remain fully aligned, so that the discount is properly supported as a customer discount allowed under the Shell Card program and is not later viewed as an undocumented price adjustment or unrelated deduction from revenue.

As regards the recovery from dealers through debit note, our view is that the debit note should be carefully worded as a **“Shell Card Discount Contribution / Funding Recovery”** and should not be described as service charges, administrative fee, marketing fee, card management fee, commission, or consideration for any service provided by WEPL to the dealer. This distinction is important because, on the confirmed facts, WEPL is not providing any separate service to the dealer; rather, WEPL is recovering part of the commercial cost of discount offered by WEPL to Shell Card customers. If the documentation is drafted in this manner, the recovery should be supportable as a commercial contribution / recovery linked with the discount program, instead of being treated as consideration for a taxable service.

From an income tax perspective, since WEPL intends to book the dealer recovery as income and offset the Shell Card discount within the same account head, the income should be offered as part of taxable receipts, while the corresponding Shell Card discount cost should remain claimable as a business expense, subject to proper documentation and reconciliation. For audit trail purposes, we would suggest maintaining clear working papers showing Shell Card volumes, per-litre contribution, debit notes issued to dealers, discounts offered to Shell Card customers, and the corresponding accounting entries. It would be preferable to maintain gross visibility of both the discount cost and dealer recovery, even if both are ultimately netted or monitored under the same accounting head.

With respect to the Rs. 0.40 per litre dealer administration margin, since you have clarified that no separate credit or payment will be made to the dealer and the same will only remain part of the dealer’s original economics under the sales invoice issued at the first stage, no separate tax treatment should arise merely on account of this component. However, the agreement and internal documentation should avoid presenting this amount as a separate fee payable by WEPL to the dealer for services, unless there is an intention to treat it as a separate service component. Otherwise, it should be described only as part of the dealer’s retained margin/economics under the retail arrangement.

From a provincial sales tax perspective, the key risk would arise only if the debit note recovery is characterized as consideration for any service by WEPL to the dealer, such as card facilitation, marketing support, customer management, promotional services, or administrative services. On the confirmed facts, this does not appear to be the substance of the arrangement. Accordingly, the documentation should clearly provide that the dealer contribution is only towards funding the discount offered by WEPL to Shell Card customers and that no separate service is being rendered by WEPL to the dealer against such recovery. This will help mitigate any potential provincial sales tax exposure on the dealer debit note.

Similarly, from a withholding tax perspective, the recovery should not be documented as a payment by the dealer for services rendered by WEPL. If the dealer is a withholding agent and the debit note is described in a manner suggesting service charges or commission, it may create unnecessary withholding tax questions. Therefore, the debit note narration and agreement clauses should be aligned with the commercial substance, i.e. “discount contribution / funding recovery based on Shell Card volumes”.

In light of the above, the proposed model may be implemented from a tax perspective, subject to careful documentation, consistent invoicing, and proper accounting trail. We would particularly recommend that the agreement title and operative clauses be reviewed to ensure that the arrangement is not inadvertently described as a service arrangement. A more appropriate title may be **“Shell Card Discount Contribution Arrangement”** or **“Shell Card Discount Funding Addendum”**, with clauses clearly stating that WEPL alone offers the Shell Card discount to customers and that the dealer’s contribution is a commercial funding recovery based on Shell Card volumes.

Please feel free to share the revised draft agreement / debit note format once available, and we can review the wording from a tax risk perspective before implementation.

Regards,  
Zuhair Ahmed Minhas

**Subject:** RE: New Supply Model – Dealers (Retailer) & Shell Card

Dear Hashim Sb,

Thank you for your confirmation and the additional clarifications.

Based on the facts now shared, our broad understanding is that the existing supply model between WEPL and the dealer/retailer will continue to operate in the ordinary course. WEPL will continue to sell petroleum products to the dealer under the existing retail supply arrangement, and the existing treatment of dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax on franchise fee and withholding tax on dealer margin will remain unchanged.

The proposed arrangement appears to be specific to Shell Card transactions, whereby WEPL will offer discount to Shell Card customers at its own discretion, and a portion of the commercial cost of such discount will be recovered from the dealer through a debit note based on Shell Card volumes. You have also confirmed that the dealer will not be concerned with the quantum or manner of discount offered by WEPL to Shell Card customers, and that the customer-facing invoice will reflect the discount offered by WEPL.

Having said that, before we draw any final tax conclusion, there are certain aspects which may require further clarity, particularly from the business / commercial team. The tax treatment would materially depend on the exact commercial substance, contractual wording, debit note narration, accounting treatment and the manner in which the transaction is represented between WEPL, the dealer and the Shell Card customer.

In particular, the key point requiring careful evaluation is whether the amount recovered from the dealer is merely a **commercial contribution / recovery towards discount funding**, or whether it can be interpreted as consideration for any service, facility, marketing support, card arrangement, customer access or administrative support provided by WEPL to the dealer. If the arrangement is documented as a pure discount funding recovery, the tax implications may be different. However, if the wording suggests that WEPL is providing any identifiable service to the dealer against the recovery, then provincial sales tax and withholding tax considerations may arise.

Similarly, while you have confirmed that the Rs. 0.40 per litre dealer administration margin will not be separately credited or paid to the dealer and will form part of the original invoice economics, we would suggest that this aspect should also be clearly understood from the business team. If this amount is merely part of the dealer’s retained commercial margin, it should not ordinarily create a separate tax event. However, if the arrangement or internal workings describe it as separate compensation to the dealer for handling Shell Card transactions, then the treatment may need to be evaluated separately.

Further, since WEPL intends to book the dealer recovery as income and offset the Shell Card discount within the same account head, it would be important to understand the accounting entries in detail. For tax and audit trail purposes, it would be preferable to maintain clear linkage between Shell Card volumes, customer discount, dealer-wise contribution, debit notes issued and the corresponding accounting entries. This will help support the position that the recovery is directly linked with Shell Card discount funding and is not an unrelated income stream or service consideration.

We would also suggest that the agreement title, operative clauses and debit note description should be reviewed carefully. Terms such as “service charges”, “administrative fee”, “marketing fee”, “card management fee” or “commission” may create unnecessary tax ambiguity. A more neutral description such as **“Shell Card Discount Contribution / Funding Recovery”** may be more aligned with the apparent commercial substance, subject of course to final confirmation from the business team.

Accordingly, at this stage, our preliminary observation is that the proposed model may be supportable from a tax perspective if the arrangement is properly documented as a discount funding / commercial recovery mechanism and not as a service arrangement. However, we would not suggest finalising the tax position until the complete commercial flow, accounting entries, debit note format and agreement wording are reviewed together.

In this regard, it would be useful to arrange a call with the concerned business / commercial team so that we can understand the practical mechanics of the model in more detail, including the customer journey, dealer involvement, invoicing flow, accounting entries and commercial rationale for the recovery from dealers. Once this is discussed, we can provide more precise comments on the income tax, withholding tax and provincial sales tax implications, as well as suggest any changes required in the draft agreement / debit note format.

Regards,  
Zuhair Ahmed Minhas

parts:
I searched this point. The **best available authority** for your argument is **MCB Bank Ltd. v Commissioner Inland Revenue, 2014 PTD 1874 [Lahore High Court]**. This judgment directly discusses section 32(2) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, Rule 32(2) of the Income Tax Rules, 2002, IAS-based accounting, and the relationship between tax accounting and financial accounting. The Court observed that companies are required to compute business income on **accrual basis**, and Rule 32(2) requires company books to be maintained in accordance with **IAS**. The Court further clarified that IAS/IFRS principles support computation of income, but taxability is ultimately governed by the Ordinance. This helps your point that IAS/IFRS-based recognition is not outside accrual accounting; rather, it is the accounting framework through which accrual-based computation is ordinarily made, subject to specific tax provisions. citeturn684870view0

The statutory anchor is also clear. The latest FBR version of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, amended up to 20 February 2026, places sections 32 to 34 under the heading **“Tax Accounting”**. Section 32(2) provides that a company shall account for income chargeable under the head “Income from Business” on an **accrual basis**, while section 34 explains that under accrual accounting, income is derived when due and expenditure is incurred when payable; section 34(3) further provides that an amount becomes payable when all events determining liability have occurred and the liability can be determined with reasonable accuracy. citeturn444599view0 citeturn195590view0 citeturn195590view2

Another useful authority is **Commissioner Inland Revenue Zone-I v M/s Excell Pakistan (Pvt.) Ltd., 2022 PTD 1535 [Sindh High Court]**. The headnote states that an entry made in accounts under the accounting system regularly employed by the taxpayer is valid if it is not contrary to law, and that under the mercantile/accrual system an ascertained liability accruing with reasonable expectation of payment is an allowable deduction. The KTBA synopsis also records that the Sindh High Court allowed exchange loss because it was accounted for as an ascertained liability under the taxpayer’s accounting system. citeturn207924view0 citeturn738145search0

For corporate-law support, section 225 of the Companies Act, 2017 requires financial statements to give a true and fair view, comply with financial reporting standards notified by SECP, and permits unreserved compliance with IFRS issued by IASB. The Fourth Schedule also states that listed companies and subsidiaries shall follow IFRS notified under section 225. This supports the broader proposition that IFRS/IAS-based accounting is part of the statutory financial reporting framework for companies in Pakistan, and therefore cannot be treated as alien to accrual accounting. citeturn698226view0

A careful way to frame the argument would be:

**“The expression ‘accrual basis’ under sections 32 and 34 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 cannot be read in isolation from the accounting framework applicable to companies. For companies, accrual-based computation is ordinarily carried out through books maintained in accordance with applicable IAS/IFRS and financial reporting standards. The Lahore High Court in MCB Bank Ltd. v CIR, 2014 PTD 1874, recognized this relationship while clarifying that accounting principles support computation, whereas ultimate taxability or deductibility remains subject to the Ordinance. Therefore, where an amount is recognized in accordance with the applicable accounting standards and the liability/income has accrued within the meaning of section 34, the same is not outside the scope of accrual accounting merely because it arises from IAS/IFRS-based measurement, unless a specific provision of the Ordinance provides otherwise.”**

One caveat: **MCB Bank** is also useful for the Department in one limited sense because it says tax law prevails over financial accounting where the Ordinance has a specific rule. So our strongest position should not be “IFRS always prevails”; rather, it should be **“IFRS/IAS recognition is part of accrual-based computation, unless specifically displaced by the Ordinance.”**

parts:
Further case-wise research gives the following position. **The strongest direct authority remains MCB Bank, 2014 PTD 1874 [LHC]**, while the remaining cases are useful to support the broader accrual/mercantile accounting principle.

### 1. **MCB Bank Ltd. v Commissioner Inland Revenue — 2014 PTD 1874 [Lahore High Court]**

This is the most relevant case for your specific point. The Lahore High Court discussed section 32(2) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 and observed that a company is required to compute its business income on **accrual basis**. The Court also noted that Rule 32(2) of the Income Tax Rules, 2002 requires company books to be maintained in accordance with **International Accounting Standards**. The judgment explains that accounting principles under IAS support the computation of income, though final taxability is controlled by the Ordinance. citeturn670036view0

**How to use it:**  
This supports the argument that IAS/IFRS-based accounting is not outside the scope of accrual accounting. Rather, for companies, accrual-based computation is ordinarily carried out through books maintained under applicable accounting standards. The caveat is that IAS/IFRS cannot override a specific provision of the Ordinance.

---

### 2. **Commissioner Inland Revenue Zone-I v M/s Excell Pakistan (Pvt.) Ltd. — 2022 PTD 1535 [Sindh High Court]**

This case is highly useful for accrual-based recognition of liabilities, particularly exchange loss. The Sindh High Court dealt with sections 20, 32, 34 and 122 and accepted the principle that entries made in accordance with the taxpayer’s regularly maintained accounting system are valid where they are not contrary to law. The case recognizes that under the mercantile/accrual system, an ascertained liability which has accrued and is reasonably determinable may be allowable. citeturn667887search6

**How to use it:**  
This case can be relied upon where the Department argues that an accounting-standard-based entry is merely bookish or notional. The answer is that if the company follows accrual accounting and the liability has crystallized with reasonable accuracy, the entry is part of accrual accounting, not something outside it.

---

### 3. **Maple Leaf Cement Factory Ltd. v Federal Board of Revenue — 2016 PTD 2074 [Lahore High Court]**

The Lahore High Court discussed the scheme of sections 32 and 34 and noted that under accrual accounting, income is recognized when due and expenditure is recognized when payable. The case also shows that accrual accounting under sections 32 and 34 must be read subject to specific provisions of the Ordinance, such as withholding-related provisions. citeturn927845search0

**How to use it:**  
This is a good supporting case for explaining the statutory scheme of tax accounting. It helps show that section 32 and section 34 form the core framework for determining when income or expense is recognized for tax purposes.

---

### 4. **WAPDA Bonds / Interest on Securities case — 2009 PTD 443 [High Court]**

In this case, the taxpayer had recognized accrued income in accounts under International Accounting Standards. However, the Court held that although income is chargeable on accrual basis, interest on time-bound securities did not accrue day-to-day where it was not due or receivable before the specified maturity/payment dates. citeturn670036view2

**How to use it:**  
This case is more of a caution. It does not weaken our argument, but it shows that an accounting entry alone is not conclusive for tax purposes. For tax accrual, there must be a legal right to receive income or an obligation to pay liability. So the correct argument should be: **IAS/IFRS recognition is relevant and part of accrual accounting, provided it satisfies section 34 and is not displaced by a specific tax provision.**

---

### 5. **2010 PTD 111 [ATIR Pakistan] — Gratuity / Ascertained Liability**

This Tribunal decision discusses the company’s obligation to maintain accounts on accrual basis under section 32 and the principle that expenditure is incurred when payable under section 34. It is useful for the concept of ascertained liability and consistency of tax treatment. citeturn200997search4

**How to use it:**  
This can be cited as a lower-level supporting authority where the issue involves provisions, gratuity, employee benefits, or other accrued liabilities. Since it is ATIR and not High Court, it should be used after stronger High Court cases.

---

### 6. **Recent SHC remand order referring to 2024 PTD 619**

There is also a recent Sindh High Court order where the issue of notional exchange loss, section 34(3), and deduction on accrual basis under sections 32 and 34 came up, and counsel relied on a judgment reported as **2024 PTD 619**. However, the High Court remanded the matter to the Tribunal for fresh adjudication because the Tribunal’s earlier order was not properly reasoned. citeturn670036view4

**How to use it:**  
This should not be treated as a final authority on the substantive issue, but it shows that the same controversy — whether accounting-based exchange loss can be allowed under accrual principles — continues to be litigated.

---

## Suggested legal proposition

You may frame the point as follows:

**“Under section 32(2) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, a company is mandatorily required to account for business income on accrual basis. Further, as recognized by the Lahore High Court in MCB Bank Ltd. v CIR, 2014 PTD 1874, the books of account of a company are required to be maintained in accordance with applicable International Accounting Standards. Therefore, IAS/IFRS-based recognition is not alien to accrual accounting; rather, it is the accounting framework through which accrual-based computation is ordinarily made by companies. However, such accounting treatment remains subject to the express provisions of the Ordinance, and may only be displaced where a specific tax provision provides otherwise.”**

For a stronger submission, I would rely on the authorities in this order:

**MCB Bank — 2014 PTD 1874 [LHC]**  
**Excell Pakistan — 2022 PTD 1535 [SHC]**  
**Maple Leaf Cement — 2016 PTD 2074 [LHC]**  
**2009 PTD 443 [High Court] as a cautionary distinction**  
**2010 PTD 111 [ATIR] as supporting authority**

Subject: Re: New Supply Model- Dealers (Retailer) & Shell Card

 

Hi Hashim Sb, hope you are doing well.

We have reviewed your email and the draft Shell Card Discount Funding Agreement shared with us. At this stage, the complete commercial, invoicing, accounting and customer-facing mechanics of the proposed model have not been fully explained in the email. Therefore, before we provide an opinion on the income tax and provincial sales tax implications, it would be appropriate to first confirm our understanding of the proposed arrangement based on the email and draft agreement.

As we understand, the existing arrangement for sale of petroleum products to the dealer/retailer will broadly continue in the same manner. WEPL will continue to supply petroleum products to the dealer/retailer under the retail supply arrangement at the applicable OGRA-notified price, and the existing mechanism for dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax on franchise fee, and withholding tax on dealer margin will continue to apply in the normal course.

The proposed change appears to be limited to Shell Card transactions. For such transactions, a separate / dedicated SOLD TO account will be maintained for the dealer/retailer. Shell Card-related volumes will be captured through this account, and based on those volumes, WEPL will debit a per-litre “Discount Contribution” to the dealer/retailer. The purpose of this contribution appears to be funding or supporting the discount which may be extended to Shell Card customers under WEPL’s Shell Card program.

Our further understanding is that this “Discount Contribution” is not intended to alter the primary sale price of petroleum products charged to the dealer/retailer, nor is it intended to change the OGRA price structure or the nature of the underlying sale of petroleum products. Instead, it appears to be a separate commercial recovery / adjustment between WEPL and the dealer/retailer, linked only with Shell Card volumes recorded under the dedicated SOLD TO account.

Based on the table shared in your email, the dealer’s existing economics remain the same up to the point of dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax and withholding tax. Under the proposed model, an additional Rs 0.40 per litre is being considered as a margin / administrative fee for the dealer/retailer for handling Shell Card-related transactions, while the balance amount is proposed to be recovered from the dealer/retailer through debit note or invoice. The recovered amount is intended to be used by WEPL for offering discounts to Shell Card customers.

Accordingly, the transaction appears to involve three separate components: first, the normal sale of petroleum products by WEPL to the dealer/retailer; second, the Shell Card discount program operated for customers; and third, the dealer/retailer’s contribution towards funding that discount through a per-litre recovery mechanism. The tax treatment may differ for each component depending on how the arrangement is documented, invoiced and recorded in the books.

Kindly confirm whether the above understanding is correct. In particular, please also confirm the following points so that we may provide our tax comments more precisely:   Yes, your understanding is correct

Whether the Shell Card customer discount will be offered by WEPL, the dealer/retailer, or jointly by both parties, only WEPL offer discount Shell Card Customer not jointly there is no concern of dealer what discount WEPL offering to Shell Card Customer.
Whether the discount will appear on the customer-facing invoice / receipt issued to Shell Card customers.   Yes, we are issuing manual invoices to Shell Card Customers with mention of discount on invoice where we are offering to discount and same declaring in Sales tax return
Whether the recovery from the dealer/retailer will be made through a debit note, tax invoice, adjustment note, or simple ledger adjustment. Recovery from Dealers will be through Debit Note (Post in customer account and will be adjusted with their payment for their next order)
Whether the PKR 0.40 per litre dealer administration margin will be separately credited / paid to the dealer or will only be treated as part of the dealer’s retained economics. No Separate credit / paid to dealer it will be part of original invoice when we will issue sales invoice to dealer at first stage
Whether the discount contribution recovered from the dealer/retailer will be booked by WEPL as income, recovery, reimbursement, reduction of discount cost, or any other accounting head. Yes, WEPL will be booked as Income and offset Shell Card Discount with same Account head (will reconfirm further form our business)
Once the above facts are confirmed, we will be in a position to advise on the applicable income tax and provincial sales tax implications, including the treatment of the dealer administration margin, discount contribution, franchise fee, withholding tax, invoicing documentation, and the most appropriate tax-compliant manner of implementing the proposed model.

I will treat the uploaded news compilation as the base material and select only the three items with the strongest public-interest angle, then convert them into ready-to-post social media copy.

Based on the uploaded compilation, these are the **three strongest public-interest posts**:

---

## **1. Budget 2026-27: Will Relief Come or Will the Same Taxpayers Pay More?**

The Federal Budget 2026-27 is expected to be presented on **June 10**, and the real question for the public is simple: will the budget bring meaningful relief, or will the burden again fall on salaried individuals, consumers, depositors, and documented businesses? The report highlights that Pakistan’s fiscal space is extremely tight, with debt servicing consuming a major portion of federal resources, while development spending, subsidies, pensions, defence, and social support still require funding. fileciteturn0file0

For ordinary citizens, this means the budget may directly affect electricity bills, fuel prices, withholding taxes, savings income, salaries, business costs, and inflation. If the government relies again on higher withholding taxes, non-filer penalties, indirect taxes, and utility-based collections, the documented and compliant segments will continue to carry a disproportionate burden.

The real test of this budget is whether it expands taxation towards under-taxed sectors such as real estate, agriculture, retail turnover, and undocumented services, instead of repeatedly increasing pressure on the same compliant taxpayers. A fair budget should not only collect more tax; it should collect tax from where real untaxed wealth exists.

---

## **2. Proposed Fixed Tax on Retailers: Simple Tax or Double Burden?**

A proposal is reportedly under consideration to impose an annual **fixed tax of Rs. 25,000 on retailers** under a simplified tax system. The business community has opposed the proposal on the ground that retailers are already subject to advance income tax under sections **236G and 236H of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**. The reported collection under these provisions is already significant, which raises an important question: is this a genuine simplification or an additional layer of taxation? fileciteturn0file0

For small shopkeepers, even a fixed amount can become a serious burden when combined with rent, electricity, inflation, supplier deductions, and reduced customer purchasing power. In practical terms, such taxes are often passed on to consumers through higher prices, which means the general public may ultimately bear the cost.

The better approach should be enforcement of existing tax laws, proper use of data, and targeted registration of genuinely untaxed businesses, rather than imposing another flat levy that may hit compliant and semi-compliant retailers without solving the real documentation problem.

---

## **3. FTO Ruling on Section 175C: Tax Recovery Cannot Be Based on Pressure**

The Federal Tax Ombudsman has reportedly ruled that collecting tax deposits during proceedings under **section 175C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**, without determining tax liability through proper legal process, amounts to maladministration. In the reported case, the taxpayer alleged that a large amount was recovered under coercive circumstances without any lawful assessment, speaking order, or determination of liability. fileciteturn0file0

This is an important taxpayer-rights development. Tax authorities have wide powers to seek information, conduct inquiry, and examine records, but recovery cannot be treated as lawful unless liability is properly created under the law. A taxpayer cannot be pushed into making “voluntary” payments merely because proceedings are ongoing.

For the general public and businesses, the message is clear: cooperation with tax authorities is important, but payments should be made against proper legal basis, documented demand, and lawful proceedings. Due process is not a technical formality; it is the foundation of fair taxation.

**Subject: Tax Year 2022 – Section 122(5A) Proceedings Concluded Without Any Disallowance / Addition**

Dear [Client Name],

We are pleased to inform you that, after rigorous efforts and detailed representations made before the Department, the proceedings initiated under section 122(5A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 for tax year 2022 have been concluded without any adverse addition or disallowance on the issues confronted in the show-cause notice. This is a positive outcome, particularly considering the quantum and technical nature of the matters raised during the proceedings.

By way of brief background, the Department had initiated proceedings through show-cause notice dated December 10, 2025 bearing IRIS barcode No. 1000002647932025, whereby various issues were confronted, including unrealized exchange losses, withholding tax compliance on royalty paid to Port Qasim Authority, reversal of diesel provision, fixed expenses, recovery of SSGC pipeline construction cost, finance cost allocation against FTR income, group taxation-related tax credit claim, and super tax under section 4C. In response, detailed replies were submitted vide our letters dated March 12, 2026 and April 23, 2026, along with supporting documentary evidence and issue-wise explanations. The matter was also discussed in detail with the Department through effective representation from both the client’s side and our side.

We are pleased to note that the Department has accepted the explanations on the substantive issues. No adverse inference has been drawn in respect of unrealized exchange loss on borrowings, unrealized exchange movements relating to lease receivables and liabilities, royalty payments to Port Qasim Authority, reversal of provision for diesel, recovery of SSGC pipeline construction cost, finance cost allegedly attributable to FTR income, and tax credit claimed in the consolidated group return. In relation to fixed expenses, the Department has also refrained from making any disallowance in the present proceedings, observing that the matter would require detailed examination beyond the scope of section 122(5A). Accordingly, the proceedings have effectively been closed with zero disallowance / addition on the issues originally confronted.

However, while reviewing the final computation forming part of the order, we have observed that there may be a computational / mathematical issue in the super tax working. The order reflects super tax under section 4C, which appears to have impacted the return-based refund position. On a preliminary review, the super tax computation and the resulting refund figure require further examination to determine whether any rectification or corrective action may be required. We are currently reviewing this aspect in detail and will update you separately once our analysis is completed.

At this stage, since no substantive disallowance or adverse addition has been made in the order, no immediate action appears to be required from your end. We will, however, continue to review the super tax computation and related refund position and will advise you on the appropriate way forward, if any corrective step is required.

Regards,  
[Your Name]

parts: I will treat this as an appellate argument issue under Sindh sales tax classification: first, the statutory classification framework; second, consistency/estoppel against shifting tariff heads; third, supporting case-law principles from tax/customs classification that can be borrowed for SRB proceedings.

Yes, this argument can be improved materially. I would build it on **three legal pillars**:

1. **Correct classification must be based on the real nature of the service.**  
2. **Specific tariff heading / sub-heading prevails over a broader, general, residual, or artificial heading.**  
3. **If the Department itself later accepts the same service as Business Support Service, that later treatment is strong evidence of the true character of the service; therefore, for earlier years, it cannot be forced into Franchise unless all ingredients of franchise are independently proved.**

### Additional supporting judgments / authorities

The most useful judgment for your exact point is the recent Sindh High Court decision in the **JS Global / stockbroker matter**. The Court discussed SRB’s attempt to tax IPO-related commission under tariff heading **9813.8100**, and noted that the Appellate Tribunal had rejected SRB’s position because the relevant sub-heading could not be expanded beyond the scope of the main tariff heading. The Court reproduced section 3 of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011, showing that taxable service must be a service listed in the Second Schedule. This helps your argument that SRB cannot select a different heading only to sustain taxability. citeturn642992view1turn642992view2

More importantly, in the same judgment, the Sindh High Court relied on **Citibank NA v Commissioner Inland Revenue, 2014 PTD 284**, and held that SRB tariff headings in the Second Schedule should be interpreted using the same classification discipline applied to Chapter 98. The Court specifically observed that the list of specific services in sub-headings cannot be rendered meaningless by relying on a broad main heading. citeturn642992view0turn642992view2

This is very strong for your case. The principle is that where the legislature has created a specific tariff structure, the Department cannot ignore the specific character of the service and bring it under a broader or different heading. Applied to your facts: once the service is properly understood as **Business Support**, it cannot be treated as **Franchise** merely because the Business Support entry was introduced later.

Another strong case is **Habib Asset Management Limited / Alfalah GHP Investment Management Limited**, where the Sindh High Court again relied on **Citibank NA**. The Court held that the Department’s argument that the description in the principal heading was operative could not be accepted, and that classification must be made by applying the relevant sub-headings. It further held that applying a broader approach contrary to the sub-heading structure was “not tenable.” citeturn509217view0turn642992view3

This can be used to say that **Franchise cannot be used as a catch-all entry**. If the service does not satisfy the legal ingredients of franchise, SRB cannot stretch the franchise heading merely because another more appropriate heading was not available in 2011–2012.

You can also rely on the Supreme Court’s classification principle in **Additional Collector of Customs v M/s K.S. Sulemanji Esmailji & Sons (Pvt.) Ltd., 2025 SCMR 121 / 2025 SCP 312**. Although it is a customs case, it is useful because the Supreme Court held that classification is a technical exercise governed by rules of interpretation, and that an “Others” heading is relevant only where the item is not more specifically covered elsewhere. citeturn166518view1

The Sindh High Court’s MDI classification judgment is also useful. In that case, the Court referred to the view that once goods were classifiable under a specified tariff heading by name, such classification could not be altered unless the tariff itself was appropriately amended. citeturn509217view1 This supports the broader proposition that a specific statutory classification should not be displaced by departmental re-characterization.

### Improved appeal argument

It may be respectfully submitted that the Department’s attempt to classify the Appellant’s services under “Franchise Services” for the tax periods 2011 and 2012 is legally misconceived. The true nature of the same services was subsequently accepted by SRB itself as falling within “Business Support Services” after the introduction of the relevant tariff heading in 2013. This subsequent treatment is not being relied upon to retrospectively apply the 2013 entry; rather, it is being relied upon as a clear admission and recognition of the true character of the activity. Once the activity is identified as business, technical, operational or commercial support, the same cannot be artificially re-described as franchise for an earlier period merely because the specific Business Support heading was not then available.

The classification of taxable services under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 is not a matter of administrative convenience. Section 3 requires that the service must be a taxable service listed in the Second Schedule. Therefore, the Department must bring the service strictly within the relevant taxable entry. The Sindh High Court has consistently held that tariff headings and sub-headings cannot be expanded beyond their proper scope and that the list of specific services cannot be rendered redundant by reliance on a broader or general description. Accordingly, where the service is more specifically and naturally classifiable as Business Support Service, it cannot be taxed under Franchise Service unless the Department independently establishes every legal ingredient of franchise.

The franchise entry has its own distinct legal character. A franchise ordinarily involves grant of a right, authority or licence by a franchisor to a franchisee to use a brand, trade name, trademark, service mark, business model, technical know-how or similar commercial/intellectual property right, usually against franchise fee, royalty or similar consideration. The mere provision of technical assistance, coordination, operational support, commercial facilitation or business support does not constitute franchise. Unless SRB establishes a franchisor-franchisee relationship and consideration for the use of franchise rights, the franchise heading cannot be invoked.

### Best concise formulation for hearing

The point may be argued in this manner:

**“The Department’s own subsequent classification of the same service under Business Support is the best evidence of the real nature of the activity. If the service is Business Support in character, it does not become Franchise merely because, in the earlier period, the Business Support heading had not yet been introduced. Absence of the correct taxable heading cannot justify artificial classification under another heading. A fiscal charge cannot be created by analogy, substitution or force-fitting. The Department must either show that the service squarely falls within Franchise, or the demand must fail.”**

### Authorities to cite in sequence

For the appeal note, I would cite them in this order:

**First:** IMS Health Pakistan Pvt. Ltd. — Business Support Services under 9805.9200; useful because it is directly on SRB Business Support classification.

**Second:** JS Global / stockbroker SRB judgment — taxable service must fall in Second Schedule; sub-heading cannot be expanded beyond main heading; SRB cannot force classification under another entry.

**Third:** Citibank NA v CIR, 2014 PTD 284 — specific sub-heading structure must be respected; broad principal heading cannot override specific services.

**Fourth:** Habib Asset Management / Alfalah GHP — reinforces Citibank and holds Department’s broader classification approach not tenable.

**Fifth:** K.S. Sulemanji Esmailji & Sons, 2025 SCMR 121 — “Others” / general headings cannot be used where a more specific classification exists.

This combination should make the argument much stronger: not just consistency, but **statutory classification discipline, strict construction of charging provisions, and specific-over-general tariff interpretation**.
