parts:
Based on the research, the strongest appellate argument should not be framed merely as “SRB once classified it under Business Support, therefore it can never change.” That argument alone may be treated as weak because classification for one period does not always operate as strict res judicata for another period. The stronger argument is this:

**Once SRB itself has accepted the true nature of the same service as “Business Support Service” under tariff heading 9805.9200 after its introduction in 2013, the Department cannot, for earlier tax periods, artificially re-characterize the very same activity as “Franchise Service” merely because Business Support was not then available in the tariff. If the proper tariff did not exist during 2011–2012, the Department cannot force-fit the service into another taxable heading unless all legal ingredients of that heading are independently satisfied.**

The Sindh Finance Act, 2013 introduced the definition of **“business support service”** as services provided in relation to business or commerce, including activities such as evaluation of prospective buyers, telemarketing/call centre facilities, accounting and transaction processing, processing of purchase orders and fulfilment services. This supports the factual point that the Legislature later created a specific classification for business/commercial support activities. citeturn425602search5turn425602search2 In **IMS Health Pakistan (Pvt.) Ltd. v Commissioner-II, Special Sales Tax Reference No. 02 of 2017**, the Sindh High Court directly dealt with tariff heading **9805.9200 – Business Support Service** and held that services involving collection/coding of data, transmission to overseas offices and coordination between the foreign principal and Pakistan customers were more appropriately classifiable as Business Support Services under heading 9805.9200. citeturn405166view0

The same judgment is very useful for your case because the Court treated the First Schedule as more general/descriptive and the Second Schedule as the list of taxable services on which tax is actually levied. The Court noted that the Second Schedule contains the services whereon tax is levied, and ultimately upheld 9805.9200 as the correct taxable heading for the relevant activity. citeturn405166view0 Therefore, for 2011–2012, if Business Support was not in the taxable schedule, the Department cannot simply say, “since this activity looks taxable in substance, let us tax it under franchise.” The charging provision must be applied to the **correct taxable service**, not to a substitute heading selected for revenue purposes.

A second strong authority is the ABAD / builders and developers judgment, **2018 PTD 1487 (Sindh High Court)**. The Court held that, for a transaction to be brought within Sindh sales tax, it must be established that there is a service within a **specific tariff heading** in the Second Schedule and that the dominant purpose of the transaction is the provision of that service. It also held that where an activity more naturally and properly falls within another tariff heading, it should not be taxed under a broader or artificial heading. citeturn967169view3turn967169view4 This principle is directly relevant: if the same activity naturally falls under Business Support, it cannot be pushed into Franchise merely because the Business Support heading was introduced later.

For strengthening the “specific heading prevails over general / residual / artificial heading” point, reliance may also be placed on customs classification principles. The Supreme Court in **2025 SCMR 121 / 2025 SCP 312** emphasized that an “Others” heading is relevant only where the goods are not covered more specifically under another sub-heading, and upheld classification based on the proper interpretative rules rather than a convenient alternative heading. citeturn927490view3 Although this is a customs classification case, the principle is persuasive for tariff-based fiscal statutes: classification must follow the true description of the activity and the most appropriate heading, not departmental convenience.

The franchise heading should be attacked independently. Franchise services generally involve an authority granted by a franchisor to a franchisee, normally involving use of brand, trademark, service mark, technical know-how, business model, system, royalty/franchise fee or similar consideration. SRB’s own materials and Rule 36 framework focus on franchise fee, royalty, technical fee or consideration under a franchise arrangement. citeturn146489search0turn146489search3 Therefore, unless the Department establishes a real franchisor–franchisee relationship, grant of right to use brand/IP/business system, and consideration relatable to such right, the service cannot be classified as franchise merely because some technical or commercial support was received.

**Suggested appellate argument paragraph:**

It is respectfully submitted that the Department has fundamentally erred in re-characterizing the Appellant’s services as “Franchise Services” for the tax periods 2011 and 2012. The very same nature of services was subsequently accepted/classified by the Department under tariff heading 9805.9200 as “Business Support Services” after introduction of the said heading through the Sindh Finance Act, 2013. This subsequent classification is a strong contemporaneous recognition of the true character of the activity, namely business/commercial support, coordination, technical and operational assistance, and not franchise. Once the nature of the service is so identified, the Department cannot, for an earlier period, artificially force the same activity into a different tariff heading merely because the appropriate heading was not available at the relevant time.

**Further paragraph on law:**

The scheme of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 requires that the taxable service must fall within a specific taxable entry of the Second Schedule. The Sindh High Court has held that the First Schedule is descriptive in nature whereas the Second Schedule contains the services on which tax is levied, and that sales tax can be charged only on the value of the taxable service listed in the Schedule. In fiscal classification, the true nature and dominant character of the activity must be examined, and where the activity more naturally and properly falls within one tariff heading, it cannot be brought to tax under another heading by implication, analogy or administrative convenience.

**Further paragraph against franchise classification:**

The Department has not discharged the burden of establishing the essential ingredients of “Franchise Services”. There is no finding that the Appellant was granted any authority by a franchisor to operate under a brand, trademark, service mark, trade name, business system or franchise model. There is also no finding that the consideration was paid for use of any franchise right. The mere provision of technical, operational or commercial support cannot be equated with franchise. Such services, if taxable after their specific introduction, may fall under Business Support Services; however, in the absence of that tariff heading during the relevant tax periods, the Department cannot create a charge by re-labelling the same activity as franchise.

**Best conclusion for appeal:**

Accordingly, the impugned demand is based on a misclassification. The Department’s own later treatment confirms that the true nature of the activity is Business Support Service and not Franchise Service. For the periods prior to the introduction of Business Support Services as a taxable heading, no charge could be created by stretching the franchise entry beyond its legal scope. The demand is therefore liable to be deleted on the ground of incorrect classification, absence of charging entry, and failure to establish the essential ingredients of franchise services.

parts:
The following additional paragraphs may be inserted in the appeal arguments, preferably under the issue relating to **Technical Service Fee / Franchise classification**:

It is also pertinent to mention that the definition of “franchise” under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services law is substantially aligned with, and in material terms borrowed from, the definition earlier contained under the federal sales tax / federal excise regime. Therefore, the interpretation of the expression “franchise” already examined in the appellant’s own federal proceedings carries strong persuasive value for the present proceedings. The same technical service arrangement was previously sought to be treated by the federal tax authorities as a franchise arrangement; however, after examining the relevant agreements, the nature of services, the commercial substance of the arrangement and the legal ingredients of “franchise”, the learned Appellate Tribunal decided the matter in favour of the appellant and held that the said technical service fee could not be classified as franchise.

The said appellate findings are directly relevant because the controversy in the present case is not merely one of rate or computation, but of the very character of the service. The technical service arrangement did not confer upon the appellant any franchise right in the legal sense. It was not an arrangement whereby the appellant was granted a right to carry on business as a franchisee under a franchisor-controlled business model against payment of franchise consideration. Rather, the arrangement was in the nature of technical assistance, business support, know-how, advice, operational guidance and related support services. These features may, at best, fall within a technical / business support framework, but they do not satisfy the essential legal requirements of a franchise arrangement.

Copies of the favourable orders passed in the appellant’s own cases are being furnished along with the present submissions for ready reference and verification. It is further understood from the appellant’s record that the department did not assail the said findings before the Hon’ble High Court; therefore, the issue stood settled at the federal level in the appellant’s own case. In these circumstances, and particularly where the statutory definition under the Sindh regime is materially similar, the same technical service fee cannot be re-characterized as franchise merely to sustain a demand for the earlier period. Any such approach would be contrary to the settled treatment of the same arrangement, the principle of consistency, and the legal requirement that a taxable entry must be applied strictly on the basis of the actual nature of the service rather than on assumptions or broad commercial association with the Shell brand.

citation.snippet: ٹھیک ہے میل، بات کریں، ہاں حسن صاحب، ہوپ یو ڈوئنگ ویل، اچھا جیسے آپ کو ایز یو ایئر کہ ہماری ایک اپیل ایس آر بی کمشنر اپیلز ان کے پاس پینڈنگ ہے فار ٹیکس پیریڈ جولائی 2011 تا دسمبر 2012، ٹھیک ہے، جس کا جو پرنسپل ڈیمانڈ کریئیٹڈ ہے وہ 287 ملین کے ہے۔ اچھا اب آپ اس میں جو ہے نا جو تین میٹرز اس نے پلیج کیے تھے ایک لائسنس فیس، لوکل لائسنس فیس کا ٹریڈ مارک مینفیسٹریشن تھا اور فیفو ٹیکنکل تھا، اچھا جو فیفو ٹیکنکل کا پوائنٹ ہے وہ تو لیگل پوائنٹ ہے اس میں تو ہمیں کوئی ڈیٹیل چاہیے نہیں وہ تو جو ہے نا وہ بزنس سپورٹ کی ٹائرفیلنگ کے بیسس پر لڑیں گے، باقی جو لوکل فرنچائز اور ٹریڈ مارک مینفیسٹریشن کے حوالے سے تھا۔ تو اوریجنل جو ایس ایس ڈی اس نے الینج کیا تھا وہ لوکل فرنچائز میں نائنٹی نائن ملین کیا تھا اور ٹریڈ مارک میں تھرٹی نائن کیا تھا جس میں سے اس نے نائنٹی نائن میں سے 28 ملین کہاں سے آلریڈی پیمنٹ ایس ایس ڈی کی آئی ہوئی ہے اور ٹریڈ مارک مینفیسٹریشن میں تھرٹی نائن میں سے 9 ملین اس نے کہاں آئی ہے۔ تو ریمننگ سیونٹی ون لوکل فرنچائز میں اور ٹریڈ مارک میں 29 ملین آؤٹ اسٹینڈنگ تھا وچ از اوبویسلی وہ آپ جانس کو اپوشن کیا ہوگا تو ہمیں ہمیں ہم نے اس اپیل کی جو ہے نا اسٹے ایپلیکیشن آج فائل کر دی ہے ٹھیک ہے جو فور کمیشنر کی اپیلز کو ہمارے پاس کمیشنر کی طرف سے کال آئی تھی کہ آپ اس کا جو ہے نا اسٹے پرسو کر لیں کیونکہ اس کی وہاں پہ کیونکہ مے اور جون ہے تو وہاں پہ پریشر ہے ریوری کے حوالے سے تو ہم نے اس کے کل ہمارے پاس کال آئی تھی اور ہم نے آج اس کی ایپلیکیشن فائل کر دی تو مین ویل آپ سے ریکویسٹ یہ ہے کہ لوکل فرنچائز جو سیونٹی ون ملین نظر آ رہے اور ٹریڈ مارک جو 29 ملین آؤٹ اسٹینڈنگ نظر آ رہا ہے وچ از اوبویسلی آپ نے فیڈرل میں یا پروونسز میں اس کا ڈسچارج کیا ہوگا تو ہمیں اس کا سپورٹنگ دینا ہے تاکہ ہم اس کو کنکلوڈ کروا سکیں تو فار یور ریفرینس ای میل پہ ہی میں بریک ڈاؤن بھی جو ہے نیچے بریک ڈاؤن بھی دے رہا ہوں ڈیمانڈ کا ٹھیک ہے یہ ذرا جو ہے نا ای میل مجھے اپلوڈ کر دینا

Hi Hashim Sb, hope you are doing well.

We have reviewed your email and the draft Shell Card Discount Funding Agreement shared with us. At this stage, the complete commercial, invoicing, accounting and customer-facing mechanics of the proposed model have not been fully explained in the email. Therefore, before we provide an opinion on the income tax and provincial sales tax implications, it would be appropriate to first confirm our understanding of the proposed arrangement based on the email and draft agreement.

As we understand, the existing arrangement for sale of petroleum products to the dealer/retailer will broadly continue in the same manner. WEPL will continue to supply petroleum products to the dealer/retailer under the retail supply arrangement at the applicable OGRA-notified price, and the existing mechanism for dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax on franchise fee, and withholding tax on dealer margin will continue to apply in the normal course.

The proposed change appears to be limited to Shell Card transactions. For such transactions, a separate / dedicated SOLD TO account will be maintained for the dealer/retailer. Shell Card-related volumes will be captured through this account, and based on those volumes, WEPL will debit a per-litre “Discount Contribution” to the dealer/retailer. The purpose of this contribution appears to be funding or supporting the discount which may be extended to Shell Card customers under WEPL’s Shell Card program.

Our further understanding is that this “Discount Contribution” is not intended to alter the primary sale price of petroleum products charged to the dealer/retailer, nor is it intended to change the OGRA price structure or the nature of the underlying sale of petroleum products. Instead, it appears to be a separate commercial recovery / adjustment between WEPL and the dealer/retailer, linked only with Shell Card volumes recorded under the dedicated SOLD TO account.

Based on the table shared in your email, the dealer’s existing economics remain the same up to the point of dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax and withholding tax. Under the proposed model, an additional Rs 0.40 per litre is being considered as a margin / administrative fee for the dealer/retailer for handling Shell Card-related transactions, while the balance amount is proposed to be recovered from the dealer/retailer through debit note or invoice. The recovered amount is intended to be used by WEPL for offering discounts to Shell Card customers.

Accordingly, the transaction appears to involve three separate components: first, the normal sale of petroleum products by WEPL to the dealer/retailer; second, the Shell Card discount program operated for customers; and third, the dealer/retailer’s contribution towards funding that discount through a per-litre recovery mechanism. The tax treatment may differ for each component depending on how the arrangement is documented, invoiced and recorded in the books.

Kindly confirm whether the above understanding is correct. In particular, please also confirm the following points so that we may provide our tax comments more precisely:   Yes, your understanding is correct

Whether the Shell Card customer discount will be offered by WEPL, the dealer/retailer, or jointly by both parties, only WEPL offer discount Shell Card Customer not jointly there is no concern of dealer what discount WEPL offering to Shell Card Customer.
Whether the discount will appear on the customer-facing invoice / receipt issued to Shell Card customers.   Yes, we are issuing manual invoices to Shell Card Customers with mention of discount on invoice where we are offering to discount and same declaring in Sales tax return
Whether the recovery from the dealer/retailer will be made through a debit note, tax invoice, adjustment note, or simple ledger adjustment. Recovery from Dealers will be through Debit Note (Post in customer account and will be adjusted with their payment for their next order)
Whether the PKR 0.40 per litre dealer administration margin will be separately credited / paid to the dealer or will only be treated as part of the dealer’s retained economics. No Separate credit / paid to dealer it will be part of original invoice when we will issue sales invoice to dealer at first stage
Whether the discount contribution recovered from the dealer/retailer will be booked by WEPL as income, recovery, reimbursement, reduction of discount cost, or any other accounting head. Yes, WEPL will be booked as Income and offset Shell Card Discount with same Account head (will reconfirm further form our business)
Once the above facts are confirmed, we will be in a position to advise on the applicable income tax and provincial sales tax implications, including the treatment of the dealer administration margin, discount contribution, franchise fee, withholding tax, invoicing documentation, and the most appropriate tax-compliant manner of implementing the proposed model.

Please read the attached recent and earlier notice from SRB. As a tax consultant, kindly prepare a thorough response on the client's behalf. Please take contentions from the petition filed before the Sindh High Court and advice from lawyers. Please also emphasis the point that our client duly included the royalty from PQA in the value of taxable services, in other words, the Sindh Sales Tax charged on gross revenue which includes royalty from PQA. Hence, your earlier contention is grossly that our client didn't pay the Sindh sales tax on royalty pay to PQA. 

Furthermore, the earlier notice imposed a tax liability under section 18 of the Sindh Sales Tax Act on Services, 2011, without acknowledging that the burden of proof lies with the tax department before they can make anyone jointly and severally liable for the payment of any unpaid tax amount. Only stating the facts without providing any evidence is merely an assumption and presumption, and it is against the spirit of Section 18 of the Sindh Sales Tax Act on Services, 2011. However, in the instant case, our client duly charged and subsequently deposited the Sindh sales tax on the gross amount charged to them, which includes the royalty payment to PQA.
Furthermore, the tax period in question relates to July 2016 to February 2018, despite the judgment of the Honorable High Court of Sindh at Karachi reported as 2021 PTD 484, which held that, due to the insertion of Section 13(3) of the Act through the Finance Act, 2019, no liability could be imposed on a withholding agent for any period prior to 01.07.2019.

Subject: Re: New Supply Model- Dealers (Retailer) & Shell Card

 

Hi Hashim Sb, hope you are doing well.

We have reviewed your email and the draft Shell Card Discount Funding Agreement shared with us. At this stage, the complete commercial, invoicing, accounting and customer-facing mechanics of the proposed model have not been fully explained in the email. Therefore, before we provide an opinion on the income tax and provincial sales tax implications, it would be appropriate to first confirm our understanding of the proposed arrangement based on the email and draft agreement.

As we understand, the existing arrangement for sale of petroleum products to the dealer/retailer will broadly continue in the same manner. WEPL will continue to supply petroleum products to the dealer/retailer under the retail supply arrangement at the applicable OGRA-notified price, and the existing mechanism for dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax on franchise fee, and withholding tax on dealer margin will continue to apply in the normal course.

The proposed change appears to be limited to Shell Card transactions. For such transactions, a separate / dedicated SOLD TO account will be maintained for the dealer/retailer. Shell Card-related volumes will be captured through this account, and based on those volumes, WEPL will debit a per-litre “Discount Contribution” to the dealer/retailer. The purpose of this contribution appears to be funding or supporting the discount which may be extended to Shell Card customers under WEPL’s Shell Card program.

Our further understanding is that this “Discount Contribution” is not intended to alter the primary sale price of petroleum products charged to the dealer/retailer, nor is it intended to change the OGRA price structure or the nature of the underlying sale of petroleum products. Instead, it appears to be a separate commercial recovery / adjustment between WEPL and the dealer/retailer, linked only with Shell Card volumes recorded under the dedicated SOLD TO account.

Based on the table shared in your email, the dealer’s existing economics remain the same up to the point of dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax and withholding tax. Under the proposed model, an additional Rs 0.40 per litre is being considered as a margin / administrative fee for the dealer/retailer for handling Shell Card-related transactions, while the balance amount is proposed to be recovered from the dealer/retailer through debit note or invoice. The recovered amount is intended to be used by WEPL for offering discounts to Shell Card customers.

Accordingly, the transaction appears to involve three separate components: first, the normal sale of petroleum products by WEPL to the dealer/retailer; second, the Shell Card discount program operated for customers; and third, the dealer/retailer’s contribution towards funding that discount through a per-litre recovery mechanism. The tax treatment may differ for each component depending on how the arrangement is documented, invoiced and recorded in the books.

Kindly confirm whether the above understanding is correct. In particular, please also confirm the following points so that we may provide our tax comments more precisely:   Yes, your understanding is correct

Whether the Shell Card customer discount will be offered by WEPL, the dealer/retailer, or jointly by both parties, only WEPL offer discount Shell Card Customer not jointly there is no concern of dealer what discount WEPL offering to Shell Card Customer.
Whether the discount will appear on the customer-facing invoice / receipt issued to Shell Card customers.   Yes, we are issuing manual invoices to Shell Card Customers with mention of discount on invoice where we are offering to discount and same declaring in Sales tax return
Whether the recovery from the dealer/retailer will be made through a debit note, tax invoice, adjustment note, or simple ledger adjustment. Recovery from Dealers will be through Debit Note (Post in customer account and will be adjusted with their payment for their next order)
Whether the PKR 0.40 per litre dealer administration margin will be separately credited / paid to the dealer or will only be treated as part of the dealer’s retained economics. No Separate credit / paid to dealer it will be part of original invoice when we will issue sales invoice to dealer at first stage
Whether the discount contribution recovered from the dealer/retailer will be booked by WEPL as income, recovery, reimbursement, reduction of discount cost, or any other accounting head. Yes, WEPL will be booked as Income and offset Shell Card Discount with same Account head (will reconfirm further form our business)
Once the above facts are confirmed, we will be in a position to advise on the applicable income tax and provincial sales tax implications, including the treatment of the dealer administration margin, discount contribution, franchise fee, withholding tax, invoicing documentation, and the most appropriate tax-compliant manner of implementing the proposed model.

Please read the attached recent and earlier notice from SRB. As a tax consultant, kindly prepare a thorough response on the client's behalf. Please take contentions from the petition filed before the Sindh High Court and advice from lawyers. Please also emphasis the point that our client duly included the royalty from PQA in the value of taxable services, in other words, the Sindh Sales Tax charged on gross revenue which includes royalty from PQA. Hence, your earlier contention is grossly that our client didn't pay the Sindh sales tax on royalty pay to PQA. 

Furthermore, the earlier notice imposed a tax liability under section 18 of the Sindh Sales Tax Act on Services, 2011, without acknowledging that the burden of proof lies with the tax department before they can make anyone jointly and severally liable for the payment of any unpaid tax amount. Only stating the facts without providing any evidence is merely an assumption and presumption, and it is against the spirit of Section 18 of the Sindh Sales Tax Act on Services, 2011. However, in the instant case, our client duly charged and subsequently deposited the Sindh sales tax on the gross amount charged to them, which includes the royalty payment to PQA.
Furthermore, the tax period in question relates to July 2016 to February 2018, despite the judgment of the Honorable High Court of Sindh at Karachi reported as 2021 PTD 484, which held that, due to the insertion of Section 13(3) of the Act through the Finance Act, 2019, no liability could be imposed on a withholding agent for any period prior to 01.07.2019.

citation.snippet: ٹھیک ہے میل، بات کریں، ہاں حسن صاحب، ہوپ یو ڈوئنگ ویل، اچھا جیسے آپ کو ایز یو ایئر کہ ہماری ایک اپیل ایس آر بی کمشنر اپیلز ان کے پاس پینڈنگ ہے فار ٹیکس پیریڈ جولائی 2011 تا دسمبر 2012، ٹھیک ہے، جس کا جو پرنسپل ڈیمانڈ کریئیٹڈ ہے وہ 287 ملین کے ہے۔ اچھا اب آپ اس میں جو ہے نا جو تین میٹرز اس نے پلیج کیے تھے ایک لائسنس فیس، لوکل لائسنس فیس کا ٹریڈ مارک مینفیسٹریشن تھا اور فیفو ٹیکنکل تھا، اچھا جو فیفو ٹیکنکل کا پوائنٹ ہے وہ تو لیگل پوائنٹ ہے اس میں تو ہمیں کوئی ڈیٹیل چاہیے نہیں وہ تو جو ہے نا وہ بزنس سپورٹ کی ٹائرفیلنگ کے بیسس پر لڑیں گے، باقی جو لوکل فرنچائز اور ٹریڈ مارک مینفیسٹریشن کے حوالے سے تھا۔ تو اوریجنل جو ایس ایس ڈی اس نے الینج کیا تھا وہ لوکل فرنچائز میں نائنٹی نائن ملین کیا تھا اور ٹریڈ مارک میں تھرٹی نائن کیا تھا جس میں سے اس نے نائنٹی نائن میں سے 28 ملین کہاں سے آلریڈی پیمنٹ ایس ایس ڈی کی آئی ہوئی ہے اور ٹریڈ مارک مینفیسٹریشن میں تھرٹی نائن میں سے 9 ملین اس نے کہاں آئی ہے۔ تو ریمننگ سیونٹی ون لوکل فرنچائز میں اور ٹریڈ مارک میں 29 ملین آؤٹ اسٹینڈنگ تھا وچ از اوبویسلی وہ آپ جانس کو اپوشن کیا ہوگا تو ہمیں ہمیں ہم نے اس اپیل کی جو ہے نا اسٹے ایپلیکیشن آج فائل کر دی ہے ٹھیک ہے جو فور کمیشنر کی اپیلز کو ہمارے پاس کمیشنر کی طرف سے کال آئی تھی کہ آپ اس کا جو ہے نا اسٹے پرسو کر لیں کیونکہ اس کی وہاں پہ کیونکہ مے اور جون ہے تو وہاں پہ پریشر ہے ریوری کے حوالے سے تو ہم نے اس کے کل ہمارے پاس کال آئی تھی اور ہم نے آج اس کی ایپلیکیشن فائل کر دی تو مین ویل آپ سے ریکویسٹ یہ ہے کہ لوکل فرنچائز جو سیونٹی ون ملین نظر آ رہے اور ٹریڈ مارک جو 29 ملین آؤٹ اسٹینڈنگ نظر آ رہا ہے وچ از اوبویسلی آپ نے فیڈرل میں یا پروونسز میں اس کا ڈسچارج کیا ہوگا تو ہمیں اس کا سپورٹنگ دینا ہے تاکہ ہم اس کو کنکلوڈ کروا سکیں تو فار یور ریفرینس ای میل پہ ہی میں بریک ڈاؤن بھی جو ہے نیچے بریک ڈاؤن بھی دے رہا ہوں ڈیمانڈ کا ٹھیک ہے یہ ذرا جو ہے نا ای میل مجھے اپلوڈ کر دینا

Subject: Re: New Supply Model- Dealers (Retailer) & Shell Card

 

Hi Hashim Sb, hope you are doing well.

We have reviewed your email and the draft Shell Card Discount Funding Agreement shared with us. At this stage, the complete commercial, invoicing, accounting and customer-facing mechanics of the proposed model have not been fully explained in the email. Therefore, before we provide an opinion on the income tax and provincial sales tax implications, it would be appropriate to first confirm our understanding of the proposed arrangement based on the email and draft agreement.

As we understand, the existing arrangement for sale of petroleum products to the dealer/retailer will broadly continue in the same manner. WEPL will continue to supply petroleum products to the dealer/retailer under the retail supply arrangement at the applicable OGRA-notified price, and the existing mechanism for dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax on franchise fee, and withholding tax on dealer margin will continue to apply in the normal course.

The proposed change appears to be limited to Shell Card transactions. For such transactions, a separate / dedicated SOLD TO account will be maintained for the dealer/retailer. Shell Card-related volumes will be captured through this account, and based on those volumes, WEPL will debit a per-litre “Discount Contribution” to the dealer/retailer. The purpose of this contribution appears to be funding or supporting the discount which may be extended to Shell Card customers under WEPL’s Shell Card program.

Our further understanding is that this “Discount Contribution” is not intended to alter the primary sale price of petroleum products charged to the dealer/retailer, nor is it intended to change the OGRA price structure or the nature of the underlying sale of petroleum products. Instead, it appears to be a separate commercial recovery / adjustment between WEPL and the dealer/retailer, linked only with Shell Card volumes recorded under the dedicated SOLD TO account.

Based on the table shared in your email, the dealer’s existing economics remain the same up to the point of dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax and withholding tax. Under the proposed model, an additional Rs 0.40 per litre is being considered as a margin / administrative fee for the dealer/retailer for handling Shell Card-related transactions, while the balance amount is proposed to be recovered from the dealer/retailer through debit note or invoice. The recovered amount is intended to be used by WEPL for offering discounts to Shell Card customers.

Accordingly, the transaction appears to involve three separate components: first, the normal sale of petroleum products by WEPL to the dealer/retailer; second, the Shell Card discount program operated for customers; and third, the dealer/retailer’s contribution towards funding that discount through a per-litre recovery mechanism. The tax treatment may differ for each component depending on how the arrangement is documented, invoiced and recorded in the books.

Kindly confirm whether the above understanding is correct. In particular, please also confirm the following points so that we may provide our tax comments more precisely:   Yes, your understanding is correct

Whether the Shell Card customer discount will be offered by WEPL, the dealer/retailer, or jointly by both parties, only WEPL offer discount Shell Card Customer not jointly there is no concern of dealer what discount WEPL offering to Shell Card Customer.
Whether the discount will appear on the customer-facing invoice / receipt issued to Shell Card customers.   Yes, we are issuing manual invoices to Shell Card Customers with mention of discount on invoice where we are offering to discount and same declaring in Sales tax return
Whether the recovery from the dealer/retailer will be made through a debit note, tax invoice, adjustment note, or simple ledger adjustment. Recovery from Dealers will be through Debit Note (Post in customer account and will be adjusted with their payment for their next order)

Based on the clauses reproduced in the SRB order, my independent view is that the **Technical Service Agreement should not be treated as a franchise agreement**. At best, it is a **technical assistance / business support / know-how support arrangement**. The order relies on selected clauses relating to confidentiality, technical information, advice, know-how, patents and intellectual property, but those clauses do not, by themselves, satisfy the legal ingredients of “franchise”. They are more consistent with a controlled technical support arrangement where Shell retains ownership of its intellectual property and only permits limited internal use of technical information for operational purposes. fileciteturn3file0

For a contract to qualify as a **franchise**, the essential requirement is that there must be a positive commercial authority granted by a franchisor to a franchisee to carry on business, sell goods, provide services, undertake a process, or operate under a trade name, brand, logo, service mark, system or business format identified with the franchisor, against consideration. Merely providing technical advice, operational guidance, know-how, expertise, confidential information or access to technical material does not automatically create a franchise. The phrase “technical fee” appearing in the definition cannot be read in isolation; it becomes relevant only where the technical fee is paid **as consideration for the grant of a franchise right**. If the payment is for technical support only, it does not convert the arrangement into franchise.

The clauses reproduced in the order actually support the appellant’s case. The agreement states that copyright, property and industrial property rights in confidential material supplied by Shell remain vested in Shell. It further refers to limited licences in relation to patents, industrial rights, processes, inventions, devices, techniques and applications. These are restrictive and protective clauses, not franchise-granting clauses. A franchise normally allows the franchisee to commercially exploit the franchisor’s brand / system in the market. Here, the reproduced clauses show that Shell’s intellectual property remains protected, controlled and retained by Shell, and the appellant is only allowed to use technical information for limited operational purposes. fileciteturn3file0

The officer’s reasoning appears to conflate three different streams: the **retail franchise / dealer licence arrangement**, the **trademark and manifestation licence arrangement**, and the **technical service arrangement**. This is a fundamental classification error. A technical support agreement cannot be taxed as franchise merely because the wider Shell business also involves brand, retail network and trademark arrangements. Each agreement must be classified on its own legal character. If the right to use trade marks, brand manifestations or retail identity is governed by separate agreements, then the technical service agreement cannot be artificially merged with those agreements to create a franchise classification.

A particularly important point is that the agreement, as reproduced, refers to technical advice, know-how, expertise and information which Shell had available and could provide within the relevant chargeable or non-chargeable time. This is the language of **technical support / advisory assistance**, not the language of a franchise grant. The dominant purpose of the arrangement appears to be to assist the appellant in improving or supporting its operations through technical input. It does not appear to grant the appellant any independent market-facing right to operate as a franchisee, appoint sub-franchisees, exploit a business format, sell services under a franchisor-controlled model, or hold itself out as having received franchise rights under the Technical Service Agreement.

Therefore, the better legal position is that this agreement is **not a franchise agreement** for the following reasons: first, it does not grant a positive commercial right to carry on business as a franchisee; second, the technical information is provided for internal operational support, not for market-facing exploitation of Shell’s brand; third, the intellectual property remains vested in Shell and is not transferred or commercially assigned to the appellant; fourth, the limited use of technical information / know-how is ancillary to service support and not the core subject of a franchise; fifth, the agreement does not appear to establish a franchisor-franchisee business model, retail network arrangement or customer-facing brand exploitation mechanism; and sixth, SRB’s own later treatment of similar technical support services as business support services strengthens the position that the arrangement is not franchise in substance.

If SRB were to allege that it is a franchise agreement, it would have to establish much more than the existence of technical know-how or confidential information. It would need to demonstrate that the agreement granted the appellant a legally enforceable commercial right to conduct business under Shell’s brand / system, that such right was the core subject of the agreement, that the appellant was authorized to commercially exploit the Shell trade name, logo, service mark, business format or process through that agreement, and that the consideration was paid for that franchise right. On the clauses presently reproduced in the order, those ingredients are not sufficiently established.

For appeal purposes, the conclusion can be framed as follows:

“On an independent examination of the clauses of the Technical Service Agreement relied upon in the impugned order, it is evident that the agreement is not in the nature of a franchise arrangement. The agreement merely provides for technical assistance, know-how, advice, expertise, confidential information and limited operational support, while the ownership of intellectual property, patents and confidential material remains vested in Shell. Such restrictive and protective clauses cannot be equated with the grant of a commercial franchise right. The impugned order has erroneously presumed that any arrangement involving technical information, know-how or Shell group support automatically falls within the ambit of franchise. This approach is legally misconceived. The taxable entry of franchise requires a positive grant of a right to operate, sell, trade, provide services or undertake a process under the franchisor’s brand, system or commercial identity. No such right is granted under the Technical Service Agreement. The agreement is, in substance, a technical / business support arrangement and not a franchise agreement.”

The impugned order proceeds on the assumption that the entire local franchise / license fee is liable to Sindh sales tax merely because the appellant is registered in Sindh and the agreements relate to Shell branded retail operations. This approach is materially defective because the fee was not wholly relatable to Sindh. The appellant’s retail network is spread across Pakistan, and the local franchise / license fee charged from dealers was linked with their respective business locations and sales activity. Therefore, the taxable value, if any, had to be attributed with reference to the relevant jurisdiction and not treated as an entire Sindh-based transaction.
It is pertinent to mention here that the appellant has already discharged tax on the relevant franchise / license fee by apportioning the value among SRB, FBR and other provincial revenue authorities, including PRA, on the basis of revenue / place of business / jurisdictional attribution. For the sake of brevity, the said reconciliation is enclosed as Annexure ‘A’, clearly demonstrate the province-wise bifurcation, the tax deposited with each authority, and the corresponding returns. The impugned order itself acknowledges SRB payments made by the appellant in relation to franchise services, but rejects the appellant’s position mainly on the ground that evidence of payment before other authorities was not adequately produced at the adjudication stage. 
It is also pertinent to mention here that the statement filed by the Chairman SRB before the Sindh High Court is very important for this issue. In that statement, SRB stated that, pending finalization of harmonized place of supply rules pursuant to the National Tax Council framework, where the taxpayer satisfies SRB through proof and verification that sales tax on franchise services has been paid to any other sales tax authority, SRB shall not charge Sindh sales tax from such taxpayer. This is a direct departmental position before the High Court in the appellant’s own matter and should be specifically relied upon.
Keeping in view of the above, appellant is not seeking exemption from tax; rather, the appellant is seeking proper recognition of tax already discharged in the correct jurisdiction. Once the reconciliation, returns and CPRs demonstrate that the relevant non-Sindh portion has already been subjected to tax before the appropriate authority, SRB cannot again assess Sindh sales tax on the same value. Such double taxation would be contrary to the constitutional scheme under which sales tax on services is a provincial levy and must remain confined to the province having the taxing nexus.
Please only read the attached order.

Below are detailed appeal argument notes on all three avenues. I have kept the reconciliation aspect in narrative form, not in tabular form, so that it can be incorporated in the appeal note together with annexures.

## 1. Local Franchise / Retail Licence Fee — primary argument is reconciliation, provincial attribution and credit of tax already paid

The impugned order proceeds on the assumption that the entire local franchise / licence fee is liable to Sindh sales tax merely because the appellant is registered in Sindh and the agreements relate to Shell branded retail operations. This approach is materially defective because the fee was not wholly relatable to Sindh. The appellant’s retail network is spread across Pakistan, and the licence / franchise fee charged from dealers was linked with their respective business locations and sales activity. Therefore, the taxable value, if any, had to be attributed with reference to the relevant jurisdiction and not treated as an entire Sindh-based transaction.

The strongest factual response should be that the appellant has already discharged tax on the relevant franchise / licence fee by apportioning the value among SRB, FBR and other provincial revenue authorities, including PRA, on the basis of revenue / place of business / jurisdictional attribution. The reconciliation to be enclosed with the appeal should clearly demonstrate the dealer-wise / province-wise bifurcation, the tax deposited with each authority, and the corresponding returns / CPRs. The impugned order itself acknowledges SRB payments made by the appellant in relation to franchise services, but rejects the appellant’s position mainly on the ground that evidence of payment before other authorities was not adequately produced at the adjudication stage. That finding can be directly met by placing the complete reconciliation, returns, CPRs and supporting documents before the Commissioner (Appeals). fileciteturn0file0

The statement filed by the Chairman SRB before the Sindh High Court is very important for this issue. In that statement, SRB stated that, pending finalization of harmonized place-of-supply rules pursuant to the National Tax Council framework, where the taxpayer satisfies SRB through proof and verification that sales tax on franchise services has been paid to any other sales tax authority, SRB shall not charge Sindh sales tax from such taxpayer. This is a direct departmental position before the High Court in the appellant’s own matter and should be specifically relied upon. fileciteturn1file0

Accordingly, the appeal argument should be framed as follows: the appellant is not seeking exemption from tax; rather, the appellant is seeking proper recognition of tax already discharged in the correct jurisdiction. Once the reconciliation, returns and CPRs demonstrate that the relevant non-Sindh portion has already been subjected to tax before the appropriate authority, SRB cannot again assess Sindh sales tax on the same value. Such double taxation would be contrary to the constitutional scheme under which sales tax on services is a provincial levy and must remain confined to the province having the taxing nexus.

The finding that the appellant “failed to provide evidence” should be attacked as a curable factual finding, not a final legal determination. The Commissioner (Appeals) may be requested to admit the reconciliation and supporting documents, verify the same, and delete the demand to the extent already discharged before SRB / FBR / PRA / other authorities. The Chairman SRB’s statement should also be used to show that the proper course is verification and credit, not duplication of demand.

## 2. Trademark and Manifestation Licence Fee — primary argument is that Sindh cannot tax the all-Pakistan royalty / licence base

For the trademark and manifestation licence fee, the order records that the appellant paid royalty / licence fee to Shell Brands International AG on the basis of net sales proceeds across Pakistan. The officer then treats the service as received in Sindh, substantially relying on the fact that petroleum products were imported through Karachi / Port Qasim and that supplies were also moved from Sindh to other provinces. This reasoning is weak because the taxable service is not “import of petroleum products” nor “movement of goods from Sindh”; the subject matter is the right to use trademarks / manifestations / brand-related intellectual property, and the value of that right is linked with sales made across Pakistan.

The appeal should emphasize that the place of import or initial physical entry of goods cannot determine the situs of a trademark / manifestation licence. The licence is commercially exploited where branded goods are sold, marketed and distributed. If the royalty / licence fee is computed with reference to net sales proceeds throughout Pakistan, then only the Sindh-attributable component can fall within SRB’s jurisdiction, while the balance has to be attributed to the relevant federal / provincial jurisdictions, depending on the period and applicable mechanism.

Here also, the appeal should rely on the same evidentiary approach: invoice-wise reconciliation, province-wise sales / royalty allocation, copies of returns, CPRs and payment evidence. The appellant should state that it is enclosing a complete reconciliation of the trademark and manifestation licence fee, together with the relevant invoices and sales tax returns, to establish that tax has already been discharged on the appropriate jurisdictional basis.

The Chairman SRB’s statement before the Sindh High Court materially supports this position as well, because the issue before the High Court itself concerned franchise fee paid by petroleum companies / sub-franchisees located outside Sindh. SRB’s own stated position was that, subject to verification of proof of payment to another sales tax authority, SRB shall not charge Sindh sales tax again on such franchise services. fileciteturn1file0

The order’s reliance on imports through Sindh ports should be specifically rebutted. A port of import is relevant for customs / goods-related movement, but it cannot convert an all-Pakistan brand royalty into a Sindh-only taxable service. The contract basis, the invoice basis and the sales base are more relevant than the logistics route of petroleum products. If the royalty / manifestation fee is linked to national sales, the tax base must follow the same allocation logic. Treating the entire amount as Sindh taxable merely because the appellant is based in Karachi or imports through Sindh would expand SRB’s jurisdiction beyond the province.

The appeal should therefore request deletion of the demand to the extent it relates to amounts already taxed / paid outside Sindh, or alternatively remand / verification of the reconciliation by the assessing officer under the principle recorded in the Chairman SRB’s statement.

## 3. Technical Service Fee — primary argument is that it is not Franchise; at most it became Business Support Service from July 2013 onward

This is the most important legal issue. The impugned order classifies the technical service fee as franchise service for July 2011 to December 2012. The officer relies on selected clauses of the technical service agreement, including confidentiality, retention of intellectual property by Shell, advice / know-how / expertise, and limited licence language. On that basis, the officer concludes that the arrangement falls within franchise. This conclusion is not sustainable.

The technical service agreement, as discussed in the order itself, relates to advice, assistance, know-how, expertise, technical information and operational support provided by Shell International Petroleum Company. These are ordinary features of a technical assistance / business support arrangement. They do not, by themselves, amount to franchise. A franchise arrangement requires the grant of a commercial right to produce, manufacture, sell, trade in goods, provide services or undertake a process identified with the franchisor’s brand / system. The technical service agreement does not grant such independent market-facing franchise rights. It only provides technical support for the appellant’s existing operations.

A very important factual rebuttal is that the officer appears to misread the agreement. The order refers to an “exclusive and non-transferable” licence, whereas the agreement language, as reproduced in the order, appears to refer to a non-exclusive / non-transferable licence for limited purposes. This distinction is material. A limited non-exclusive right to use technical information, processes, inventions or know-how for internal operational purposes cannot be equated with a franchise right to commercially exploit a brand or business format. fileciteturn0file0

The appeal should clearly separate three agreements / streams: retail franchise / dealer licence arrangements, trademark and manifestation licence arrangements, and technical service / technical assistance arrangements. The officer’s fundamental error is that he has merged the technical service agreement with the trademark / franchise arrangements. The mere fact that all agreements relate to the Shell group or Shell business operations does not mean that every payment is franchise consideration. Each stream has to be classified independently based on its legal character, contract terms and taxable entry.

The strongest legal point is SRB’s own subsequent conduct. From July 2013 onward, SRB itself classified the same / similar technical support services under “Business Support Services” and not as “Franchise Services”. Business Support Services under tariff heading 9805.9200 were introduced through Sindh Finance Act, 2013 / related SRB tariff framework effective from 1 July 2013. The SRB working tariff also reflects Business Support Services under heading 9805.9200 and references the 1 July 2013 notification framework. citeturn350301search2turn350301search0

This subsequent classification is highly relevant. It shows that, even according to SRB’s own understanding, the nature of the service is business / operational support, not franchise. However, because the specific taxable heading for Business Support Services was introduced from July 2013, SRB cannot retrospectively tax the same service for July 2011 to December 2012 by artificially forcing it into the general franchise entry. A service cannot be taxed under a wrong heading merely because the correct specific heading did not exist during the earlier period.

The Sindh High Court judgment concerning Business Support Services is useful here. The Court recognized tariff heading 9805.9200 as applicable where activities are undertaken to support business transactions and activities, and also observed that only the revenue component representing the value of services should be taxed. citeturn886893view0 This supports the appellant’s broader classification argument: services involving operational support, technical coordination, advice, assistance and business facilitation belong to the business support / technical support category, not franchise, unless the franchise ingredients are independently established.

The principle of specific-over-general classification should also be emphasized. The Supreme Court in K.S. Sulemanji Esmailji & Sons held, in the classification context, that classification is a technical exercise requiring examination of relevant documents, classification rules and technical material, and that an “others” / general category is not to be used where the subject matter is more specifically covered elsewhere. citeturn886893view1 By analogy, once the service is specifically identifiable as business support / technical support, it cannot be placed under the broader franchise heading merely to create tax liability for a period before the specific entry became taxable.

The appeal should therefore state that the technical service fee cannot be taxed as franchise for the pre-July 2013 period. If SRB’s own later orders and appellate history classify the same service as Business Support Services, the earlier period cannot be re-characterized as franchise without proving the essential elements of franchise. The burden was on the department to establish that the technical service agreement granted a franchise right. The impugned order does not discharge that burden; it merely refers to advice, know-how, expertise and limited licence clauses, which are not sufficient.

Finally, penalty and default surcharge should be challenged separately. At the minimum, the matter involves a bona fide classification dispute, supported by SRB’s own later classification, the Chairman SRB’s statement before the High Court, and payments made / claimed before relevant authorities. There is no concealment, suppression or deliberate non-payment. Therefore, even if any principal liability survives after reconciliation / verification, penalty and default surcharge should be deleted.

citation.snippet: ٹھیک ہے میل، بات کریں، ہاں حسن صاحب، ہوپ یو ڈوئنگ ویل، اچھا جیسے آپ کو ایز یو ایئر کہ ہماری ایک اپیل ایس آر بی کمشنر اپیلز ان کے پاس پینڈنگ ہے فار ٹیکس پیریڈ جولائی 2011 تا دسمبر 2012، ٹھیک ہے، جس کا جو پرنسپل ڈیمانڈ کریئیٹڈ ہے وہ 287 ملین کے ہے۔ اچھا اب آپ اس میں جو ہے نا جو تین میٹرز اس نے پلیج کیے تھے ایک لائسنس فیس، لوکل لائسنس فیس کا ٹریڈ مارک مینفیسٹریشن تھا اور فیفو ٹیکنکل تھا، اچھا جو فیفو ٹیکنکل کا پوائنٹ ہے وہ تو لیگل پوائنٹ ہے اس میں تو ہمیں کوئی ڈیٹیل چاہیے نہیں وہ تو جو ہے نا وہ بزنس سپورٹ کی ٹائرفیلنگ کے بیسس پر لڑیں گے، باقی جو لوکل فرنچائز اور ٹریڈ مارک مینفیسٹریشن کے حوالے سے تھا۔ تو اوریجنل جو ایس ایس ڈی اس نے الینج کیا تھا وہ لوکل فرنچائز میں نائنٹی نائن ملین کیا تھا اور ٹریڈ مارک میں تھرٹی نائن کیا تھا جس میں سے اس نے نائنٹی نائن میں سے 28 ملین کہاں سے آلریڈی پیمنٹ ایس ایس ڈی کی آئی ہوئی ہے اور ٹریڈ مارک مینفیسٹریشن میں تھرٹی نائن میں سے 9 ملین اس نے کہاں آئی ہے۔ تو ریمننگ سیونٹی ون لوکل فرنچائز میں اور ٹریڈ مارک میں 29 ملین آؤٹ اسٹینڈنگ تھا وچ از اوبویسلی وہ آپ جانس کو اپوشن کیا ہوگا تو ہمیں ہمیں ہم نے اس اپیل کی جو ہے نا اسٹے ایپلیکیشن آج فائل کر دی ہے ٹھیک ہے جو فور کمیشنر کی اپیلز کو ہمارے پاس کمیشنر کی طرف سے کال آئی تھی کہ آپ اس کا جو ہے نا اسٹے پرسو کر لیں کیونکہ اس کی وہاں پہ کیونکہ مے اور جون ہے تو وہاں پہ پریشر ہے ریوری کے حوالے سے تو ہم نے اس کے کل ہمارے پاس کال آئی تھی اور ہم نے آج اس کی ایپلیکیشن فائل کر دی تو مین ویل آپ سے ریکویسٹ یہ ہے کہ لوکل فرنچائز جو سیونٹی ون ملین نظر آ رہے اور ٹریڈ مارک جو 29 ملین آؤٹ اسٹینڈنگ نظر آ رہا ہے وچ از اوبویسلی آپ نے فیڈرل میں یا پروونسز میں اس کا ڈسچارج کیا ہوگا تو ہمیں اس کا سپورٹنگ دینا ہے تاکہ ہم اس کو کنکلوڈ کروا سکیں تو فار یور ریفرینس ای میل پہ ہی میں بریک ڈاؤن بھی جو ہے نیچے بریک ڈاؤن بھی دے رہا ہوں ڈیمانڈ کا ٹھیک ہے یہ ذرا جو ہے نا ای میل مجھے اپلوڈ کر دینا

Subject: Re: New Supply Model- Dealers (Retailer) & Shell Card

 

Hi Hashim Sb, hope you are doing well.

We have reviewed your email and the draft Shell Card Discount Funding Agreement shared with us. At this stage, the complete commercial, invoicing, accounting and customer-facing mechanics of the proposed model have not been fully explained in the email. Therefore, before we provide an opinion on the income tax and provincial sales tax implications, it would be appropriate to first confirm our understanding of the proposed arrangement based on the email and draft agreement.

As we understand, the existing arrangement for sale of petroleum products to the dealer/retailer will broadly continue in the same manner. WEPL will continue to supply petroleum products to the dealer/retailer under the retail supply arrangement at the applicable OGRA-notified price, and the existing mechanism for dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax on franchise fee, and withholding tax on dealer margin will continue to apply in the normal course.

The proposed change appears to be limited to Shell Card transactions. For such transactions, a separate / dedicated SOLD TO account will be maintained for the dealer/retailer. Shell Card-related volumes will be captured through this account, and based on those volumes, WEPL will debit a per-litre “Discount Contribution” to the dealer/retailer. The purpose of this contribution appears to be funding or supporting the discount which may be extended to Shell Card customers under WEPL’s Shell Card program.

Our further understanding is that this “Discount Contribution” is not intended to alter the primary sale price of petroleum products charged to the dealer/retailer, nor is it intended to change the OGRA price structure or the nature of the underlying sale of petroleum products. Instead, it appears to be a separate commercial recovery / adjustment between WEPL and the dealer/retailer, linked only with Shell Card volumes recorded under the dedicated SOLD TO account.

Based on the table shared in your email, the dealer’s existing economics remain the same up to the point of dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax and withholding tax. Under the proposed model, an additional Rs 0.40 per litre is being considered as a margin / administrative fee for the dealer/retailer for handling Shell Card-related transactions, while the balance amount is proposed to be recovered from the dealer/retailer through debit note or invoice. The recovered amount is intended to be used by WEPL for offering discounts to Shell Card customers.

Accordingly, the transaction appears to involve three separate components: first, the normal sale of petroleum products by WEPL to the dealer/retailer; second, the Shell Card discount program operated for customers; and third, the dealer/retailer’s contribution towards funding that discount through a per-litre recovery mechanism. The tax treatment may differ for each component depending on how the arrangement is documented, invoiced and recorded in the books.

Kindly confirm whether the above understanding is correct. In particular, please also confirm the following points so that we may provide our tax comments more precisely:   Yes, your understanding is correct

Whether the Shell Card customer discount will be offered by WEPL, the dealer/retailer, or jointly by both parties, only WEPL offer discount Shell Card Customer not jointly there is no concern of dealer what discount WEPL offering to Shell Card Customer.
Whether the discount will appear on the customer-facing invoice / receipt issued to Shell Card customers.   Yes, we are issuing manual invoices to Shell Card Customers with mention of discount on invoice where we are offering to discount and same declaring in Sales tax return
Whether the recovery from the dealer/retailer will be made through a debit note, tax invoice, adjustment note, or simple ledger adjustment. Recovery from Dealers will be through Debit Note (Post in customer account and will be adjusted with their payment for their next order)
Whether the PKR 0.40 per litre dealer administration margin will be separately credited / paid to the dealer or will only be treated as part of the dealer’s retained economics. No Separate credit / paid to dealer it will be part of original invoice when we will issue sales invoice to dealer at first stage
Whether the discount contribution recovered from the dealer/retailer will be booked by WEPL as income, recovery, reimbursement, reduction of discount cost, or any other accounting head. Yes, WEPL will be booked as Income and offset Shell Card Discount with same Account head (will reconfirm further form our business)
Once the above facts are confirmed, we will be in a position to advise on the applicable income tax and provincial sales tax implications, including the treatment of the dealer administration margin, discount contribution, franchise fee, withholding tax, invoicing documentation, and the most appropriate tax-compliant manner of implementing the proposed model.

Regards

Zuhair Ahmed Minhas

Please read the attached recent and earlier notice from SRB. As a tax consultant, kindly prepare a thorough response on the client's behalf. Please take contentions from the petition filed before the Sindh High Court and advice from lawyers. Please also emphasis the point that our client duly included the royalty from PQA in the value of taxable services, in other words, the Sindh Sales Tax charged on gross revenue which includes royalty from PQA. Hence, your earlier contention is grossly that our client didn't pay the Sindh sales tax on royalty pay to PQA. 

Furthermore, the earlier notice imposed a tax liability under section 18 of the Sindh Sales Tax Act on Services, 2011, without acknowledging that the burden of proof lies with the tax department before they can make anyone jointly and severally liable for the payment of any unpaid tax amount. Only stating the facts without providing any evidence is merely an assumption and presumption, and it is against the spirit of Section 18 of the Sindh Sales Tax Act on Services, 2011. However, in the instant case, our client duly charged and subsequently deposited the Sindh sales tax on the gross amount charged to them, which includes the royalty payment to PQA.
Furthermore, the tax period in question relates to July 2016 to February 2018, despite the judgment of the Honorable High Court of Sindh at Karachi reported as 2021 PTD 484, which held that, due to the insertion of Section 13(3) of the Act through the Finance Act, 2019, no liability could be imposed on a withholding agent for any period prior to 01.07.2019.

citation.snippet: ٹھیک ہے میل، بات کریں، ہاں حسن صاحب، ہوپ یو ڈوئنگ ویل، اچھا جیسے آپ کو ایز یو ایئر کہ ہماری ایک اپیل ایس آر بی کمشنر اپیلز ان کے پاس پینڈنگ ہے فار ٹیکس پیریڈ جولائی 2011 تا دسمبر 2012، ٹھیک ہے، جس کا جو پرنسپل ڈیمانڈ کریئیٹڈ ہے وہ 287 ملین کے ہے۔ اچھا اب آپ اس میں جو ہے نا جو تین میٹرز اس نے پلیج کیے تھے ایک لائسنس فیس، لوکل لائسنس فیس کا ٹریڈ مارک مینفیسٹریشن تھا اور فیفو ٹیکنکل تھا، اچھا جو فیفو ٹیکنکل کا پوائنٹ ہے وہ تو لیگل پوائنٹ ہے اس میں تو ہمیں کوئی ڈیٹیل چاہیے نہیں وہ تو جو ہے نا وہ بزنس سپورٹ کی ٹائرفیلنگ کے بیسس پر لڑیں گے، باقی جو لوکل فرنچائز اور ٹریڈ مارک مینفیسٹریشن کے حوالے سے تھا۔ تو اوریجنل جو ایس ایس ڈی اس نے الینج کیا تھا وہ لوکل فرنچائز میں نائنٹی نائن ملین کیا تھا اور ٹریڈ مارک میں تھرٹی نائن کیا تھا جس میں سے اس نے نائنٹی نائن میں سے 28 ملین کہاں سے آلریڈی پیمنٹ ایس ایس ڈی کی آئی ہوئی ہے اور ٹریڈ مارک مینفیسٹریشن میں تھرٹی نائن میں سے 9 ملین اس نے کہاں آئی ہے۔ تو ریمننگ سیونٹی ون لوکل فرنچائز میں اور ٹریڈ مارک میں 29 ملین آؤٹ اسٹینڈنگ تھا وچ از اوبویسلی وہ آپ جانس کو اپوشن کیا ہوگا تو ہمیں ہمیں ہم نے اس اپیل کی جو ہے نا اسٹے ایپلیکیشن آج فائل کر دی ہے ٹھیک ہے جو فور کمیشنر کی اپیلز کو ہمارے پاس کمیشنر کی طرف سے کال آئی تھی کہ آپ اس کا جو ہے نا اسٹے پرسو کر لیں کیونکہ اس کی وہاں پہ کیونکہ مے اور جون ہے تو وہاں پہ پریشر ہے ریوری کے حوالے سے تو ہم نے اس کے کل ہمارے پاس کال آئی تھی اور ہم نے آج اس کی ایپلیکیشن فائل کر دی تو مین ویل آپ سے ریکویسٹ یہ ہے کہ لوکل فرنچائز جو سیونٹی ون ملین نظر آ رہے اور ٹریڈ مارک جو 29 ملین آؤٹ اسٹینڈنگ نظر آ رہا ہے وچ از اوبویسلی آپ نے فیڈرل میں یا پروونسز میں اس کا ڈسچارج کیا ہوگا تو ہمیں اس کا سپورٹنگ دینا ہے تاکہ ہم اس کو کنکلوڈ کروا سکیں تو فار یور ریفرینس ای میل پہ ہی میں بریک ڈاؤن بھی جو ہے نیچے بریک ڈاؤن بھی دے رہا ہوں ڈیمانڈ کا ٹھیک ہے یہ ذرا جو ہے نا ای میل مجھے اپلوڈ کر دینا

Please read the below email trail and attached supporting documents and prepare email through which give answer to queries. 

Dear Baqar

 

Please refer to email below. For the purpose of WEPL’s supply through non resident suppliers, the supplier needs a guarantee and WEPL is planning to take one instead of option of getting it done through a bank. In lieu of this, the WEPL’s holding associate Assyad is ready to provide a guarantee to these suppliers at a fee of 1.5% of the amount. Your advice is required on the following:

 

Will it be chargeable to tax under ITO, 2001 read with treaty? Assyad is registered in Saudi.
Will it be considered as services? If yes, what will be the tax implication?
Will it be allowed as expenses, input tax claimable (sales tax) purposes?
Any other TP requirements which we need to fulfil before finalizing the arrangement.
 

We would appreciate your brief preliminary response as early as possible.

 

Regards

Komal

 

From: Saleem, Nida WEP-FDR/REP <Nida.Saleem@wafi-energy.com>
Sent: Thursday, September 4, 2025 8:46 PM
To: Ali, Komal WEP-FDR/REP <Komal.Ali@wafi-energy.com>
Cc: Muhammad Sarosh <Muhammad.Sarosh@Wafi-Energy.com>; Aabis, Umer WEP-FDR/REP <Umer.Aabis@wafi-energy.com>; Elahi, Faizan WEP-FDR/REP <Faizan.Elahi@Wafi-Energy.com>
Subject: FW: PCG - Lubricant

 

Dear Komal,

 

Asyad has issued a parental guarantee to Shell Lubricant Suppliers; SMME (UAE based) and SLSC (Netherlands) of cumulative USD 15.3 Mn – signed document attached. In lieu of this Asyad will charge Wafi PK a guarantee fee of 1.5% per annum of the guarantee amount.

 

To pay this amount to Asyad we have to secure SBP permission, hence I have made a draft agreement which I have sent to bank for its review. You are requested to review the tax clauses in the word file or add/delete anything as per your opinion. Further please confirm the nature of taxes that will be applied along-with their rates. Please note it is yet not decided who will bear the tax impact, the costings will be shared with Zarrar once the draft is finalized.

 

Appreciate your revert on this at earliest. Thanks.

 

Regards,

Nida

Please see below items to be considered and procedure for the same. Happy to have a brief call to discuss the same. Thanks

 

Regards

Umer Aabis

 

From: Saleem, Nida WEP-FDR/REP <Nida.Saleem@wafi-energy.com>
Sent: Tuesday, September 2, 2025 12:40 PM
To: Aabis, Umer WEP-FDR/REP <Umer.Aabis@wafi-energy.com>

Subject: RE: PCG - Lubricant

 

Hi,

 

Please note as per my discussion with SCB an agreement under the category” Guarantee Fee Letter” should be drafted. Such commission are not mentioned under specific FE Manual category hence it will be put up for permission on special request basis to SBP for approval. Precedents apply with a company paying its parent company monthly payment whereby they have not taken permission upfront rather they put it on monthly basis after month close.

 

The fee letter can be a short 2-3 pager letter with agreement essential topics like governing law, severability etc amongst specific points to be covered:

 

Parties
Scope/Recitals
Guarantee Amount – better to have this locked in PKR to avoid FX Loss. SBP have approved such guarantee fee previously in PKR.
Effective date
Calculation and Payment frequency – payment either monthly or quarterly. My recommendation is to try get an upfront SBP approval for full year amount but with payment frequency  on quarterly basis. Or we can pay full year amount at each anniversary lump sum
Termination – open ended
 

 

The SBP application would accompany:

 

Cover letter application
Debit Note from Parent based on payment frequency
Calculation in excel
PSG Guarantee Letter
 

Regards,

Nida

 

 

From: Aabis, Umer WEP-FDR/REP <Umer.Aabis@wafi-energy.com>
Sent: Thursday, August 28, 2025 9:14 AM
To: Saleem, Nida WEP-FDR/REP <Nida.Saleem@wafi-energy.com>

Subject: RE: PCG - Lubricant

 

Can you please compile and share the list of queries / items that should be covered in the agreement? Thanks

Subject: Re: New Supply Model- Dealers (Retailer) & Shell Card

 

Hi Hashim Sb, hope you are doing well.

We have reviewed your email and the draft Shell Card Discount Funding Agreement shared with us. At this stage, the complete commercial, invoicing, accounting and customer-facing mechanics of the proposed model have not been fully explained in the email. Therefore, before we provide an opinion on the income tax and provincial sales tax implications, it would be appropriate to first confirm our understanding of the proposed arrangement based on the email and draft agreement.

As we understand, the existing arrangement for sale of petroleum products to the dealer/retailer will broadly continue in the same manner. WEPL will continue to supply petroleum products to the dealer/retailer under the retail supply arrangement at the applicable OGRA-notified price, and the existing mechanism for dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax on franchise fee, and withholding tax on dealer margin will continue to apply in the normal course.

The proposed change appears to be limited to Shell Card transactions. For such transactions, a separate / dedicated SOLD TO account will be maintained for the dealer/retailer. Shell Card-related volumes will be captured through this account, and based on those volumes, WEPL will debit a per-litre “Discount Contribution” to the dealer/retailer. The purpose of this contribution appears to be funding or supporting the discount which may be extended to Shell Card customers under WEPL’s Shell Card program.

Our further understanding is that this “Discount Contribution” is not intended to alter the primary sale price of petroleum products charged to the dealer/retailer, nor is it intended to change the OGRA price structure or the nature of the underlying sale of petroleum products. Instead, it appears to be a separate commercial recovery / adjustment between WEPL and the dealer/retailer, linked only with Shell Card volumes recorded under the dedicated SOLD TO account.

Based on the table shared in your email, the dealer’s existing economics remain the same up to the point of dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax and withholding tax. Under the proposed model, an additional Rs 0.40 per litre is being considered as a margin / administrative fee for the dealer/retailer for handling Shell Card-related transactions, while the balance amount is proposed to be recovered from the dealer/retailer through debit note or invoice. The recovered amount is intended to be used by WEPL for offering discounts to Shell Card customers.

Accordingly, the transaction appears to involve three separate components: first, the normal sale of petroleum products by WEPL to the dealer/retailer; second, the Shell Card discount program operated for customers; and third, the dealer/retailer’s contribution towards funding that discount through a per-litre recovery mechanism. The tax treatment may differ for each component depending on how the arrangement is documented, invoiced and recorded in the books.

Kindly confirm whether the above understanding is correct. In particular, please also confirm the following points so that we may provide our tax comments more precisely:   Yes, your understanding is correct

Whether the Shell Card customer discount will be offered by WEPL, the dealer/retailer, or jointly by both parties, only WEPL offer discount Shell Card Customer not jointly there is no concern of dealer what discount WEPL offering to Shell Card Customer.
Whether the discount will appear on the customer-facing invoice / receipt issued to Shell Card customers.   Yes, we are issuing manual invoices to Shell Card Customers with mention of discount on invoice where we are offering to discount and same declaring in Sales tax return
Whether the recovery from the dealer/retailer will be made through a debit note, tax invoice, adjustment note, or simple ledger adjustment. Recovery from Dealers will be through Debit Note (Post in customer account and will be adjusted with their payment for their next order)
Whether the PKR 0.40 per litre dealer administration margin will be separately credited / paid to the dealer or will only be treated as part of the dealer’s retained economics. No Separate credit / paid to dealer it will be part of original invoice when we will issue sales invoice to dealer at first stage
Whether the discount contribution recovered from the dealer/retailer will be booked by WEPL as income, recovery, reimbursement, reduction of discount cost, or any other accounting head. Yes, WEPL will be booked as Income and offset Shell Card Discount with same Account head (will reconfirm further form our business)
Once the above facts are confirmed, we will be in a position to advise on the applicable income tax and provincial sales tax implications, including the treatment of the dealer administration margin, discount contribution, franchise fee, withholding tax, invoicing documentation, and the most appropriate tax-compliant manner of implementing the proposed model.

Please read the attached recent and earlier notice from SRB. As a tax consultant, kindly prepare a thorough response on the client's behalf. Please take contentions from the petition filed before the Sindh High Court and advice from lawyers. Please also emphasis the point that our client duly included the royalty from PQA in the value of taxable services, in other words, the Sindh Sales Tax charged on gross revenue which includes royalty from PQA. Hence, your earlier contention is grossly that our client didn't pay the Sindh sales tax on royalty pay to PQA. 

Furthermore, the earlier notice imposed a tax liability under section 18 of the Sindh Sales Tax Act on Services, 2011, without acknowledging that the burden of proof lies with the tax department before they can make anyone jointly and severally liable for the payment of any unpaid tax amount. Only stating the facts without providing any evidence is merely an assumption and presumption, and it is against the spirit of Section 18 of the Sindh Sales Tax Act on Services, 2011. However, in the instant case, our client duly charged and subsequently deposited the Sindh sales tax on the gross amount charged to them, which includes the royalty payment to PQA.
Furthermore, the tax period in question relates to July 2016 to February 2018, despite the judgment of the Honorable High Court of Sindh at Karachi reported as 2021 PTD 484, which held that, due to the insertion of Section 13(3) of the Act through the Finance Act, 2019, no liability could be imposed on a withholding agent for any period prior to 01.07.2019.
