Subject: Re: New Supply Model- Dealers (Retailer) & Shell Card

 

Hi Hashim Sb, hope you are doing well.

We have reviewed your email and the draft Shell Card Discount Funding Agreement shared with us. At this stage, the complete commercial, invoicing, accounting and customer-facing mechanics of the proposed model have not been fully explained in the email. Therefore, before we provide an opinion on the income tax and provincial sales tax implications, it would be appropriate to first confirm our understanding of the proposed arrangement based on the email and draft agreement.

As we understand, the existing arrangement for sale of petroleum products to the dealer/retailer will broadly continue in the same manner. WEPL will continue to supply petroleum products to the dealer/retailer under the retail supply arrangement at the applicable OGRA-notified price, and the existing mechanism for dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax on franchise fee, and withholding tax on dealer margin will continue to apply in the normal course.

The proposed change appears to be limited to Shell Card transactions. For such transactions, a separate / dedicated SOLD TO account will be maintained for the dealer/retailer. Shell Card-related volumes will be captured through this account, and based on those volumes, WEPL will debit a per-litre “Discount Contribution” to the dealer/retailer. The purpose of this contribution appears to be funding or supporting the discount which may be extended to Shell Card customers under WEPL’s Shell Card program.

Our further understanding is that this “Discount Contribution” is not intended to alter the primary sale price of petroleum products charged to the dealer/retailer, nor is it intended to change the OGRA price structure or the nature of the underlying sale of petroleum products. Instead, it appears to be a separate commercial recovery / adjustment between WEPL and the dealer/retailer, linked only with Shell Card volumes recorded under the dedicated SOLD TO account.

Based on the table shared in your email, the dealer’s existing economics remain the same up to the point of dealer margin, franchise fee, provincial sales tax and withholding tax. Under the proposed model, an additional Rs 0.40 per litre is being considered as a margin / administrative fee for the dealer/retailer for handling Shell Card-related transactions, while the balance amount is proposed to be recovered from the dealer/retailer through debit note or invoice. The recovered amount is intended to be used by WEPL for offering discounts to Shell Card customers.

Accordingly, the transaction appears to involve three separate components: first, the normal sale of petroleum products by WEPL to the dealer/retailer; second, the Shell Card discount program operated for customers; and third, the dealer/retailer’s contribution towards funding that discount through a per-litre recovery mechanism. The tax treatment may differ for each component depending on how the arrangement is documented, invoiced and recorded in the books.

Kindly confirm whether the above understanding is correct. In particular, please also confirm the following points so that we may provide our tax comments more precisely:   Yes, your understanding is correct

Whether the Shell Card customer discount will be offered by WEPL, the dealer/retailer, or jointly by both parties, only WEPL offer discount Shell Card Customer not jointly there is no concern of dealer what discount WEPL offering to Shell Card Customer.
Whether the discount will appear on the customer-facing invoice / receipt issued to Shell Card customers.   Yes, we are issuing manual invoices to Shell Card Customers with mention of discount on invoice where we are offering to discount and same declaring in Sales tax return
Whether the recovery from the dealer/retailer will be made through a debit note, tax invoice, adjustment note, or simple ledger adjustment. Recovery from Dealers will be through Debit Note (Post in customer account and will be adjusted with their payment for their next order)
Whether the PKR 0.40 per litre dealer administration margin will be separately credited / paid to the dealer or will only be treated as part of the dealer’s retained economics. No Separate credit / paid to dealer it will be part of original invoice when we will issue sales invoice to dealer at first stage
Whether the discount contribution recovered from the dealer/retailer will be booked by WEPL as income, recovery, reimbursement, reduction of discount cost, or any other accounting head. Yes, WEPL will be booked as Income and offset Shell Card Discount with same Account head (will reconfirm further form our business)
Once the above facts are confirmed, we will be in a position to advise on the applicable income tax and provincial sales tax implications, including the treatment of the dealer administration margin, discount contribution, franchise fee, withholding tax, invoicing documentation, and the most appropriate tax-compliant manner of implementing the proposed model.

Regards

Zuhair Ahmed Minhas

Please read the attached recent and earlier notice from SRB. As a tax consultant, kindly prepare a thorough response on the client's behalf. Please take contentions from the petition filed before the Sindh High Court and advice from lawyers. Please also emphasis the point that our client duly included the royalty from PQA in the value of taxable services, in other words, the Sindh Sales Tax charged on gross revenue which includes royalty from PQA. Hence, your earlier contention is grossly that our client didn't pay the Sindh sales tax on royalty pay to PQA. 

Furthermore, the earlier notice imposed a tax liability under section 18 of the Sindh Sales Tax Act on Services, 2011, without acknowledging that the burden of proof lies with the tax department before they can make anyone jointly and severally liable for the payment of any unpaid tax amount. Only stating the facts without providing any evidence is merely an assumption and presumption, and it is against the spirit of Section 18 of the Sindh Sales Tax Act on Services, 2011. However, in the instant case, our client duly charged and subsequently deposited the Sindh sales tax on the gross amount charged to them, which includes the royalty payment to PQA.
Furthermore, the tax period in question relates to July 2016 to February 2018, despite the judgment of the Honorable High Court of Sindh at Karachi reported as 2021 PTD 484, which held that, due to the insertion of Section 13(3) of the Act through the Finance Act, 2019, no liability could be imposed on a withholding agent for any period prior to 01.07.2019.

Yes, the appropriate legal expression here is **“in pari materia”**, meaning that two statutory provisions are on the same subject and materially similar in substance. You may use the following improved version:

It is also respectfully submitted that the definition of “franchise” under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act / Rules is **in pari materia** with the definition of “franchise” contained under the federal sales tax / federal excise regime. The relevant statutory expressions are materially similar and operate on the same legal premise, namely that there must be an identifiable franchise arrangement involving the grant of a right, authorization or permission by a franchisor to a franchisee to undertake business under a trade name, brand, system, process or other similar commercial arrangement. Therefore, the interpretation already rendered in the appellant’s own federal proceedings, while examining the same technical service arrangement, carries substantial persuasive value for the present controversy.

In this regard, it is pertinent to mention that the federal tax authorities had also previously attempted to treat the very same technical service fee / FIFO technical services as consideration for “franchise”. However, after examining the relevant agreements, the nature of the services, the commercial substance of the arrangement and the essential legal ingredients of a franchise, the learned Appellate Tribunal, in the appellant’s own cases, decided the issue in favour of the appellant. The Tribunal held, in substance, that the arrangement did not constitute a franchise arrangement and that the technical service fee could not legally be brought within the ambit of franchise merely because the services were being provided by an associated / group concern or because the business was being carried on under the Shell brand.

The aforesaid findings are directly relevant for the present proceedings. The dispute is not merely computational in nature; rather, it goes to the very root of classification. A limited arrangement for technical assistance, operational guidance, know-how, advisory support, business support and related technical input does not, by itself, amount to a franchise unless the statutory ingredients of franchise are independently satisfied. The impugned order has proceeded by broadly associating the technical service arrangement with Shell’s brand structure, whereas the correct legal test is whether the agreement itself granted any franchise right in the legal sense. On a proper reading of the agreements, no such franchise right was granted.

Copies of the favourable orders passed in the appellant’s own federal cases are being furnished along with the present submissions. It is further understood from the appellant’s record that the department did not assail the said findings before the Hon’ble High Court and, therefore, the matter attained finality at the federal level in the appellant’s own case. In such circumstances, where the Sindh definition is **in pari materia** with the federal definition, the same arrangement cannot be re-characterized as franchise for Sindh sales tax purposes without any distinguishing factual or legal basis. Any contrary treatment would offend the principles of consistency, finality and certainty in tax administration, particularly where the same taxpayer, same agreement and same nature of payment have already been examined and decided in favour of the appellant.

Certainly. A more refined version is as follows:

The impugned order proceeds on the erroneous assumption that the entire local franchise / licence fee is liable to Sindh sales tax merely because the appellant is registered in Sindh and the underlying arrangements relate to Shell-branded retail operations. This approach is materially flawed, as the fee was not wholly attributable to Sindh. The appellant’s retail network extends across Pakistan, and the local franchise / licence fee charged from dealers was directly linked with their respective business locations and sales activity. Accordingly, the taxable value, if any, was required to be attributed on a jurisdictional basis, having regard to the place of business / revenue generation, instead of treating the entire transaction as a Sindh-based taxable service. The impugned order itself acknowledges certain SRB payments made by the appellant in relation to franchise services, but proceeds to sustain the demand primarily on the ground that evidence of payment before other revenue authorities was not adequately produced at the adjudication stage. fileciteturn0file0

In this regard, it is respectfully submitted that the appellant has already discharged sales tax on the relevant franchise / licence fee by apportioning the taxable value amongst SRB, FBR and other provincial revenue authorities, including PRA, on the basis of revenue / place of business / jurisdictional attribution. For ease of reference and verification, a detailed reconciliation is enclosed as **Annexure ‘A’**, which clearly demonstrates the province-wise bifurcation of the value, the tax deposited with each relevant authority, and the corresponding sales tax returns / payment evidence. The appellant is, therefore, not seeking any exemption from tax; rather, the appellant is only seeking due recognition and credit of tax already discharged before the competent revenue authorities in respect of the same taxable value.

The statement filed by the Chairman SRB before the Hon’ble High Court of Sindh in the appellant’s own matter also assumes significant relevance. In the said statement, SRB categorically took the position that, pending finalization of harmonized place-of-supply rules pursuant to the National Tax Council framework, where the taxpayer satisfies SRB through proof and verification that sales tax on franchise services has already been paid to any other sales tax authority, SRB shall not charge Sindh sales tax from such taxpayer. This constitutes a clear departmental position placed before the Hon’ble High Court and is directly applicable to the present controversy. fileciteturn1file0

In view of the above, once the enclosed reconciliation, returns and payment evidence establish that the relevant non-Sindh portion of the franchise / licence fee has already been subjected to tax before the appropriate revenue authority, SRB cannot again assess Sindh sales tax on the same value. Such duplication would not only result in double taxation but would also be inconsistent with the constitutional scheme under which sales tax on services is a provincial levy and must remain confined to the province having the appropriate taxing nexus. The demand created under the impugned order, to the extent it disregards tax already paid before other competent revenue authorities, is therefore liable to be deleted, or at the very least, the matter may be verified in light of the reconciliation and supporting record now placed on file.

---

## **1. Small Traders May Get a Simpler Tax Scheme — But Bank Records Will Matter**

FBR is expected to introduce a new simplified tax scheme for small traders and shopkeepers in the Federal Budget 2026–27. The proposed scheme may cover businesses having annual turnover up to approximately **Rs. 20 million**, with easier registration through IRIS, mobile app, authorised tax practitioners, or facilitators.

The real attraction for small businesses is the possibility of a reduced tax rate, simplified record keeping, and lower audit exposure. However, this does not mean “no documentation.” Traders will still need to maintain basic records of sales, purchases, expenses, and banking transactions.

The most important point is that FBR may compare declared income with bank activity, business scale, assets, and lifestyle. So, the message is clear: the scheme may be simple, but declarations must still be realistic and properly supported.

---

## **2. FBR’s Next Budget Strategy: More Audits, More Enforcement, More Revenue**

FBR is planning aggressive enforcement measures for fiscal year 2026–27, with an estimated revenue generation target of around **Rs. 700 billion** through audits, production monitoring, sales tax checks, and other enforcement actions. Field formations may also be assigned specific audit-based collection targets.

This indicates that the upcoming budget may not rely only on new taxes; it may focus heavily on better recovery from existing taxpayers, stricter monitoring, and deeper scrutiny of declared figures. Sectors with weak documentation, unexplained sales patterns, or inconsistent input/output tax positions may face greater attention.

For businesses, this is the right time to review tax positions, reconcile sales tax returns with financial accounts, check withholding compliance, and ensure that bank transactions match declared income. In the coming year, weak documentation may become more costly than tax itself.

---

## **3. Royalty on Cement Bags? Court Questions Whether It Is Actually a Tax**

The Federal Constitutional Court has raised an important question in relation to royalty imposed on cement production. The Court observed that royalty is generally linked with minerals, and imposing it on a finished product such as cement bags may, prima facie, appear to be equivalent to a tax.

This matter is important because any additional levy on a finished product normally becomes part of the final price paid by consumers. The Court also noted that factory owners may pass this cost to the public, meaning the burden may ultimately fall on consumers rather than manufacturers.

The case highlights a wider principle: governments must be careful in designing levies, charges, royalties, and taxes. If a levy is imposed in the wrong form or at the wrong stage, it can create legal disputes, increase consumer prices, and disturb industry pricing structures.

**Subject:** Tax Year 2024 – Order under Section 122(5A) – Update on Proceedings

Dear [Client Name],

We are pleased to inform you that the order under section 122(5A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 for Tax Year 2024 has been issued, and after effective representation and detailed submissions filed on behalf of the Company, all substantive issues confronted by the department have been decided in favour of the Company. No adverse inference has been drawn in respect of the matters relating to unrealized exchange loss, withholding tax on royalty payments, Workers Welfare Fund, recovery of SSGC pipeline construction cost, and allocation of finance cost against FTR income.

Based on our review of the order, the only demand now appearing in the order amounts to **Rs. 27,477,400**, which has arisen due to computation of super tax under section 4C on the FTR component. As you are aware, at the time of filing of the return, the Company had not charged super tax on the FTR income component based on the then-prevailing decision of the Islamabad High Court. However, the said decision has now been overturned by the Federal Constitutional Court, due to which the department has included the FTR component for purposes of super tax computation, resulting in the above demand.

In view of the Federal Constitutional Court’s decision being the prevailing field position from the highest forum, there does not appear to be any further sustainable contest or appeal point available against this demand. Accordingly, no further appeal is recommended on this specific issue.

The practical way forward would be either to discharge the demand through payment or, where any available refund exists, to seek adjustment of the demand against such refund. We will coordinate further with your team for the preferred course of action.

Regards,  
[Your Name]

**Subject: Follow-up on Input Tax Details for Appeal Proceedings**

Dear Sir,

We refer to our earlier email wherein we had explained that the narration provided by you in respect of input tax claimed in the appeal proceedings does not clearly bring out the nature and admissibility of the claim. In particular, we had highlighted that certain input tax appears to relate to building/construction or allied activities, which may create difficulty in view of the recent judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court.

**Subject: Correction of Tax Period in Return Filing**

Hi Nabeel,

Thank you for your email.

We would like to update you that yesterday we met with your concerned Commissioner and apprised him of the entire matter in detail. We explained that, while filing the return, the tax period field is generally system-generated and not editable by the taxpayer. Accordingly, the taxpayer cannot select or amend the tax period at its own discretion. In the present case, while filing the tax year 2025 return, due to an apparent IRIS/system glitch, the tax period was reflected as July to June instead of January to December.

We also discussed the option suggested by your team regarding filing the return again. In our view, this approach should be avoided, as it may result in two return submissions appearing on the system — one for the July to June period and another for the January to December period — which may create further complications.

Further, we do not believe that revision of return is the appropriate route unless IRIS specifically allows amendment of the tax period during the revision process. Generally, revision of return is meant for changes in figures, computations, declarations, etc., whereas the tax period appearing on the top of the IRIS return form is a system-generated field and does not directly form part of the taxpayer’s computation. You may, however, please check whether IRIS is allowing the tax period to be amended through the revision module. If the system allows the same, we may proceed with filing a revision application accordingly. However, if the tax period is not editable under the revision process, then revision would not practically resolve the issue.

In that case, as already suggested earlier, the appropriate course would be to submit a formal letter/application to the concerned tax office requesting correction of the tax period through the backend/IT support of IRIS. We have already shared the draft letter for your review. Please go through the same and provide your go-ahead so that we may proceed with its submission.

For future filings, the tax period will need to be carefully reviewed at the time of return filing to ensure that IRIS reflects the correct January to December period, instead of automatically picking the July to June period.

As regards the refund application, the system appears to be picking the January to December period. However, we have not yet proceeded with actual submission. If you advise, we can attempt to file the refund application for the January to December period and see whether the system accepts it without any issue.

Regards,  
[Your Name]

You are right. The earlier version should not have stated a straight “standard Federal GST @ 18% across provinces” as the clean answer. The more accurate response should distinguish **EV vehicle concession**, **EV charging tariff concession**, and **possible service-tax characterization**.

Revised draft below:

---

**Subject:** RE: Sales Tax on EV sales

Hi Hashim,

Thanks for your email.

We have reviewed the matter. At the outset, the reduced / concessional sales tax treatment available for electric vehicles appears to be specific to the prescribed categories of EVs / hybrid vehicles under the Sales Tax Act, 1990. The said concession should not be applied to EV charging transactions carried out through charging points.

Separately, the Government / NEPRA has introduced a special regulatory framework for EV charging stations. However, this is essentially a concession / rationalization in the electricity tariff applicable to EV charging stations, and not a separate reduced GST rate for onward charging-point sales.

From a tax perspective, where Wafi charges customers for EV charging on a per-kWh / charging-unit basis, the underlying electricity purchased from DISCO / K-Electric would already be subject to applicable electricity tariff, GST and other electricity-bill levies at utility billing stage. Accordingly, the EV vehicle concession should not be applied to such charging transactions.

Further, since NEPRA has characterized the activity of an EV charging station as provision of “charging service”, the invoicing model should also be reviewed from a provincial sales tax on services perspective, particularly where any separate service fee, facilitation fee, access fee, parking fee, subscription fee or margin is separately charged to the customer. In such a case, provincial sales tax exposure may need to be evaluated based on the province in which the service is provided / consumed and the manner in which the invoice is structured.

For immediate site enablement, our recommendation would be to configure the billing description as **EV charging / charging service on per-kWh basis**, and not to apply the reduced GST rate available for EV vehicles. The commercial price may be determined after factoring the applicable electricity tariff, taxes charged by the utility, and Wafi’s margin. We can separately review the proposed invoice / POS format to confirm whether any additional Federal or provincial sales tax reporting is triggered.

Please also note that if the query relates to sale of EV charging equipment / charging hardware, rather than charging units / kWh from charging points, the tax treatment would need to be examined separately with reference to the relevant HS classification and import / local supply status.

Regards,  
Zuhair

---

Basis for the correction: the Eighth Schedule concessions are framed for specified electric / hybrid vehicles, not charging-point sales; NEPRA’s EVCS decision refers to EV charging stations providing “charging service” and being billed by DISCOs under A-2(d) tariff; and the Power Division announcement relates to discounted electricity tariff for EV charging stations, not a GST concession. citeturn165746view0turn293765view0turn727453view3

parts:
Subject: RE: Sales Tax on EV sales

Hi Hashim,

Thanks for your email.

Based on our review, the concessional / reduced sales tax treatment available under the law appears to be specific to certain categories of electric vehicles and hybrid electric vehicles, subject to the conditions prescribed under the Eighth Schedule to the Sales Tax Act, 1990. It does not appear to extend to sale of electricity / charging units through EV charging points.

Accordingly, where Wafi is charging customers for EV charging units at its sites, the safer position would be to treat the same as a taxable supply subject to standard Federal sales tax at 18%, unless any specific exemption or reduced-rate notification is separately issued for EV charging points. Since this is essentially linked with supply of electricity / charging units, the treatment should remain uniform across provinces for Federal sales tax purposes, rather than being subject to different provincial rates.

Having said that, the commercial model should be carefully reviewed from an invoicing perspective. If the customer is charged only for charging units / electricity consumption, Federal sales tax treatment should apply. However, if any separate amount is charged for parking, access, facilitation, subscription, service fee, or site support, provincial sales tax on services exposure may need to be evaluated separately depending on the province and the exact description of the charge.

In view of the above, Midhat’s understanding is broadly correct that the EV vehicle concession does not automatically apply to sales from charging points. For site enablement purposes, we would recommend configuring the billing / invoicing model on the basis of standard Federal sales tax at 18%, while keeping the description aligned with sale of EV charging units / electricity consumption and avoiding unnecessary segregation of any separate service component unless commercially required.

This position may, however, be revisited if any specific notification or amendment is introduced for EV charging infrastructure / charging point sales in the upcoming budget or through a subsequent SRO.

Regards,  
Zuhair

For reference: the standard Federal sales tax rate under section 3 is 18%, while the reduced EV entries in the Eighth Schedule are framed for specified electric / hybrid vehicles, not EV charging point sales. citeturn228183view0 citeturn233315view0

Subject: Rectification of Demand for Tax Year 2024

Dear Sir,

Thank you for your email.

The difference appearing for Tax Year 2024, resulting in the creation of demand, is due to the following errors in the order:

Firstly, while computing super tax in the return, there was an error in the calculation. The impact of WWF was not deducted while computing super tax, and the super tax was applied on total income instead of taxable income. This needs to be corrected.

Secondly, the capital gain of PKR 10 million has been accounted for twice in the order. The said capital gain was already included in our computation; however, the officer has again applied tax on the gross capital gain separately, which has resulted in an incorrect addition.

Thirdly, the CPR/payment shared by you has not been given credit in the order.

Accordingly, these three errors have resulted in the incorrect demand for Tax Year 2024. We are preparing the rectification application and will share it with you shortly. Once these errors are rectified, the demand should be eliminated and the excess amount should become refundable.

Regards,  
[Your Name]

**Subject:** Difference in Tax Year 2022 Computation

Hi Haasan,

Thanks for your email.

With respect to the difference appearing for tax year 2022, the main reason appears to be the treatment of the professional debt amount. In our computation, an amount of PKR 100 million was reflected under the exempt portion, since part of the relevant period pertained to the exempt period.

However, while computing super tax, the department has taken this amount into account. It is important to note that this specific treatment was neither confronted in the notice nor otherwise discussed during the proceedings. Accordingly, there appears to be a clear basis to seek rectification of the computation to this extent.

Having said that, this particular issue may not be fully resolved through rectification alone, and an appeal may also be required to safeguard the Company’s position on this point. We will therefore evaluate both available avenues, i.e. rectification as well as appeal, and proceed accordingly.

We are currently preparing the rectification application and will share the same with you shortly for your review and onward action.

Regards,  
Zuhair

**Draft Rectification Application under Section 221 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**  
**Tax Year 2024 — Engro Elengy Terminal (Private) Limited**

---

**The Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue / Commissioner Inland Revenue**  
[Jurisdiction]  
Large Taxpayers Office  
[City]

**Subject: Application for Rectification under Section 221 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 against Order passed under Section 122(5A) for Tax Year 2024**

Dear Sir,

We, on behalf of **M/s Engro Elengy Terminal (Private) Limited** “the Company”, refer to the assessment/amended assessment order passed under section **122(5A)** of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 for **Tax Year 2024**, whereby certain computational errors apparent from the record have resulted in creation of an incorrect tax demand.

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the errors highlighted below are purely computational / arithmetical in nature and are duly verifiable from the return, computation, payment challans and other documents already available on record. Accordingly, the same are squarely rectifiable under section **221** of the Ordinance.

### 1. Double taxation of capital gain already included in returned income

While processing the amended assessment, an error has occurred whereby the capital gain has effectively been taxed twice.

In this regard, it is submitted that the Company had already included capital gain of **Rs. 264 million** in the relevant return / computation of income. However, while passing the impugned order, the same amount has again been taken into account separately, resulting in duplication of income and consequential excess tax demand.

Further, a capital gain amounting to **Rs. 10 million**, which was already incorporated in the return and formed part of the taxable income / computation submitted by the Company, has also been considered again while computing the tax liability, including the super tax impact. This has resulted in double taxation of the same income, which is an error apparent from the record and requires rectification.

It is respectfully submitted that once the capital gain has already been made part of the returned income, the same cannot again be independently added / taxed in the amended assessment. The duplication may kindly be deleted and the tax liability may be recomputed accordingly.

### 2. Non-consideration of super tax already paid

It is further submitted that the Company has already discharged its super tax liability for Tax Year 2024. However, while passing the impugned order, the payment already made by the Company has not been properly accounted for / adjusted, resulting in an incorrect outstanding demand.

The relevant payment details are as under:

| Particulars | Amount |
|---|---:|
| Super tax paid for Tax Year 2024 | Rs. 26 million |
| CPR / PSID No. | [●] |
| Date of payment | [●] |

The above payment is duly verifiable from the CPR and the tax payment record available with the Department. Therefore, the tax demand may kindly be rectified after allowing credit of the aforesaid payment.

### 3. Incorrect computation of super tax due to use of total income instead of correct taxable income after allowable deduction

It is also submitted that while filing the return, an inadvertent computational error occurred in the super tax working, whereby the deductible allowance / WWF adjustment was not reduced while computing the base for super tax. Consequently, the figure of total income was used instead of the correct taxable income after admissible deduction / adjustment.

Since this computational error has also been carried into the impugned order, the super tax liability has been overstated. The correct computation requires that the admissible deduction / adjustment be reduced from the relevant income base before applying super tax.

Accordingly, the super tax computation may kindly be rectified by considering the correct taxable income base, after allowing the relevant deduction / adjustment, instead of applying super tax on the gross / total income figure.

### Prayer

In view of the above, it is respectfully requested that the impugned order passed under section **122(5A)** for Tax Year 2024 may kindly be rectified under section **221** of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 by:

1. deleting the duplication of capital gain already included in the return / computation of income;  
2. allowing proper credit / adjustment of super tax payment of **Rs. 26 million** already made by the Company;  
3. recomputing super tax on the correct income base after allowing the relevant deductible adjustment; and  
4. revising the demand accordingly.

The Company reserves the right to submit further explanations, reconciliations, CPRs and supporting documents as may be required by your good office.

Thank you.

Yours faithfully,  
For and on behalf of  
**Engro Elengy Terminal (Private) Limited**

Authorized Representative  
[Name]  
[Designation]  
[Date]

**Subject: Application for Rectification under Section 221 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 against Order passed under Section 122(5A) for Tax Year 2024**

Dear Sir,

We, on behalf of our above-mentioned client, respectfully refer to the amended assessment order passed under section 122(5A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 for Tax Year 2024, whereby certain apparent computational errors have resulted in an excessive and incorrect tax demand against our client.

At the outset, it is submitted that the errors highlighted in the ensuing paragraphs are apparent from the record and are verifiable from the return of income, computation of tax, super tax working and CPRs / payment record already available with the Department. Accordingly, the same warrant rectification under section 221 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

### Double inclusion of capital gain while computing super tax liability

It is respectfully submitted that while passing the impugned order, an apparent computational error has occurred in respect of capital gain considered for the purpose of super tax. The total capital gain for the year amounted to approximately Rs. 267 million. Out of the said amount, capital gain of Rs. 10 million had already been duly incorporated by our client in the return / computation while determining the super tax liability.

However, in the impugned order, gross capital gain of Rs. 264 million has again been considered separately for the purpose of computing super tax, without appreciating the fact that Rs. 10 million had already been included in the returned computation. Consequently, the said amount of Rs. 10 million has effectively been considered twice, once in the return / computation already filed by our client and again through separate consideration of gross capital gain in the impugned order.

This has resulted in overstatement of super tax liability due to double inclusion of the same income. Since the error is purely computational and apparent from the record, it is respectfully requested that the super tax computation may kindly be rectified by excluding the duplicate impact of Rs. 10 million already included in the return / computation.

### Non-adjustment of super tax payment already made

It is further submitted that our client had already discharged super tax liability amounting to Rs. 26 million for Tax Year 2024. However, while passing the impugned order, the said payment has not been duly accounted for / adjusted against the demand created, resulting in an incorrect outstanding liability.

The payment of Rs. 26 million is duly supported by the relevant CPR / PSID bearing No. [●] dated [●], and the same is verifiable from the tax payment record available with the Department. Therefore, the demand created through the impugned order may kindly be rectified after allowing proper credit of the aforesaid super tax payment already made by our client.

### Incorrect continuation of error relating to deductible allowance / WWF adjustment

It is also submitted that at the time of filing the return, while computing super tax liability, an inadvertent computational error occurred whereby the deductible allowance / WWF adjustment was not properly taken into account. As a result, the super tax was computed on a higher income base instead of the correct figure after accounting for the admissible deduction / adjustment.

The same computational error has now continued in the impugned order, resulting in further overstatement of super tax liability. Since the correct income base for super tax purposes ought to be determined after considering the relevant deductible allowance / WWF adjustment, it is respectfully requested that the computation may kindly be revised accordingly and the excess demand arising on this account may be deleted.

### Prayer

In view of the above submissions, it is respectfully requested that the impugned order passed under section 122(5A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 for Tax Year 2024 may kindly be rectified under section 221 of the Ordinance by removing the duplicate impact of capital gain already incorporated in the return / computation, allowing credit of super tax payment of Rs. 26 million already made by our client, and revising the super tax computation after considering the relevant deductible allowance / WWF adjustment.

The aforesaid rectification will correctly reflect the tax liability of our client and remove the excessive demand created due to the apparent computational errors highlighted above. Our client reserves the right to submit any further reconciliation, working, CPR or supporting document as may be required by your good office in this regard.

Yours faithfully,  
For and on behalf of  
**[Name of Client]**

## **Post 1: Faceless Tax System — Less Harassment or More Data-Based Scrutiny?**

Pakistan is moving towards a **centralized and faceless tax model**, where audits and assessments may no longer be handled by local field officers. Instead, separate digital wings in Islamabad will conduct risk-based audits, issue assessment orders, and manage taxpayer cases through an online system.

The objective is clear: reduce direct interaction between taxpayers and tax officers, limit discretion, curb harassment, and improve transparency. The proposed model will use banking data, property records, vehicle ownership details, withholding data, and other information to identify under-reporting and concealed income.

For genuine taxpayers, this may reduce unnecessary physical visits and officer-dependent compliance. However, for non-compliant persons, especially those showing low or nil income despite large bank balances or asset transactions, the system may create serious exposure. The future of tax compliance is becoming more data-driven, and taxpayers should ensure that their returns properly match their actual financial profile.

---

## **Post 2: 18% Sales Tax on Stationery — Education May Become More Expensive**

A major budget proposal reportedly cleared for Finance Bill 2026 is the increase in sales tax on stationery items from **10% to 18%**, effective from July 1, 2026.

This change may directly affect students, parents, schools, offices, bookshops, and small retailers. Items such as notebooks, registers, paper products, pens, and other stationery essentials may become more expensive if the higher tax is passed on to consumers.

At a time when education costs are already rising, taxing basic learning materials at the standard sales tax rate raises an important policy question: should essential educational supplies be treated like ordinary commercial goods, or should they receive special relief to support students and families?

---

## **Post 3: Budget 2026-27 — Industry Wants Relief, FBR Wants Documentation**

Business associations have strongly pushed for relief in the upcoming budget, including reduction in GST rates, restoration of final tax regime for exporters, faster refund processing, lower withholding tax, and relief from excessive audit and enforcement actions.

At the same time, the government is moving towards stricter documentation through AI-based monitoring, faceless audits, data integration, and stronger enforcement against sectors such as tobacco, real estate, banking transactions, and under-reported income.

This budget may therefore become a balancing exercise: businesses want liquidity, lower tax rates, and simpler compliance, while the government wants higher collection, less evasion, and a broader tax base. The real test will be whether Budget 2026-27 brings genuine simplification or merely adds another layer of digital enforcement.
